en: Now begins the third chapter:
I worship that Leader of Sītā, whom those endowed with dispassion, who discern the meaning of "That" and "Thou," and who are self-controlled, attain through spiritual means. (1)
START BsRp_3,1.1.1:
At the time of entering that [other body], he goes forth enveloped, according to the question and its explanation.
BBs_3,1.1: At the time of entering that [other body], he goes forth enveloped, according to the question and its explanation.
Having restated what has been discussed, he states the subject matter of the third chapter with the words "In the second," and so forth.

There is a relationship of cause and effect between these two [chapters]: when the meaning of the Vedānta texts is established as non-contradictory, there arises the occasion for an inquiry into the means of attaining knowledge thereof.

Furthermore, once the subtle body (*liṅga*) and its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are established, there follows an inquiry into the transmigratory state of the individual soul (*jīva*) as conditioned by them; thus, there is a logical connection between the sections (*pādas*) as well.
In this [work], detachment is treated in the first chapter;
in the second, the referent of the term "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha) and the reality of Brahman are explained through the description of states such as dreaming;
in the third, the meaning of the Great Sentence (vākyārtha) and the meditations (upāsanā) for that purpose are investigated.
He states the meaning of the fourth quarter [of the verse] with the words "from right vision" (*samyagdarśanāt*).
The means of vision are renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and so forth.
Regarding the fruit, which is liberation, there is an absence of any rule of gradation as there is with heaven; that is to say, it is of a single uniform nature.
The refutation of the body as the self has arisen incidentally.
The meditation on the five—namely, the sky, rain, earth, man, and woman—as being fires constitutes the Pañcāgni-vidyā (the Knowledge of the Five Fires).

Since there is misfortune consisting of coming and going by means of *karma*, it is taught for the purpose of detachment (*vairāgya*), because we hear in the conclusion of the Pañcāgni-vidyā that one should cultivate "disgust," "aversion," and "detachment" toward the fruit of action.
This is the logical connection (*anvaya*).
In the first aphorism of the *Śāstra*, dispassion (*vairāgya*) produced by the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal was described;
here, for the sake of strengthening that, dispassion produced by the contemplation of the afflictions of going and returning is described, and thus there is no tautology.
He states the subject matter of the discussion: "the individual soul" (jīva).
"Ignorance" (avidyā) is well-known;
if the reading is "knowledge" (vidyā), then meditative worship (upāsanā) is to be understood.
Karma is that which is termed dharma and adharma;
prior wisdom (pūrvaprajñā) refers to the latent impressions (saṃskāra) from previous births.
Now, at the time of death, the vital breaths (prāṇas) become unified with the individual soul (jīva) in the heart; this is the meaning.
"Form" (rūpa) refers to the body; "subtle elements" (bhūtasūkṣma) refers to the portions of the fivefold-composed elements that undergo transformation into the subsequent body.
This is because all the topical sections (adhikaraṇa) constitute an inquiry into the means for attaining knowledge of the meaning of the Vedānta.
The connections with the scriptures and the study of the treatises are as follows: because this [section] has dispassion (*vairāgya*) as its fruit, it is connected to this chapter (*pāda*).

In the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) was stated for the sake of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); here, that very transaction is being investigated. Thus, the relationship between the means and the end (*phala-phalibhāva*) constitutes the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*). Here, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [it is argued that] there can be no movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) without a substratum.
There is no detachment;
in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), detachment consists in the departure of the vital breath from its support in the elements—this is the difference in result.
The "measures of light" (*tejomātrā*) are the eyes and other sense organs.

The ellipsis [of the sentence] is "he sees" and "he smells. King Pravāhaṇa’s question to Śvetaketu is: "Do you know how water, when offered in the five fires and offered as the fifth oblation, becomes designated by the word 'person' (puruṣa) and transforms into the nature of a person?"
And when he did not understand the answer to that, the King said to his father: "In that world, O Gautama, this is indeed the fire; there, the water called faith is the oblation.
In this world, at the Agnihotra sacrifice, the waters in the form of curd and other substances, offered with faith, become connected to the sacrificer;
having reached the heavenly world, they abide in the form of a divine body known as Soma, and at the conclusion of the ritual, they flow forth."

It has been established that "the waters are offered into the rain-cloud; from there, taking the form of rain, they become food on the earth; in the person, they take the form of semen; and when offered into the woman, those waters—denoted by the word 'person' (puruṣa)—become male in nature.
Now, one might object: "Is it not improper to say that after leaving this body and traveling with the waters, one subsequently attains another body?"

He raises an objection based on a contradiction with scripture: "But [it is] otherwise," meaning that just as a caterpillar, having grasped another blade of grass, leaves the previous blade, so too the individual soul (jīva), having grasped another body, leaves the previous body.

He resolves this by stating: "Even there," meaning that the meaning of the scripture is that even here [in this life], one grasps the future body dependent upon karma through such contemplations as "I am a god" and so forth, and thereby leaves the previous body;
thus, there is no contradiction.
The "prolongation" (*dīrghībhāva*) of meditation refers to its having the future body as its object.

The individual soul (*jīva*), conditioned like the space within a jar, goes to another world by means of its subtle adjuncts; this is the method taught in the *Pañcāgni-śruti*. Because other theories contradict this, they are all to be disregarded—this is the logical connection.
He states the Sāṅkhya theory with the words: "Of those that are all-pervading," etc.
He states the Sugata’s (Buddhist) conception with the words "of the pure [self]," meaning that the self,

which consists of a continuum of non-conceptual knowledge, acquires a function called conceptual cognition of sound and so forth in another body. He states the Kaṇāda’s (Vaiśeṣika) conception with the word "mind."
Only the mind goes toward another body, while the sense organs are newly produced; this describes the Digambara conception—that the soul [is what transmigrates]. //1//
But [the distinction is made] because of the threefold nature [of the elements] and because of their predominance. (BBs 3.1.2)

[Objection: Is it not improper to say that the body consists of three elements because the three effects of cooking (pāka), moisture (sveda), and odor-color (gandharūpa) are perceived? For the body actually consists of five elements due to the perception of both vital air (prāṇa) and space (avakāśa). Anticipating this dissatisfaction, he provides another explanation with the words "furthermore" (punar ca). The grammatical connection is as follows: because they sustain the body, they are called *dhātus*; since there are three such *dhātus*, the body is said to consist of three elements (*tryātmaka*).
The sense is that if the body consisted solely of water, then *vāta* (wind) and *pitta* (bile), which are respectively of the nature of air (*vāyavya*) and fire (*taijasa*), would not exist.
Water is predominant when compared to the other elements.
Furthermore, because the actions (*karman*) that cause the body are predominantly aqueous, the other elements are indicated by them; thus he says, "And action," and so forth. //2//
And because of the departure of the vital breaths. (BS 3.1.3)

He states [the reason] as "and because of the departure of the vital breath" (prāṇagateś ca) //3//: at the time of departure, the vital breaths have as their substratum the five elements which are the seeds of the body, because they are vital breaths, just like the vital breath residing in a living body.
If it be argued that [the soul does not go to Brahman] because of scriptural statements regarding its going to Agni and others, we say no, because those statements are figurative. (BS 3.1.4)

Anticipating the objection that the destination of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) is unestablished, he refutes it with the words "agnyādi" (fire, etc.). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "because [the movement] of the herbs and trees is not observed.
The meaning is that they enter even the body hairs.

The meaning is that if the dissolution of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) into fire and the other elements were taken in its primary sense, it would be impossible for the individual soul (*jīva*) to undergo departure and experience [in another world]; therefore, because of the clear scriptural statement that "all the vital breaths depart after [the soul]" and because of the mention of a figurative dissolution in things such as the body hairs, [the dissolution of the breaths] is to be understood in a secondary sense.
"If it is argued that [the waters] are not mentioned in the first [case], we say no; for they are indeed [mentioned] because of the logical possibility.

Having explained the movement of the waters when conjoined with other elements, and having raised an objection regarding their being designated as "man" (*puruṣavacastva*), the author provides a resolution starting with the words "In the first. One might object: "But the word 'first' is redundant, since the waters are not mentioned even in the subsequent fires. Anticipating this, he replies that because soma, rain, food, and semen are of the nature of water, there is indeed mention of those waters later on.

He says "not the first" with the words "if indeed... The meaning of the objection is this: even if it were established that water is the oblation in the five fires, its state of being called "man" would occur at the fifth oblation; however, that is not established because water is not an oblation in the first fire. This is so provided that water is understood by the word "faith" (*śraddhā*).
Because the questions, answers, and conclusions are connected and possess a single meaning, they are established as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*).
However, if this were not grasped, since water is the oblation in all four fires, one would have to say "in the fourth oblation";
therefore, because both the question and the conclusion state "in the fifth," [the two must refer to the same thing].
The purpose of the resolution is that even in the first fire, only water is to be taken;
"anapaḥ" means other than water;
"etadeva" means this very thing.
The meaning is that he demonstrates that the word *śraddhā* (faith) has the sense of "water.
He states another meaning for the term *upapatteḥ* (because it is logical): "the effect of faith" (*śraddhākāryam*).
By the passage beginning with "from that oblation of faith, soma is produced," [the author] shows that faith, soma, and the others are successive transformations of one another.

The meaning is that, because faith undergoes transformation into fluidity (*drava-pariṇāma*), it possesses the nature of water; furthermore, since faith consisting of conviction (*pratyayātmaka*) cannot logically be the oblation, [faith] is identified with water.

Having explained the secondary application (*vṛtti*) of the word "faith" to water by way of the quality of subtlety, he states the connection—either as a cause or as sharing a single ritual action—with water in order to explain its figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*): "preceded by faith" (*śraddhā-pūrvaka*) for this sacrificer (*asmai yajamānāya*).
The meaning of the Vedic text is that the waters bow down with faith, generating [the power] for the sake of bathing and other such acts. //5//
If it be argued that [the ascent] does not occur because it is not mentioned in scripture, we say no; for those who perform sacrifices and other rites are known [to ascend].
Having established the movement of water, he now explains the movement of living beings along with that water by means of the passage beginning with "Now moreover" (athāpi).

Having stated that King Soma arises from the oblation of faith in the fire of the heavenly world, the remainder of the passage describes those who perform sacrifices and other rites as reaching the moon from the ether via the path of smoke and so forth, identifying them as "this King Soma.

Therefore, the meaning is that because of this commonality of the term "King Soma," the movement of the living beings of those who perform sacrifices and other rites, together with the waters denoted by the word "faith," is understood here in the statement regarding the oblation of faith.

Explaining their connection with the waters that have been quintuplicated (pañcīkṛta), which consist of subtle substances and prior forms, he clarifies their co-migration with the words: "And of them, at the Agnihotra...
Death is *nidhana*; the performance of the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) occasioned by it; and "this one" refers to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
The meaning of the mantra is: "May it go to heaven.
To show that water, in the form of the substance offered in the oblation, indeed goes [to heaven], he cites another scriptural passage with the words "And likewise" (*tathā ca*).
In the section on the Agnihotra, Janaka said to Yājñavalkya: "But surely you have not [observed] the departure of these two evening and morning oblations..."

"You do not know the destination, nor the resting place, nor the satisfaction, nor the return, nor the world that rises up to meet them"—these are the six questions posed; and their explanation was given by the king himself:
"When these two oblations are offered, they rise up; they go to heaven through the gateway of the intermediate space; they take heaven itself as their resting place; they satisfy heaven."

Then they return again; then, when [the oblation] has been offered into the earth, into the man, and into the woman, they arise in the form of a man—thus it is established by the remainder of the passage. //6//
Or rather, [the designation "Self"] is figurative because of the lack of knowledge of the Self; for thus the scripture shows. (BS 3.1.7)
Now, he raises an objection that is to be refuted by the subsequent sūtra with the words "How? and so forth.

Here, in order to dispel the misconception that the moon named Soma is the food [of the gods] rather than the performers of sacrifices such as the *iṣṭāpūrta*, he cites another scriptural passage: "They [make him] the moon.

Just as in a sacrifice, the officiating priests repeatedly cause the Soma in the cup to swell, saying "Swell! (using the imperative for repeated action), and having repeatedly caused it to swell and repeatedly diminished it, they consume it.

The meaning is that in this way the gods consume those who perform undesirable acts (aniṣṭādikārin) by making them into the form of food. "Adhikāra" means that a person is qualified [for action] or connected with an injunction; it refers to the desire for a result.
The intention is that the status of being food is figurative, in order to avoid rendering the scripture purposeless.

To the question, "By what defect do they become objects of enjoyment for the gods? he says: "And because of being non-knowers of the Self" (*anātmavitvāt*). The meaning is that just as an animal is an object of enjoyment, so too the ignorant person who possesses the notion of duality is an object of enjoyment for the gods. Having explained a portion of the Sūtra by relying on the primary sense of the word *ātman*, he offers another interpretation—namely, that the five fires under discussion are metaphorically designated as the "Self" by the author of the Sūtra—beginning with the words "non-Self," etc.
He explains the remainder of the Sūtra—"for thus [it is said]"—to show that being food is not primary for the purpose of praising knowledge;
in this way, it is established that dispassion arises from reflecting upon the course of transmigration. //7//
Upon the exhaustion of [the results of] what has been performed, one who possesses residual karma (anuśaya) returns by the same way and not by that way, as is seen from both scripture and tradition.
Now he examines the return that occurs after the other state of existence, beginning with the words "kṛtātyaye" (when the performed [deeds] have passed away).
The meaning of the word "atha" (then) is immediate succession following the completion of the karma to be experienced.
The construction is as follows: the scriptural passage beginning with "yathetam" (as they went) and ending with "śvādiyoniṃ" (the womb of dogs, etc. is handed down [in the text].

Regarding this, he states a doubt based on the qualification "as far as the completion [of their experience]" and the statement "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*). In that context, *anuśaya* refers to karma;

here, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since there is an absence of karma, there is no restriction regarding the descent [from heaven], and thus there is a firmness of dispassion (*vairāgya*).

The distinction [between the two views] is that, according to the Siddhānta, because the restriction of the path of return is established by the continued existence of karma, there is a firmness of detachment (*vairāgya*). The meaning is that another scriptural passage also states that the entire karma of those performers of sacrifices and other rites is exhausted in the world of the moon: "When that karma of theirs comes to an end—that is, when it is completely worn away—then they return. Thus, it is declared that all karma is experienced in the lunar realm.
He says "not so" because a restriction of the words is not appropriate, as it would contradict other scriptural passages (*śruti*).
The meaning of the scripture is this: whatever action this person performs here in this world, having obtained its final fruit in the next world, he returns again for the sake of action.
Having stated the scriptural authority regarding the absence of action, he states the logical argument with the words "furthermore" (*api ca*).
"Manifestation" (*abhivyakti*) means being oriented toward its fruit;
since all karma manifested by death necessarily results in experience in the next world, the meaning is that there is an absence of [remaining] karma.
When it might be concluded that descent occurs from mere conduct (*cāritra*), he explains the thesis of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words beginning "by which" (*yena*).

Among those living beings descending there, those who in this land of action (karmabhūmi) have performed pleasant deeds, whose actions were meritorious, and who possess a meritorious womb—it is "near" (*abhyāśaḥ*) to them, meaning it is certain; whereas for those of foul conduct, it is "evil" (*kapūyam*), meaning sinful.
Having explained the literal Vedic sense of the word *dṛṣṭa*, he states another meaning: "And it is seen."

From such scriptural passages as, "One becomes virtuous through virtuous action and sinful through sinful action," it is understood that pleasure and pain have merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) as their causes.

Consequently, the existence of residual karma (*anuśaya*) is established by the following inference: the enjoyment experienced from birth onwards is caused by karma, because it is an enjoyment, just like the enjoyment of heaven.

The meaning is that, in the absence of a cause for the opposite case, there would follow the consequence of experience being accidental. The connection [of the words] is as follows: "Those who have dwelt in the stages of life," that is, those belonging to the stages of life (*āśramiṇaḥ*), having died—that is, having passed away—after experiencing the fruit of their actions in another world, then, by means of the remainder—that is, by other action distinct from what was experienced and called *anuśaya* (latent tendency)—they undergo rebirth.
Those [places] in which there are ten qualities beginning with excellence of location and ending with intelligence are described as such;
"learning" (śruta) means knowledge,
and "conduct" (vṛtta) means behavior.

He asks—"But who [is it]?"—in order to state his own preferred view regarding the latent disposition (*anuśaya*). He presents the explanation of a certain partial school (*ekadeśin*) with the words "some say" (*kecit*), etc., stating that when there is enjoyment in heaven of the karma already performed, the residue (*leśa*) of that karma which has been enjoyed is the latent disposition; one descends while possessing that, because a trace of oil is observed in a vessel, and because of the Smṛti statement, "Then by what remains."
"Being emptied" means being deprived of its oily essence (*sneha*).
He raises an objection with "nanu": "Is it not the case that a residue of karma is not logical, since karma is destroyed by experience? [The response is:
When the experience of all karma has occurred, destruction would take place.
The meaning of the rebuttal is that experience has not arisen.
He raises an objection, saying "But surely," on the grounds that it is incorrect to say that experience does not arise.
He provides the resolution, beginning with "Certainly," etc., by stating that experience has arisen with a remainder.
He refutes this explanation of the "partialist" (ekadeśin) with the words "And not...

The meaning is that by such scriptural injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," action is enjoined for the purpose of experiencing heaven; therefore, if the remainder of that [action] were to be the cause of mortal experience, there would be a contradiction with scripture.

Furthermore, he states "And necessarily... to show that there would be a contradiction with the scriptural teaching regarding the attainment of a foul womb during descent from heaven due to the remainder of karma that causes rebirth in heaven.
He states his own intended view of residual karma (anuśaya) with "Therefore...
and refutes the seed of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) with the words beginning "That which... and so forth.
The construction is as follows: it is understood from the statement "having exhausted [the results], they return again" that [only] what has reached its end [is meant].

This is because there is a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning "pleasant and foul conduct," which—beginning from birth—are supported by the signs of experienced enjoyments and are intent upon qualifying specific residual actions (*anuśaya*) pertaining to this world;

therefore, the intention is that the contraction of the general terms *yat kiñcit* ("whatever") and *yāvat-sampātam* ("as far as the completion") to refer specifically to matters pertaining to the next world is logical.

He says "that too" [in the verse], meaning that it is incorrect to claim that death manifests all karma, because that would contradict the scriptural passages concerning the latent dispositions (anuśaya) already mentioned.

And because there is an obstruction by powerful karma that has already begun its fruition (*ārabdhakarma*), there is no manifestation of all karma; this he states with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth.
The sense is that there is no cause for that [destruction] to be the manifestor of all karma.
Anticipating the question, he offers a response with the words "That which has begun" (*ārabdha*).

He provides the resolution with the words "Just as... (*yathā*): because even a weak [action] can act as a powerful obstructer of that which has already begun, there is no manifestation for the sake of yielding the fruit of every action.

Having raised the objection that all actions might manifest because they are equally unmanifested in their results, he explains that it is impossible for mutually contradictory fruits—such as bodies leading to heaven or hell—to originate from a single body; this is stated in the words "For not... (*na hi*). Then, [the opponent] suggests:
"In that case, let there be the destruction of the weak action," to which [the author] replies: "Nor also... (*nāpi*).

"The statement that 'unexperienced karma does not perish' is an absolute general rule (*utsarga*), and it is set aside by expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), the knowledge of Brahman, and meditation—not merely by death; this is the meaning.
He states that "Smṛti" is the authority for the fact that weak karma is not destroyed by death.

Having rejected the position that karma is destroyed [by death], he points out another defect in the position that all previously performed karma is manifested [at death], saying "And if..."* *Note: The ellipsis refers to the subsequent argument in the source text regarding the impossibility of simultaneous manifestation of all karmas.*
The meaning is this: since all karma would be exhausted through experience within a single birth as a god or other being, there would be no further birth;

yet, due to the absence of knowledge, there would be no liberation. Thus, the ignorant deity would be in a miserable intermediate state. [As it is said: "Of dogs, pigs, donkeys, and camels; of cows, goats, sheep, deer, and birds..."

Furthermore, because it contradicts such Smṛti texts as, "The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of Caṇḍālas and Pulkasas," [the author] states "Brahma" [in the verse], meaning that not all karmas initiate a single birth.
Now, one might ask: how can a single action have multiple births as its fruit?
He says "not so" because it has not been observed.
Furthermore, even if death were a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), would it be postulated as the manifestor of all karma, or as the manifestor of only some karma?

It cannot be the first, because in this world, the results of actions such as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice—which are causes for results to be experienced right here—could not possibly be manifested by death; thus he says "not so."
Refuting the second [position], he dismantles the example stated by the opponent with the words "pradīpa" (lamp) and so forth.

The meaning is that, like lamps [revealing] forms, death is not the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) of any karma whatsoever; rather, when there is an absence of obstruction by a powerful karma, a weak [karma] is manifested.

Thus, by not accepting that death is a manifestor [of karma], the analogy of the lamp has been refuted; yet, even if it were accepted, he states that it is an unfavorable analogy with the words "sthūla" (gross), etc.
The remainder of the sense is: since the subtle [karma] is unmanifested in form, the manifestation of all karma at the time of death is not established.

Thus, he concludes the refutation of the view that the entire collection of karma (*karmasaṅgha*) initiates a single birth—that is, that *karmāśaya* is "belonging to one existence" (*aikabhavika*)—with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

The meaning is that [the existence of unmanifested karma persists] due to the scriptural statement regarding conduct (*caraṇa*), the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) beginning with "Then by the remainder," and the logical principle (*nyāya*) of "obstruction by a stronger [force].
[Objection: But since liberation would otherwise be impossible, one must accept that [karma] belongs to a single existence; to this, he replies: "By the remainder" (*śeṣa*).
He explains the remainder of the Sūtra with the words beginning "And those," etc.
The path of descent is heard thus: "Having dwelt there until the exhaustion of their merits, they then return again by this very same path as they came—to space;
from space, to air; having become air, he becomes smoke; having become smoke, he becomes mist; having become mist, he becomes a cloud."
Having come into being, it rains; from that, rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans are produced here.
Indeed, it is more difficult for one to emerge from this state—whosoever eats food and whosoever sheds semen, he becomes that very thing again.
Thus, those whose conduct here has been pleasant attain a pleasant womb.

Having stated that they return by this path "as they went" and "as they came"—meaning they return by the same path starting from smoke—it was thought that the night and so forth situated on the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) characterized by smoke, etc., had not been mentioned, while additional elements such as the clouds had been mentioned; therefore, the author of the Sūtras said, "as they went and not so.
The meaning of the remaining portion of the Śruti will become clear later. //8//
If it be argued that [the term "conduct"] refers to the Vedic school (caraṇa), Kārṣṇājini says: no, for it is intended as an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa).

Now, the author of the Sūtras explains the word *caraṇa* as it occurs in the Śruti by way of an objection: "If it be said, on account of conduct (*caraṇāt*). In the Smṛti it is stated: "Non-malice toward all beings in action, thought, and speech;

kindness and knowledge—this the wise know to be *śīla* (conduct). Thus, non-malice and the rest, which consist of knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures, are declared to be *śīla*, an auxiliary to all ritual acts. The word *caraṇa* indicates that [conduct] which is an auxiliary to the principal [act].

The view of Kārṣṇājini is that [the term ‘karman’] indicates rites such as those prescribed in the Śruti; since the subsequent state of the action itself is what is called *dharma* and *adharma*, known as the *apūrva*, the existence of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) known as the *apūrva*—which are non-different from that [action]—is established through the indication of the action itself. //9//
If it is argued that [the injunction] is purposeless, we say no, because it depends upon that. 3.1.10.
He states that very point through the resolution of a doubt by means of the Sūtra beginning with "If it be argued that [the injunctions] would be purposeless," and so forth.

Having raised the objection that since the literal meaning denoted by the word *caraṇa* (conduct) itself can be grasped, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not appropriate, he says: "But surely...
Prohibited conduct consists of anger, falsehood, and the like.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for ethical conduct (*śīla*) to be fruitless, he states "and necessarily" (*avaśyaṃ ca*) to show that its fruit is the attainment of the source of learning (*śrutayoni*), and not the latent disposition (*anuśaya*).

According to the *Smṛti*, the Vedas, their meanings, and ritual acts do not bear fruit without proper conduct; thus, because ethical conduct is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to ritual action, there is no expectation of a separate fruit, as it is rendered purposeful by the fruit of the principal act (*aṅgin*).
Nor should it be said that the result is merely the attainment of birth in another womb;

for since a subsidiary element cannot have a fruit of its own, it is impossible to accept the primary meaning of "conduct" (ācāra), and thus figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is appropriate—this is the sense of the resolution.

Furthermore, he states, "even if it serves the purpose of man," meaning that even if conduct, like bathing and other rites, is for the sake of the person as a human refinement (puruṣasaṃskāra), there is still no contradiction.
The meaning is that, like the meditations connected with the limbs [of the sacrifice], conduct (ācāra) is purposeful.

Anticipating the objection that "rebirth may then result from conduct alone, known as moral discipline (śīla)," he says "and action" (karma ca), because such a view would contradict scriptural texts such as, "Verily, by a meritorious deed one becomes meritorious. "Pārayamāṇaḥ" means capable. //10//
"But Bādari [says] that it is indeed good and evil deeds," (BS 3.1.11).

Although virtue (*śīla*)—consisting of non-anger and so forth—is of the nature of common attributes and thus not distinct from action (*karman*) in its specific form, nevertheless, the words *caraṇa* and *ācāra* denote only action and do not denote virtue; therefore, there is no occasion for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, he states Bādari’s opinion, which represents the primary established doctrine: "By well-performed [actions]," and so forth.
He concludes the meaning of the word *caraṇa* with the words "conduct (*ācāra*) also.
To the question, "If conduct is indeed action, how can there be a mention of distinctions such as 'according to his actions' (*yathākārī*) and so forth?", he replies: "The designation of distinction.
From the word *ācāra* when used without an accompanying prefix, a specific quality in the form of "good conduct" (*sadācāra*) shines forth.

Therefore, the term "yathākārī" (acting as one acts), which is uttered in conjunction with that [term], denotes the general category of action while intending its specific counterpart; likewise, "faultless actions" is the general statement, whereas "our own well-performed deeds" is the specific instance—this is the distinction.
Consequently, it is established that detachment arises from the realization that one must inevitably return due to the force of residual karma (*anuśaya*). //11//
Moreover,
it is heard in scripture regarding those who perform sacrifices other than the prescribed ones. (BS 3.1.12)

Having thus established detachment by reflecting on the coming and going of those whose nature is meritorious, he now establishes it for sinners by reflecting upon their fate, beginning with the words: "Even for those who perform undesirable acts," etc.

Since there is a doubt arising from the non-specific scriptural statement, "Whoever they may be," and from the scriptural statement, "The son of Vivasvat is the gathering place of men," he explains the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra—beginning with "Therein," etc.—by way of a connection that challenges the rule established in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*).
The meaning of the Vedic text is: "Propitiate Yama, who is rightly the destination of sinful people, with an oblation.

According to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), since there is no restrictive rule that the journey to the moon belongs to the meritorious alone, the result [of this teaching] is the realization of the futility of merit and the strengthening of detachment from sin.

In the established doctrine (siddhānta), even the sight of the world of the moon does not exist for sinners; thus, the fruit [of this teaching] is the meaningfulness of merit and the firmness of dispassion (vairāgya).

Since there is a rule that the commencement of a body occurs in the fifth fire, it must be stated that even sinners reach the first fire, which is the heavenly world (dyuloka); to this he says: "the commencement of a body.
The sense is that although sinners lack the enjoyment of heaven, they still proceed to the moon because there is no other path. //12//
But in the case of Saṃyamana, others experience [the results] after having experienced [them]; there is ascent and descent because their course is seen to be such. (3.1.13)
He explains the sūtra of the established conclusion (*siddhāntasūtra*) with the words beginning "the word *tu*," and so forth.

The construction of the sūtra should be understood as follows: having experienced the torments inflicted by Yama in the world of Yama (the realm of the twins) during their confinement, they descend; thus there are both ascent and descent. [The term] *prayatām* refers to those who have departed after dying.
*Sāṃparāya* refers to the next world (*paraloka*), because it is properly attained thereafter; *sāṃparāyika* refers to the means for attaining that.
It does not shine forth for the fool—the ignorant one—especially for him who is deluded by attachment to wealth and thus practices negligence out of delusion.
And that fool, who is conceited enough to think, "This world of women, wealth, and so forth exists, but the next world does not exist," falls under my power—that is, under the power of Yama.

The sense is that, based on the force of specific Śruti and Smṛti texts stating that sinners fall under Yama's control, the non-specific Śruti passage beginning with "Whosoever they may be" (*ye vai ke ca*) should be interpreted as referring specifically to those who perform sacrifices and other rites. //13//
And they record this in their tradition. (Sūtra 14)
The commentary on these three sūtras is easy to understand. // 14 // // 15 // // 16 //
Moreover, there are seven. (BBs 3.1.15)
And even in that case, there is no contradiction because of its operation upon that [object]. (BBs 3.1.16)
"But [the reference is] to knowledge and action, because they are the subject under discussion. (BS 3.1.17)
As for the claim that even sinners attain the state of the moon because there is no other path, that is not so;
for there is the scriptural mention of a third path, as he says: "Of knowledge and action... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2].
In the Śruti, the word *atha* (now) signifies the commencement of the exposition of the third path immediately after the description of the two paths.

Those persons who are not endowed with either of these two means—knowledge and ritual action—which serve as the instruments for the two paths, become the beings situated on the third path, which consists of the cycle of birth and death;
[this is expressed] in the *loṭ* (imperative) mood to denote a recurring action.
The meaning of the Śruti is that because there is no movement toward the moon for sinners, the world of the moon is not filled.
"In the case of attainment" (pratipattau) means in the case of the means of reaching [the goal].

Furthermore, the logical connection is as follows: if that world were filled by sinners descending from the moon, then the scriptural response, "And therefore it is not filled," would result in a contradiction.

He says, "Not so, because it is not stated [in scripture]," meaning that the non-filling of the world due to descent should not be assumed, as that would entail the abandonment of what is actually heard in scripture.
He then says, "Of the descent," because the descent itself is declared by scripture to be the third place.

The meaning is that the phrase "they return again by this path" is redundant; for since the descent of those who perform sacrifices and other rites (*iṣṭādikārin*) is stated, the descent of those who do not perform such rites (*aniṣṭādikārin*) is already established by implication. Furthermore, [if one were to interpret it as referring to the path], there would be a contradiction with the commencement of a different path in the phrase "now of these two," and a contradiction with the word "third. Therefore, it should be understood that the word *sthāna* (place) indicates the path. //17//
Not in the third [life], because it is not perceived in that way. (BBs 3.1.18)

Having thus refuted the two seeds of the prima facie argument—namely, that there is no distinction [in the scriptural texts] and that there is no other path—he introduces the sūtra beginning with "yat punar" (as for what again... in order to refute the third seed.

The meaning is that since those devoid of knowledge and ritual action are observed to undergo incessant birth and death in the form of worms, insects, and so forth, as indicated by the scriptural text "Be born," etc., there is no regard for the number of oblations.
He says "apica" (moreover) because it is so from the word "puruṣa" (person).
He states, beginning with "Moreover" (apica), that there is no fixed rule regarding the number of oblations even for the human body;
the meaning is that a syntactical split (vākyabheda) would occur if there were two distinct meanings consisting of both a prescription and a prohibition. //18//
Moreover,
it is also recorded in common worldly usage. (BBs 3.1.19)
To confirm the memory regarding this lack of restriction, there is the Sūtra: "It is also remembered" (smaryate 'pi).
That by which something is perceived is called "loka"; thus, the *Mahābhārata* and other such works are meant. He also states the primary meaning: "Balākā" [is used here]. //19//
And because it is observed [in scripture]. (3.1.20)

Relying on the scriptural authority of the passage, "those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouts," he explains the Sūtra with the words "Moreover" (api ca).
The meaning is that this applies elsewhere as well, namely to those who perform undesirable acts and so forth. //20//
The inclusion [of the third type] by the word "third" refers to that which arises from contact with heat. (BBs 3.1.21)

He introduces the Sūtra as a response to the objection: "How can fourfold birth be stated by this Śruti, given the contradiction with the restrictive statement in another Śruti that there are only three? He begins with the words "Now, [is it not so... etc. "Born from a living being" refers to the womb-born, such as humans; "born from the earth" refers to trees and the like, which grow by breaking through the ground.
The distinction is that mobile beings such as lice are born by piercing through water;
*saṃśoka* refers to perspiration. //21//
The attainment of the same nature [as the deity] occurs because it is logically consistent. (BS 3.1.22)

Having thus considered the going and coming of sinners, he now states the specific detail regarding the descent of those who perform sacrifices and other meritorious acts (iṣṭādikārin): "Because of the attainment of similarity of nature" (sābhāvyāpatti).
According to the manner previously described—namely, "as they came and not so"—they return again by the same path of smoke and so forth.
Having returned, those possessing residual karma (anuśayin), at the conclusion of their karma, having cast off their bodies, reach the ether (ākāśa) and become similar to the ether.
Immediately after becoming like space, they become condensed, endowed with an extremely subtle *liṅga*, and as they are carried here and there by the wind, they become equal to the wind.
That aggregate of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), having become equal to the wind, becomes equal to smoke when joined with smoke; having become equal to smoke, it becomes equal to a cloud.
"It carries water," thus it is called *abhra* (cloud);

"it sprinkles or pours," thus it is the cloud that is the agent of rain. Having become equal to that [water], it enters the earth by way of rain-showers and becomes rice, barley, and so forth—this is the meaning of the scriptural passage according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). The two preceding and succeeding arguments should be understood as referring to the seed of the doubt.

Having stated two types of paths in the preceding section, it was appropriate for the word "place" (*sthāna*) to indicate the path because it was spoken of as being the third; however, in this case, since in common usage such as "milk becomes curd" the verb "becomes" (*bhavati*) is primary in the sense of attaining the nature of a transformation, there is no basis for a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) meaning the attainment of similarity. Thus, there is a connection [to the previous discussion] by way of a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*).
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the fruit [of the path] is the preeminence of hearing (*śruti*).

The author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "In this way" (*evam*) and so forth, on the grounds that it is impossible for those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) to attain the very nature of the ether and other elements as previously established; rather, it is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
The meaning of the words in the aphorism is as follows: *sābhāvya* refers to the state of having a common nature (*samāna-bhāva*), which is to say, similarity (*sāmya*).
"Thus indeed this is so": the meaning is that this very existence arises in such a form of similarity.

He states that the characteristic of similarity is also established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the departure of those possessing latent tendencies from space and so forth, saying: "having the nature of space."
Anticipating the objection that this might be characterized as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), he says: "Because of omnipresence" (*vibhutvāt*).
The meaning is that if it were characterized as conjunction, it would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) due to the use of the verb "to become" (*bhavati*).
He concludes the section on dispassion (*vairāgya*) by reflecting that one becomes equal to various elements during the descent [from heaven]: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*) //22//
Not for very long, because of a specific distinction. (BBs 3.1.23)
Not long after [this was said].

Having relied upon the aforementioned similarity, the author raises a doubt based on the observation in the world that travelers take either a long or short time to reach their destination, and thus sets forth the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument beginning with "In that regard" (*tatra*).
The result of this prima facie argument is that, due to the lack of a fixed rule, the attainment of a new womb may sometimes occur after a delay.

In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, because the state of rice, barley, and so forth involves a delay for those with residual karma (*anuśayin*), there is a distinction: from the state of ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth, there is a swift departure. Thus, through the contemplation that the attainment of a womb occurs without delay, detachment (*vairāgya*) becomes firm; this is the discernment (*viveka*). Now, one might object: "Since pleasure is experienced by those with residual karma in ether and so forth, while pain is experienced in rice, barley, and so forth, it appears from the words [of the text] that the departure is not delayed in the former cases but is delayed in the latter; it does not indicate a difference in the speed of departure. To this, he says: "And this is merely a distinction between pleasure and pain."
The limit is time. //23//
In the case of those [seeds] presided over by another, it is as before, because of the statement [of the Sūtra]. (BBs 3.1.24)
The sequence of the topics is to be understood from other statements, from the sequence of the Vedic text (*śrutikrama*), and from the sequence of their meanings (*arthakrama*).

The meaning of the scriptural passage is that those possessed of latent tendencies (*anuśayin*), having fallen upon this earth by way of showers of rain, are born in the likeness of rice and other grains.
Regarding this, he states a doubt based on the Vedic text "they are born here" and because of the previously mentioned similarity [of the path] to space and so forth up to rain;
the meaning of "in this interval" (*atra*) is "immediately after the similarity to rain.
It is not appropriate to explain the word *durniṣprapatara* as signifying a long duration of emerging.

He presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) through the connection of an objection—namely, that "exit [from the body] occurs with difficulty" because it is possible as a primary [event]—with the words beginning "What, then...

The distinction here is as follows: in this prima facie view, there is a great effort required by the qualified seeker (*adhikārin*) to avoid becoming stationary; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is ease of effort merely to avoid the simple conjunction with rice and so forth, as well as the firmness of dispassion (*vairāgya*).

Now, one might object that the birth of living beings occurs through the production of a body and not inherently by themselves, and that things such as rice and the like do not possess the nature of a body; to this, he says: "of the state of being stationary," citing the scriptural text:
"Some enter into stationary objects," and so forth.
"The man goes to the state of an immobile being through the defects of actions born of the body"—such is the Smṛti.
Now, one might ask: since those in heaven lack sin, how can they attain the state of an immobile being?
To this, he says: "As animals," and so forth.
The meaning of words such as "eating the remnants of Soma" and "drinking the Sura" [is explained as follows].

The Sāṅkhyas say that even for acts such as ritual slaughter (*kratvarthahiṃsā*), because they possess the common characteristic of being "slaughter" (*hiṃsātva*) and so forth, it is not contradictory for them to produce a latent demerit (*duritāpūrva*) by virtue of their being prohibited by scriptures such as "one should not kill.

In this context, the state of becoming rice and so forth for those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) is not something produced (*janyarūpa*), because it is stated here without reference to any specific [new] karma.
He establishes the final conclusion with the words "thus, when this has been reached," etc., stating that it is like the previously mentioned states of ether and so forth.

The term "as before" (pūrvavat) has been explained both as an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) and as a constituent part of the logical reason (hetu). Furthermore, he provides a negative example (vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta) by saying "but where... to indicate that which refers to a specific action within this context, namely, "that birth."
Furthermore, in the supplementary portion of the scripture, it is stated: "For whoever eats the food and whoever pours the semen into the woman, he becomes that very thing again.

Thus, the connection of the group of residual souls who have entered into rice and other grains with a man who emits semen is heard to occur by way of the food. Since this would otherwise be impossible, the scriptural mention of birth cannot be taken in its primary sense; this is what [the author] expresses with the words beginning "Moreover" (apica).

The meaning is that, since liberation necessarily occurs for embodied beings upon the destruction of the body in the form of rice and so forth, there would be no union with a seed-discharger (retassig-yoga).
"By this" refers to the aforementioned inference and presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

The meaning is that one should respond to the objection regarding the primary sense of the scriptural statement "it is born" and the fact that rice and other grains serve as the locus for the experience of those with residual karma (*anuśayin*).

Now, if it is argued that by not accepting rice and other grains as the locus of experience, there would be a contradiction of the previously cited scriptures, traditional texts (*smṛti*), and common consensus, he says: "And not... (24).
If it is argued that [the world] is impure, we say no, because of the Word (Śabda). 3.1.25.
He elaborates on the meaning of the Sūtra— "Vedic action does not become impure because it is ordained by the Śāstra"— with the words beginning "This is Dharma. The meaning is that the conclusion—

that the Agnihotra performed in a pure place at morning or evening for the sake of livelihood and so forth constitutes Dharma, whereas the same rite performed in an impure place at midnight for the sake of death and so forth becomes Adharma— is achievable solely through the Śāstra.
To this, he says: "And from scripture.
Now, one might object: is it not improper here for the general rule (*utsarga*) that "whatever is violence is unrighteousness" to be sublated by a specific injunction?

For, just as the prohibited *śyena* sacrifice is understood to serve the purpose of the person because it is forbidden, there is no contradiction in prohibited violence and the like serving as an auxiliary to the ritual (*kratu*).
Regarding this, he says: "In the case of the general rule and the exception.

This is the meaning: in all instances of optional (kāmya) ritual action, engagement occurs out of passion (rāga) with respect to the instrumental factor (karaṇāṃśa), whereas with respect to the auxiliary factors (aṅga), it occurs by virtue of scriptural injunction (vidhi); such is the established position.

And thus, even though the ritual act called Śyena is prohibited, activity toward it would still occur due to the intensity of passion; however, in the case of violence that is an auxiliary to a sacrifice (*kratvaṅga-hiṃsā*), activity must be said to arise from the injunction itself.
If that injunction were not to sublate the fact that [violence] is a cause of harm—which is established by general rule—then it could not be an instigator of action;
or, if it were an instigator, the injunction would lead to what is harmful.
Therefore, the injunction, being without scope [elsewhere], establishes the general rule—which has scope—within those instances of killing and so forth that are not enjoined.

And this was stated by accepting that the prohibitory scripture operates through the commonality of "being killing" (*hiṃsātva*) and so on. In reality, however, since that [prohibition] concerns killing prompted by passion (*rāga*), it does not apply to killing performed under scriptural injunction (*vaidha-hiṃsā*); thus, one should understand that there is no occasion for the suspicion of impurity [in such cases].
The construction is: "It is not the case that its fruit is a corresponding form of suffering.
It has been stated here that in the state of being rice and so forth, there is no specific entitlement (*adhikāra*) nor any reference to karma. //25//
Now follows the connection with the progenitor of semen. 3.1.26.
Now, immediately after the state of being rice and so forth, the state of being one who sheds semen (*retas-sic*) is mentioned in the scripture.

In that context, since those with residual karma (*anuśayin*) residing in food cannot logically be the agents of shedding semen, it must be understood as mere contact (*yoga-mātra*). Likewise, in the opening passage as well, only contact should be accepted;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction between the beginning and the conclusion. With this in mind, it was stated: "Thus, there is no contradiction. (26)
From the womb, the body [is produced]. (BBs 3.1.27)
The meaning of the sūtra is that, because the scripture speaks of the body as arising from the womb, those who possess residual karma (anuśayins) do not have rice and the like as their bodies.

Thus, concluding the meaning of the chapter, he states "it is established" (iti siddham), summarizing that by reflecting on how the cycle of going and returning for those who perform actions is difficult to avoid, detachment from the fruits of action— which is the means to the knowledge of reality— is established.

Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the illustrious Govinda Bhagavatpāda.
The second quarter of the third chapter begins here.
"In the intermediate state there is creation, for so [the scripture] says. (BBs 3.2.1).
"In the intermediate state there is creation, for so [the scripture] says.

He states the connection between the two chapters as that of cause and effect—where the former is the means and the latter is the goal—by saying, "That which has been transcended," etc., meaning that in this chapter the discrimination between the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*, which is to be accomplished through the detachment already described, is established as the means for the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).
Because this section (pāda) consists of an investigation into the means of realization (*sādhana*), it is logically connected to this chapter.

In this section, prior to the sūtra "Not even from a different state" (*na sthānato 'pi*), the meaning of the term *jijñāsitatva-pada* (the object of inquiry, i.e., the individual self) is first analyzed by way of its various states;
from that point until the end of the section, there is an analysis of the meaning of the term *tat-pada* (the Supreme Self), which is the subject to be established.

In this regard, having first described the waking state through the investigation of going and coming, [the author] now takes up the dreaming state as taught in the Śruti; expressing a doubt based on the description of the creation of chariots and so forth in that dream, as well as the statement of their absence, he applies the sūtra of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) with the words beginning "therein, a doubt... and so on.

The meaning of the doubt is whether dream-chariots and the like possess empirical existence (*vyāvahārikasattā*) like waking chariots and the like, or whether they are merely apparent (*prātītika*) like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
This should be understood because the ultimate reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) was negated in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*.
In this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the dream state cannot be established, as it would be just like the waking state.

In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the result is the establishment of self-luminosity through discrimination, by virtue of being the witness (*sākṣin*) of the perceptible objects that appear [only] phenomenally.

For one who is about to die, because all the senses have been withdrawn, there is no experience of this world; yet, while remembering this world through mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there occurs a dream consisting of the manifestation of the next world within the heart by means of the mind through the power of karma.
This is the "intermediate dream" (*saṃdhya-svapna*), occurring at the junction between the two worlds.
And thus says the Śruti: "Standing in that intermediate state (saṃdhye sthāne), one perceives both these states—this world and the state of the next world.

Because this [ordinary] dream is merely occasional, the author, out of dissatisfaction with that view, has stated that the eternal dream occurs at the junction of waking and deep sleep (prabodha-saṃprasāda).
Others, however, define the "next world" as the direct perception of forms and so forth produced by means other than the mortal eyes and other such organs.

They explain that because the state of possessing those [objects] not produced by the divine eye and so forth—which is the characteristic of the mortal world—exists in a dream, it touches upon both worlds by way of its definition; thus, eternal sleep itself is the junction between the two worlds, just as a path touching two villages is the junction between them.
He states that the objects of dreams are not only conventionally real according to scripture, but also because they have an agent: "For he is the agent. (1)
And some [maintain that the intermediate being is] a creator, as well as sons and so forth. (BBs 3.2.2)

Furthermore, he states the meaning of the sūtra with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth: "And moreover, the objects of dreams are real, because they are created by an intelligent being, like space and so on."
Fearing that [the term] might be taken in its conventional sense, he refutes this by means of the phrase beginning with "nanu" (but surely).
The meaning is: that which remains awake while the instruments (senses) are asleep and inactive—that alone is the pure, self-luminous Brahman.
[This is contrasted] with the dream state [which consists of] waking objects.

He states that the purpose of the scriptural declarations regarding their occupying the same location and the declarations regarding their non-difference is to establish their reality: "Now, indeed, they say... (2).
But it is mere illusion, because its true nature is not manifested in its entirety. (BS 3.2.3)

He establishes the final conclusion—that dream chariots and the like are merely apparent because they are seen even without the causal materials (sāmagrī) postulated for waking chariots and so forth, just like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—by means of the word "but" (tu) and the subsequent passage.

It has been stated in the Sūtra and Bhāṣya that Māyā is Nescience (avidyā) residing in pure consciousness, which, by virtue of its limitation as the intellect (cittva), exists in the individual soul (jīva) as well in the form of chariots and other objects;

this is said for the purpose of making known the non-difference between Māyā and avidyā. By the word "mere" (mātra), however, there is a rejection of empirical reality (vyāvahārikasatyatva), which consists in being unsublated as long as the knower (pramātṛ) exists.
The property of being produced by that complete causal complex which is present here in the waking state is the characteristic of the waking object, which is a real entity.
This property pervades reality; its absence in the dream state is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "Not indeed" (na tāvat), and so forth.
In a place that is enclosed and crowded,
for the purpose of going forth to travel or returning to come back.
The awakened person causes [others] to hear it—
meaning those standing nearby—
in such a way that this becomes as if it were a dream.

The meaning is that at the time when one moves by means of the state of dreaming, one moves as one pleases within one's own body. "As if outside" means that the immortal Self, having moved as if outside the nest— namely, the body— goes wherever it desires, that is, it roams according to its will.
He states the [positive] quality [of the dreamer] with the words "for he" (yo hi).
The meaning is that, by virtue of the quality of being free from identification with the body, although situated within the body, he is said to be "outside," as if standing externally.
This being so, the meaning is that according to both scripture and reasoning, the dream exists only within.
Deception and confusion arise from the absence of a suitable place; having stated this, he speaks of the absence of time with the word "kāla" (time).
Here, even at the time of night, there is daylight in other regions such as Ketumāla; therefore, the term "Bhārata" was used [to specify the context].

The purport of the Sūtra is that in the example of the objects seen while awake, the state of being produced by fire and the suitability for non-sublation are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for the previous inferences. //3//
For there is scriptural indication, and those who know it declare this as well. (BS 3.2.4)

He explains another sūtra—beginning with "māyā" and so forth—as a response to the objection that if a dream were merely an illusion, then even an object indicated by it could not be real. [The objection is:
"If dreams are indicators of reality through mantras, divine grace, or the use of medicinal herbs, then they themselves must be real. To this he says: "In that case too, let it be granted...
The underlying sense is that even a false silver seen in a mother-of-pearl shell, which is a cause for true joy, is never observed to be real.

Just as the plough is the cause for the livelihood of cattle and other animals through the medium of agriculture, so too the dreamer is the cause of the creation of the dream through the medium of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit);

however, there is no direct agency in creating the dream on the part of the dreamer, as in the case of a potter with respect to a jar, because [such direct agency] has been refuted by the absence of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) and by logical contradiction. Thus he says, beginning with "yad uktam" (as it was stated).
Thus, the sense is that since the dream lacks a primary agent, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is unestablished (*asiddhi*).
Furthermore, he states "Moreover" (*api ca*) to show that the reality of dreams is not tenable because it contradicts the purport of the scriptures.
*Vyatikara* means confusion or intermixture.
The meaning is "by the scripture's intent";
the sense is that there is no distinction from the waking state.
He states the conclusion: "Therefore," etc.
"By this" means by way of being figurative.

Furthermore, as for the reason stated in the second sutra— that the dream state has the wise one (*prājña*) as its agent— is that established by scripture, or is it established because the wise one is the Lord of all?
He says "not so today," beginning with the words "as for what was said," etc.;
having himself paralyzed the waking body, making it motionless,
or having himself fashioned it through latent impression (*vāsanā*).

The meaning is that one experiences the dream by means of one's own light—that is, by the activity of one's own intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) and by one's own radiance, which is the consciousness of one's true nature (*svarūpa-caitanya*).
He states, "here too," because the individual soul's agency in dreaming is not heard of only in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, but also in the *Kaṭhaka*.
To the objection that there would be a contradiction with the context concerning Brahman if the individual soul were mentioned here, he says, "But of that [soul]..."

Having thus refuted that the reason is established by scripture (*śruti*), he accepts the second alternative with the words "Nor by us... Anticipating the objection that the dream must therefore be real because its cause is established, he considers the alternatives as to whether this reality is conventional (*vyāvahārika*) or ultimate (*pāramārthika*). Since it is observed to be sublated at the time of ordinary transaction, the first [conventional] option is not tenable; thus he says: "But the ultimate..."
Regarding the second [point], he states "nor... because the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*).
Anticipating the question, "What then is the distinction here between a dream and waking [experience]?", he states "prior... to indicate its status as a mere appearance (*prātibhāsikatva*). //4//
"But it is concealed by the meditation on another; for from that come its bondage and its opposite. (BS 3.2.5)

Having raised the objection that it was incorrect to state that a dream is an illusion because of the absence of previously prepared causal materials—since a real creation could possibly occur even through mere true resolve—he explains the Sūtra while offering a rebuttal, beginning with "But it might be argued... and so forth. The meaning of the rebuttal is that while for one whose resolve is true, creation becomes real by virtue of that resolve, the fact that the individual soul (jīva) possesses false resolve is directly perceived.
In that case, one might raise the objection: "Since the individual soul possesses contradictory attributes, its being the Lord is simply non-existent.

To this he replies, "It is not that it does not exist," meaning that while it is not non-existent, it remains obscured; however, through the grace of the Lord, it is manifested to someone. This refers to one whose darkness has been dispelled, who is free from sin, who is perfected, and who is endowed with powers such as *aṇimā*.

Having known and directly realized the Lord as "I am indeed Brahman," there occurs the removal and destruction of all fetters—the afflictions such as ignorance and the rest—and one becomes of that very nature.

When the afflictions are exhausted, there is the dissolution of the bondage consisting of birth and death, which are their effects; thus the fruit of knowledge devoid of attributes (nirguṇavidyā) has been described.
He now states the fruit of knowledge with attributes (saguṇavidyā): "Of him... [tasya].

By meditating with a sense of "I" directed toward another [the deity], out of a desire for liberation from bondage, or by considering the two types of loss mentioned in the *Mantra*, one attains the third state: universal sovereignty (*viśvaiśvarya*) consisting of powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth. This occurs when the mortal body has fallen away and a perfected body (*siddhadeha*) has been attained;

subsequently, through the knowledge of the Self, one becomes solitary (*kevala*), free from duality (*dvaitaśūnya*), and one whose desires are fulfilled (*āptakāma*), having attained the bliss of self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiḥ*). This is the meaning of "gradual liberation" (*kramamukti*). //5//
Or rather, that [bondage] also exists due to the connection with a body. (BBs 3.2.6)
The aphorism is intended to state that the cause of the concealment of the aforementioned sovereignty is the identification with the body;
to refute the doubt regarding this, he says, "Why?
Having accepted that there is no real obscuration, he establishes the imagined obscuration with the words beginning with "It is said."

Raising the objection that it is better to assume the soul's distinctness from God than to assume the existence of an obscuration while accepting its identity with God, [the author] refutes it by means of scripture, beginning with the words "But surely" (nanu).
If light and so forth were real even in a dream, then the self-luminosity of the Self would not be clear, as it is in the waking state.

However, if they are merely illusory (prātibhāsika), then even in the absence of light, the senses, and other factors, the immediate perception of the object is established clearly as belonging to the light of the Self alone.
Therefore, the statement regarding the similarity of place and so forth refers to the intention that a dream has an appearance equal to that of the waking state; such is the meaning. //6//
The absence [of that dream-experience] occurs in the channels and in the Self, because of scriptural statements to that effect. (BS 3.2.7)

Thus, when the external organs have ceased their activity, having reflected upon the dream state— which consists of the play of ignorance ignited by mental impressions— for the sake of demonstrating the self-luminosity of the Self as the witness, he now investigates deep sleep, which consists of the dissolution of the mind in the state of dreaming, through the relationship of subject and object: "Its absence [occurs] in the channels and in the Self, because of the scriptural statement."
This "sleeping" (svapana) occurs in such a manner that at the time one is asleep—

meaning deeply asleep (suṣupta), with all [faculties] withdrawn, external organs stilled, and because of the dissolution of the mind, there is a complete absorption (sampra-saṅga)— this is the meaning.

Having stated the location of the channels (nāḍīs) during sleep, he states the scriptural texts concerning the combination of the channels and the heart (purītat), as well as the channels and the Supreme Self (paramātman), in the passage beginning with "elsewhere" (anyatra).
He cites the scriptural passages concerning the Supreme Self alone with the words "And so elsewhere," and so forth.

He states the doubt arising from the use of the locative case regarding the channels (nāḍīs), the pericardium (purītat), and Brahman, as well as from the scriptural mention of their conjunction, with the word "Therein.
According to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), because there is an option of locations, there would be no definitive conclusion regarding the soul's identity with Brahman.

The distinction is this: according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), having reached the pericardium (purītat) by means of the channels (nāḍīs), one rests in Brahman alone within the heart; thus, because of their combination, that [resting] is determined. An objection is raised: "The mutual independence of rice and barley as serving the purpose of a single sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is observed, but how can the channels and so forth be independent locations for the single purpose consisting of sleep? To this, he says: "And of the channels, etc. The meaning of the doubt is that since Brahman exists, the third case ending (instrumental) applies according to the third scriptural mention, and not the seventh case ending (locative).
He says, "This is not a fault," because from the word *āyatana* (abode), the sense of the locative case—namely, the state of being a substratum—is understood.

The meaning is that the individual soul (*jīva*), exhausted in the other two states [waking and dreaming], approaches the True Brahman called *prāṇa*, which is the place of rest, during deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Since the locative hearing (*saptamī-śruti*) indicates an independent substratum, one must accept an option (*vikalpa*); that is, the status of being a locus belongs to the channels (*nāḍīs*) and so forth either alternatively or even collectively. Thus, there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning their collective status; such is the meaning of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
He establishes the final conclusion with the words "thus it follows.
In the Sūtra, the word "ca" (and) serves to include the pericardium (*purītat*).

If the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) were the place of deep sleep, then the pericardium would not be the place; thus, there would be a contradiction of the scriptural statement regarding the location [of the soul] in that alternative view.
He says that this is not tenable: "For there is an option among these," because the sense is that an option between rice and barley exists only as a last resort (*agatyā*).
As for the claim that the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth have a single result based on the hearing of the locative case-ending (*saptamī-śruti*), [that is also incorrect].

To this he says "no," for [it is not so] because there is not one [case-ending]. The purpose of the palace is to support the couch, whereas the purpose of the couch is to serve as a bed; thus, even though there is a difference in their respective results, a single case-ending is observed [to apply to both].
Furthermore, because they serve as means of resting whether through intervention or non-intervention, there is a conjunction;
likewise here too, since the soul’s sleep occurs in Brahman alone by way of its movement through the channels (nāḍīs) and the pericardium (purītat), there is a conjunction—this is the meaning.
He states that there is a mutual conjunction between the channels and the vital breath (prāṇa) because they are presented in a single sentence, saying: "by a single sentence."

The meaning of the locative case is merely "being a substratum" (ādhāratva) and not "independence"; therefore, there is no sublation of the conjunction by the locative. Thus he says: "And even so... The meaning is: "even in the case of conjunction.

Here, regarding the scriptural mention of the channels (nāḍī), the sleeper's state of rest within the channels is not intended to be expressed, because [the passage] aims at praising the path consisting of the channels connected with the rays. Thus he says: "Moreover... (api ca).

The meaning is that because there is an absence of perceiving objects due to the bile (pitta), there is an absence of pleasure and pain; thus, there is no contact with evil (pāpman), which consists of those dharmas that cause them.
Or, he says "Alternatively" to indicate that there is no contact with evil due to the attainment of Brahman, which is free from evil (apahatapāpman).
Regarding this interpretation, he states the advantage: "And this being so..."
The meaning is that a combination [of the two paths] is resorted to, based on the scriptural text: "Then he becomes one with them; then he becomes one in this very breath.

Just as there is a combination of the channels (nāḍīs) and Brahman during sleep by way of a subordinate and a principal relationship, so too is there a combination of the pericardium (purītat) and Brahman; this he states with the words beginning with "tathā" (so too).
Having begun with "He lies in the ether, which is Brahman," it is further stated: "Having returned from those [channels], he lies in the pericardium."

Thus, the combination [of the two paths] is established, as he goes to the *purītat* by way of the channels and then rests in Brahman; this is what he states with the words "In that way, the channels...

Since scripture mentions both "he becomes united with the Being" (*sat*) and "he is embraced by the Intelligent One" (*prājña*), there would otherwise be five places of sleep; therefore, he says "of the Being and the Intelligent One.

Furthermore, in the case of rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*), an option is appropriate because they are each independently capable of accomplishing the single sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) required for the Darśa and other rites under discussion, without depending on one another.

However, since the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth lack the capacity to serve as the substratum for the soul during deep sleep independently of Brahman, there is no optionality [between them]. Thus he says: "Moreover, the channels...

The channels and the pericardium (*purītat*), which are the supports of the subtle body (*liṅga*)—the limiting adjuncts—must be said to be the support of the soul as qualified by those adjuncts through a mediated succession;
yet even that is not possible in the state of deep sleep.
The meaning is "due to the dissolution of limiting adjuncts" (*upādhilayāt*).
Now, one might object: "Even Brahman cannot be the primary locus of the individual soul (*jīva*), because there is non-difference [between them]. To this he says: "being the substratum of Brahman.

The meaning is that while the soul's abiding in Brahman occurs through non-difference, for the soul whose limiting adjuncts have dissolved in the channels (*nāḍī*) and the pericardium (*purītat*), mere existence is not even possible; therefore, since there is no capacity for a single purpose [in both], there can be no option (*vikalpa*).

He says "Moreover" (apica) because, since the limiting adjuncts that differentiate the individual soul (jīva) have dissolved during deep sleep (suṣupti), it is not logical to conceive of any distinction from its natural state of non-difference with Brahman.
Furthermore, even by one who maintains that deep sleep occurs in any one of the various locations such as the channels (nāḍīs), it must be admitted that the state of deep sleep is not differentiated;
yet that cannot be maintained. Thus he says: "Moreover, regarding the location... (apica sthāna...).
The absence of difference is indeed the cause for the absence of the cognition of difference;

however, the meaning is that for the individual soul (jīva) residing within the channels (nāḍīs), because it exists in a state of difference, there is no instrument for the non-cognition of difference.
He raises an objection regarding the cause for the non-cognition of duality even while in a state of duality: "But [if you say] 'difference'... and so on.
Whether the distance of the seer from the seen is natural or adventitious—
having restated the first position with its supporting example, he replies with the words beginning "Certainly" (*bāḍham*);
having restated the second, he refutes it with the words "It belongs only to the limiting adjunct" (*upādhigatam eva*).

If the soul were merely conjoined with its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then during sleep within the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence of cognizing certain nearby objects; thus, deep sleep (*suṣupti*) would be contradicted.
