However, since the soul cannot abide elsewhere once the adjuncts have dissolved, one must maintain that sleep occurs in Brahman itself—this is the meaning.

Having thus rejected the alternative views, he refutes the idea of a mere equal conjunction of the channels, the pericardium (*purītat*), and Brahman as being fruitless, and concludes by establishing their conjunction through the relationship of subordinate and principal—beginning with the words "Nor do we... and so on.
Therefore, awakening arises from this. (BBs 3.2.8)

Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement regarding the soul's emergence from Brahman, the author of the Sūtras states that Brahman alone is the locus of deep sleep: "Therefore, [the soul's] awakening [is from Him]" (Sūtra 3.2.8).
The meaning is that since the channels (nāḍīs) and the pericardium (purītat) are nowhere heard of as the source (apādāna) of emergence, they cannot be the locus of deep sleep.

Therefore, when the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) dissolve, the soul is non-different from Brahman; thus, difference is merely adventitious (aupādhika). Consequently, it is established that the non-difference of the meanings of the words [denoting the soul and Brahman] is realized through discrimination. //8//
But that same [self] [returns], on account of the continuity of action, memory, scriptural testimony, and injunctions. (BS 3.2.9)
"But that same [jīva] [returns], on account of the scripture concerning the remembrance of actions and the injunctions regarding words.

Since there is doubt—arising from the observation of the remembrance of actions and so forth despite the destruction of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) during deep sleep—it was previously stated that Brahman alone is the locus of deep sleep because of the scriptural teaching on the jīva’s emergence from Brahman. However, this is challenged by the objection that since the emergence of someone other than the one who slept is also possible, it is possible for the one in deep sleep to have the channels (*nāḍīs*) and so forth as his locus. With this objection as the point of transition, the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—"There is no fixed rule, due to the absence of a restrictive factor"—beginning with the words "tasyāḥ punaḥ" (But of that...).
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), knowledge is useless because liberation in the form of non-return is established by deep sleep alone;

however, in the final view (*siddhānta*), since one who exists as the Self of Brahman while it remains unknown is necessarily bound to arise again through the power of ignorance, there is a need for knowledge to destroy that ignorance—this is the result [of the inquiry]. The phrase "or the Lord" was stated to reinforce the lack of restriction [regarding the agent of creation].

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is simply that "it is either he or another. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is set forth by the words "But it is he indeed" (*sa eva tu*), etc., [as follows]: since there is no absolute destruction of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*) apart from [the cessation of] cognition, the individual soul (*jīva*) which was conditioned by a particular intellect and remained in deep sleep in the form of a cause, arises again conditioned by that very same [intellect] which possesses the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the experience of various karmas.

The over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would be the consequence that a single sacrifice, such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, whether half-performed or fully performed by one person, would result in having multiple sacrificers.
Having stated the traditional authority (*smṛti*), he states the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) indicated by the word "again" (*anu*): "I am that very same [person].
*Ayana* means going; *āya* is the act of coming.
"Yoni" refers to the location of each respective sense organ.
The meaning of the Vedic text is that one returns to each respective womb (*pratiyoni*) in such a way as to ensure a specific destination for the sake of awakening.
The statement "he does not find [it]" indicates the necessity of the sleeper's rising from sleep due to the presence of ignorance.
The meaning is that those who exist in the previous awakening are the very same ones who exist in the subsequent awakening.

He explains the injunction with the word "karma" (action); the meaning is that it is determined that "he alone arises. Right here, he states another argument not found in the sūtra itself, beginning with "apica" (furthermore).

The meaning is that if [the soul] were to arise from something else, pleasure and so forth would not be the effects of prior karma; thus, there would be the acquisition of pleasure and so forth not earned by oneself, and the destruction of karma performed by a living being during a previous state of sleep.
He refutes the example cited by the opponent through the disparity [of their cases], starting with the words "But as for... (yat punar...).

Thinking that the Lord, depending on the unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa) of living beings, performs even that discrimination which is impossible for people like us, he states the example: "And it is seen... (dṛśyate ca).
And because the individual soul (*jīva*) is non-different from Brahman, there is no disparity [between the soul and] a drop of water; thus he says, "Moreover" (*apica*).

Anticipating the objection that if there is non-difference, the question of whether "that one" or "another" arises has no room for consideration, he says, "This being so," [meaning] that the consideration arises because the individual souls are distinct due to the distinctions of their intellects (*buddhi*).

Since, upon waking from deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the intellect is destroyed, the daily empirical usage of a single soul would not be possible due to the distinction of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the intellect; therefore, he says, "He is this very same person."
The meaning is that a single limiting adjunct (upādhi) exists in both gross and subtle forms. //9//
The state of being in a swoon is a partial attainment [of death], because of the remainder. (BS 3.2.10)
Having distinguished the Self from the three [other] states, he distinguishes it from swoon (*mūrchā*): "In swoon there is a partial attainment [of the state of deep sleep], because of the remainder.
[The opponent asks: Is swoon included within the well-known states, or is it a fifth state?
Since the four states are established and because swoon is distinct from them, when one has arisen with the recognition "I am that very same person," there arises a doubt.

He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) through the connection with the example that fainting is included within deep sleep, based on the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that it is indeed deep sleep because of the common mark of the absence of specific cognition, just as in the case of the non-difference [of the self] while asleep. He says, "There are three," etc. In the prima facie view, the result is the failure of effort to achieve the discrimination of the self from fainting as a state distinct from the well-known states.

In the Siddhānta (the final conclusion), the distinction is that there is a persistence of separate effort; demonstrating this by way of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), he establishes the Siddhānta with the words beginning "Not, indeed... (*na tāvat...*).
The meaning is: "even while waking," that is, even in the state of wakefulness.

He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating the disparity through the words beginning with "No" (*na...*), noting that sensory cognition of objects and the maintenance of the body exist for one who is awake, but not for one who is in a swoon (*mugdha*).
Having stated the distinction between fainting and waking, he states the distinction from sleep and death with the words beginning "Nor... (*nāpi*).
They "touch" (*ālabhante*) means they contact [the body].
"Diṣṭam" means death.
He says "no" because, although there is some similarity between deep sleep and fainting, they are distinct due to many differences.

Having stated the difference in their characteristics, he states the difference in their causes with the words "by cause. He further states that recognition is not established either with the words "nor... [no].

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: through the aforementioned similarities and dissimilarities, the state of being "half-attained" (*ardhasampatti*) is established; the person in a swoon (*mugdha*) is not in deep sleep because he is not endowed with all the characteristics of deep sleep, nor is he dead because he is not endowed with all the characteristics of the state of death; rather, he has entered a different state.
Regarding this Sūtra, one who is mistaken thinks that the "half-attainment" of the individual soul (*jīva*) by Brahman is being described here, and thus asks: "How so?"
The scriptural statement that one who is asleep has become united with Being (*sat*) intends to convey the absence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Since the absence of limiting adjuncts applies to me even when I am in a state of swoon (*mugdha*), the meaning is that there is indeed a complete union [with Being].

Having raised the objection—"If there is no connection with karma at the time of deep sleep, how is there a subsequent rising?"—the author replies with the words "For in the case of the individual soul" (*jīve hi*), stating that the mention of the lack of connection is due to the absence of its effects (i.e., the absence of manifesting karma).
Brahmā, having accepted the notion of "complete attainment," refutes it by saying, "We do not say so.

For the state of being "half-awake" (mugdhatva) is characterized as a "half-attainment" in the sense that it possesses the attributes of deep sleep (suṣupta), such as unconsciousness, to one half, while it possesses the attributes of death (maraṇa), such as trembling and the like, to the other half. This is the meaning.
He states "and the door" to show that there is a difference from deep sleep even for this reason as well.
Having granted the lack of established proof, he says "and it is established" to show that there is indeed established proof.
Āyurveda is the science of medicine.

Anticipating the objection, "How can there be a dispute regarding what is well-known?", he says "ardha" (half), meaning that people have the notion of its inclusion [within the states] due to the partial attainment of the characteristics of deep sleep and death. //10//
The Supreme [Self] does not possess both characteristics even from the standpoint of its various locations, for it is so everywhere. (BS 3.2.11)

Desiring to demonstrate that you are an object (*artha*) untainted by all states of existence, [the author] first states its quality of being devoid of distinctions: "Not even on account of location does the Supreme possess both characteristics, for it is everywhere.

He explains the connection of the present topic (*avasara-saṃgati*) as occurring immediately after the cessation of the inquiry into the meaning of the term *tvam* (the "you"), which is the subject of the proposition: "by which...

The meaning is that there exist Vedic texts possessing "both characteristics"—those by which both the absence of distinction and the presence of distinction are indicated (*liṅgyate*), that is, made known—and these serve as the seeds of doubt.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, just as the state of being "stupefied" (*mugdhatva*) consists of both contradictory forms—deep sleep and death—so too, on the authority of scripture, Brahman should be meditated upon as having both forms; this is established by means of an analogy.
The author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that Brahman is to be known as exclusively one form, devoid of distinctions, with the word "thus" (*evam*).
Is this possession of both forms inherent (*svataḥ*)?

Furthermore, is the specific quality of possessing all fragrances and so forth in the inherently attributeless [Brahman] real only due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), or is Brahman itself inherently possessed of such distinctions?
Having set aside the first alternative, he restates and refutes the second: "Let it be so, then," and so forth.
The locus is the limiting adjunct (upādhi). The meaning is that the distinction in Brahman is imagined, because it arises from a limiting adjunct, like the redness of a crystal.

Even if a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) were real, it is observed that what is produced by it is false; however, since the limiting adjuncts themselves are false in the case of Brahman, what need is there to say that the distinction produced by them is false? Thus he says: "Of the limiting adjuncts" (*upādhīnām*).
He refutes the third [position] with: "And therefore" (*ataśca*); the meaning is:
precisely because every distinction is merely imagined (*kalpita*).
And because of the scriptural statement of prohibition, he says "thus" with the words "for everywhere," etc. (Sūtra 11).

If it is argued that [the whole] does not exist because of the difference [of its parts], we say no; for [the scripture] does not state that [the whole is non-existent] with respect to each [part]. (BBs 3.2.12)
"Bheda" means that which is divided, i.e., a distinction (*viśeṣa*).

He explains the doubt—that even though there is a scriptural statement regarding the absence of distinctions (*nirviśeṣatva*), since distinction is also heard in scripture, there might be a dual nature—by saying, "Now, it might be argued.
He recalls the previously mentioned contradiction by saying, "But has it not been stated?"

The meaning of the resolution is that there is no contradiction because one accepts a distinction of forms based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for the sake of validating the scriptural texts concerning difference.

Is it that a distinction of forms residing solely in the adjuncts is figuratively attributed to Brahman for the purpose of meditation, or does Brahman actually come to possess a distinct nature through its connection with the adjuncts, such that a real difference arises?
In the first case, our desired conclusion is established.
He refutes the second [position] by means of the scriptural text concerning non-difference, saying: "We say, no. //12//
Moreover, some [teachers] hold this view as well. (BBs 3.2.13)
He states the meaning of the Sūtra—that the reality is without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*)—by means of the teaching of non-duality preceded by a censure of duality, with the words "Moreover" (*apica*).

Having reflected upon the enjoyer, which is the individual soul (*jīva*), the objects of enjoyment, such as sound and so forth, and the impeller of those two, which is the Lord (*īśvara*), one should understand that all this which has been declared to me is indeed the threefold Brahman alone; such is the meaning. //13//
For that [meditation] is indeed like that which is formless, because it has that as its primary object. (BS 3.2.14)

An objection is raised: "How then [is it determined] when there are two kinds of scriptural texts?"—namely, what is the determining factor regarding the absence of distinctions? He states that the principle "that which is devoted to the primary meaning prevails over that which is not" (*tatparātatparavirodhe tatparaṃ balavad iti*) is the determining factor, saying: "Just as formless" (*arūpavadeva*). Having raised the doubt that even if there is no intent regarding a specific form in passages devoted to meditation (*upāsanā*), a form might still be established—as in the case of the physical forms of deities—he says: "Because they do not exist in those [passages]," thereby stating that this cannot be so due to the contradiction with the scriptures whose primary intent is the non-dual, undifferentiated reality (*niṣprapañca*). //14//
And [the Lord is] like light, because [His teaching] is not purposeless. (BS 3.2.15)

Furthermore, because they allow for the possibility of imagined duality, the scriptural passages concerning the world of manifoldness (*saprapañca*) are weak; thus he says, "And like light" (*prakāśavad ca*). Now, one might ask: why is it described that sentences regarding forms possess a subject matter consisting of qualities such as omnipresence (*sarvagandhatva*) imagined through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), when their mere futility could simply be asserted?
To this he replies: "For [there is no] lack of purpose in Vedic sentences... (*na hi vedavākyānām...*) .
"Even so" means:
even though the scriptures are established as having both forms by accepting the aforementioned manner [of their operation].

It was previously stated that the reality of having both forms is not [ultimately] true, because the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are imagined and what is conditioned by them (*aupādhika*) is [only] conventionally real.

Now, he states, "We say no," [meaning] that even if one accepts both forms—truth being non-differentiation and falsity being differentiation—there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

Anticipating the objection that if duality were false, then because it would be sublated by knowledge, practical activities such as meditation (*upāsanā*) would not be possible, he says, "It is true," [meaning] that such activity exists prior to sublation. //15//
And it is said: "It is merely that. (BBs 3.2.16)
Since scripture declares that pure consciousness alone is real and that all distinctions are false, he states the meaning of the Sūtra with the words "And it says":
"Like a mass of rock salt" (saindhavaghana), meaning a lump of salt. //16//
Furthermore, it is shown [in scripture], and moreover, it is also recorded in the Smṛti. (BS 3.2.17)
Furthermore, because the Śruti and Smṛti teach Brahman by means of the negation of the "other," he says, "And [the scripture] shows [that Brahman is devoid of phenomenal expansion].
The meaning is that after the statement regarding duality, the instruction "not this, not this" (neti neti) is given for the purpose of producing knowledge.
To him—who was persistent, saying "Teach me something else, sir, teach me again"—he spoke, having abandoned silence in response to his second and third questions.
He is tranquil, with duality cast away;
therefore, for him, silence alone is the answer, and thus the word "ataḥ" in the Sūtra has that meaning. That which is not a beginningless effect is "anādimat.
"Sat" means perceptible by the senses.
The meaning is that it is not non-existent or imperceptible because it is self-luminous.

That you see me in a manifest form endowed with the divine attributes of all beings, such as fragrance and the like, is *māyā*; therefore, you ought not to see me as "the Blessed One who possesses duality," for in reality I am beyond duality. //17//
And for this very reason, there is a comparison [of the soul] with the reflection of the sun and so forth. (3.2.18)

Furthermore, just as attributes such as difference and motion are attributed to the sun and the moon through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) like water, so too are they attributed to the Self; this is established by both scriptural illustration and direct statement that reality is without distinctions. For this very reason, the scripture says "and therefore the simile" (*ata eva copamā*).
The suffix *-ka* in the term *sūryaka* is used to indicate that the sun appears as a mere reflection in its form as residing in water.
Just as this luminous Vivasvat, though inherently one, appears manifold when following the waters divided by the differences of jars.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: "In this way, this unborn Self, the self-luminous God, though one, becomes differentiated in form as it follows after [the various] fields (kṣetra) through the limiting adjunct (upādhi), which is Māyā. (18)
But because it is not grasped like water, it is not so [as the reflection]. (BS 3.2.19)
Regarding this, the sūtra raising the doubt that the aforementioned analogy does not apply to the Self is: "Like water" (ambuvat).

The meaning is that because the Self is formless and because there is no proximate limiting adjunct (upādhi), a distinction of reflections within the intellect and so forth through Māyā is not tenable. //19//
The participation in increase and decrease occurs because of inclusion; thus, there is consistency with both [theories]. (3.2.20)

By including the substrate (*upādhi*), the intended portion here is the possession of those properties imagined therein; thus, by way of that similarity, the sūtra provides the resolution: "In accordance with increase and decrease" (*vṛddhihāsasama*).

Even though there is similarity in the example, one might ask: how can a reflection of a formless self be imagined through one's own intellect? To this he says: "And this is not [so]" (*na cedam*). The meaning is that it is heard [in scripture], it is not imagined.
To the question, "What is the purpose of introducing the illustration of the sun and so forth for one who has heard [the teaching]? he says: "By the scripture," etc.
The meaning is that the result is the non-differentiated nature of the Self. "Non-contradiction" means the absence of any disparity.
In the inference "The self is devoid of reflection because it is a formless substance, like air," there is a deviation [from the rule] with respect to space.
The sense is that since the reflection of the sky is seen even in a small amount of water, the distance of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is sometimes irrelevant. //20//
And because it is observed [in scripture]. (BBs 3.2.21)
The author of the Sūtras states, "And because of the scriptural mention of entering," indicating that the aforementioned inference is contradicted by scripture.
He says, "And because of seeing [it].

Having made two-footed cities—human bodies and the like—and having made four-footed cities—animals—he, the Lord, becoming a bird, that is, possessing a subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), entered the cities prior to the manifestation of the eyes and other organs.
And the meaning is that even though that person has entered [the body], he remains full.
Since the Taittirīyaka mentions wings and so forth as attributes of the *liṅga* (the subtle body), it should be understood as having the nature of a bird.
Thus, because distinctions and the like are merely imagined through the state of being a reflection, he concludes his own view—that Brahman is without attributes—with the words "Therefore."
He introduces the interpretation of a certain school of thought with the words "herein":
the section beginning with "not even from the standpoint of place" (*na sthānato 'pi*) constitutes one topical section (*adhikaraṇa*);

once it has been established therein that Brahman is devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*), the second topical section, beginning with "like light" (*prakāśavad ca*), proceeds to address the doubt as to what the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman are.
Brahman is not merely of the nature of existence (*sat*), but is also of the nature of consciousness (*cit*), like light.
Why? Because of non-meaninglessness.

Since both scriptural passages—"Truth, Knowledge" and "Being alone, my dear"—are meaningful only if Brahman possesses these two forms, such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) states: [The scripture] says it is only that [existence].
The Śruti declares that Brahman is pure existence (sanmātra), because "knowledge does not exceed [the nature of] existence.
The following refutes this second position: "In this regard, we [say]..."

Regarding the second section, one might propose the following alternatives: does its fruit consist in the refutation of Brahman’s having multiple forms, or the refutation of its being of the nature of consciousness, or the refutation of its existence? Expanding upon the futility of all these positions, [the author] states that the first is redundant: "If, for a start...
He states that the second is not the case: "Nor yet..."

He says, "Or how? [meaning] that if Brahman's nature as consciousness were rejected, it would be insentient, and thus there would be a contradiction with the scriptures regarding its non-difference from the individual soul (jīva).

He says, "Nor even... [meaning] that the third alternative is not possible. And he says, "How? [meaning] that if existence itself were rejected, consciousness would become a mere nothingness (tucchatva).
Nor should it be argued that consciousness is not non-existent because it does not exceed existence;
for if the referents of the words "existent" (*sat*) and "consciousness" (*bodha*) did not exceed one another, it would follow that they are synonyms.
Having thus refuted the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) by way of the absence of its result, he refutes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "nor indeed" (*nāpi*).
He states the very consequence: "existence" (*sattā*).
"Differentiation" (*vyāvṛttatva*) means being distinct.

The meaning is that because it contradicts the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of having a single nature free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding a dual nature consisting of both [existence and differentiation] cannot arise.
He raises the objection that [the two] arise by the force of both types of scriptural revelation, stating "because it is so heard.

He replies, "No," for it is not tenable—even by a hundred scriptures—to suspect non-difference with Brahman between two cognitions of existence (*sat*) and consciousness (*bodha*), whose respective existences are mutually distinct like Mount Meru and the Vindhya mountains.
Is there a difference between existence and consciousness, or not?

It was stated that in the first case, no prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) can arise because it is impossible for even the Śruti to have a contradictory meaning. Now, he raises the second objection: "Or rather, it is existence itself" (atha sattaiva).

The meaning is that although there is a difference between the denoted meanings (vācya) of the words "Being" (sat) and "Cognition" (bodha), the identity of their indicated referents (lakṣya) is possible because of the acceptance of an indivisible meaning (akhaṇḍārtha).

The position that [the Brahmasūtras] have an indivisible meaning (akhaṇḍārtha) cannot be the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), because it is actually the established conclusion (siddhānta). Furthermore, he says "even so" (tathāpi) to show that doubt in this regard is also improper. To the question, "How are the sūtras to be interpreted if they belong to a single topic (ekādhikaraṇa)? he replies, "the sūtras" (sūtrāṇi).
He says "moreover" (*apica*) to show that there is consistency with the aphorism (*sūtra*) within his own position.

The sense is that because the subsequent aphorisms necessarily require the meaning of "going" (*gati*) and thus form a single syntactical unit with the preceding one, there is no division of the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).
He has stated his own view that for those who hear of [the Lord's] forms, the "going" consists of imagined forms.

However, those who maintain the doctrine of the dissolution of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca-vilaya-vādin*) state that the purport of scriptural passages such as "consisting of mind, having breath for its body, whose desires are true" is the dissolution of all forms other than that [Brahman].
As for the meaning of "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), it means being devoid of any limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) other than the mind.
Thus, by the phrase "the body of vital breath" (*prāṇaśarīra*), since adjuncts other than the vital breath are negated, the non-existence of the mind is also established.
Having thus restated that doctrine—that all words refer exclusively to the formless Brahman—he refutes it with the words beginning "yadapi" (as for what [has been said]).
Does the negating intent apply to words denoting form occurring in the context of the knowable Brahman, or even to those occurring in the context of meditative worship (*upāsana*)?

Therein, he accepts the first [view] with the words "ye hi" (for those which...). Regarding this Lord who has attained the state of the individual soul (*jīva*), there are ten *haris*—that is, the objects; because they carry away [the senses], they are the ten sense organs (*indriyas*). With respect to different classes of living beings, these become hundreds and thousands. Anticipating the doubt that these might be distinct from the Lord, he says "ayam" (this one), meaning that the Lord himself is the *haris*.
He refutes the second [position] with the words "But those who...

Since it is possible for words such as "mind-made" (*manomaya*) and so forth to refer primarily to qualities (*guṇa*), he states that even an indication through negation (*niṣedhalakṣaṇā*) is not appropriate, saying "And by scripture... Furthermore, since there is a twofold division of scriptural texts regarding form and formlessness, the doubt arises: "What is the determining factor (*vinigamaka*) here that Brahman is indeed formless? In response, it is stated that the determining factor is the purport of scriptures such as "not coarse" (*asthūla*) and so forth, which aims at its being formless.

For what purpose does this Sūtra become meaningful? He says, "And of all," [implying] that if all Śruti passages were intended for negation, no doubt would arise, and thus the restrictive Sūtra would be redundant. Now, one might object: since sentences whose purpose is meditation (upāsana) lack a fruit in their own right, they must be subordinate to negative statements that possess a fruit. Anticipating this, he says, "The fruit also," [meaning] that because a fruit is explicitly heard in the text, these passages are not subordinate to anything else.
And because there is no unity of purpose, there is no single sentence; thus he says, "How then?
He raises the objection regarding the unity of purpose:

"As one," meaning that just as there is a single-sentence status for the sentences concerning the subsidiaries and the primary rite due to the unity of the injunction known as the supreme apūrva which possesses a fruit, so too [is it] for one desiring the realization of reality.

The meaning is that all sentences—whether they possess a formal structure or lack one—are a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) because there exists a single object consisting of an injunction (*niyoga*) whose content is the dissolution of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
He refutes this by means of the non-establishment of the injunction with the word "no" (*na*).
He raises an objection regarding the object [of the injunction] with the words "But [is it not the case] that duality... (*nanu dvaita...*).
"Antagonistic" means an obstacle.

Now, one might object that upon the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), there would be the dissolution of Brahman as well, due to their non-difference; to this he says: "For the phenomenal world has the very nature of Brahman.
Since the cause is indeed the essential form (*svarūpa*) of the effect, the cause does not undergo dissolution even when the effect is destroyed.
The meaning is that even when the jar is destroyed, the clay is still perceived.

Having raised the alternative—that there is an injunction regarding the dissolution of the phenomenal world (prapañca), whether it be real or imagined—the author refutes the first position with the words "tatra yadi tāvat" (if, in that case, first...).

Since that which is real cannot be destroyed by knowledge alone, and since the total destruction of duality by means such as a mallet is impossible, this injunction has an unattainable object, like an injunction to swallow space.
Furthermore, the meaning is that through the liberation of Śuka and others, there would follow the liberation of everyone.
Having restated the second [position], he refutes it with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth.

The meaning is that since the dissolution of ignorance and its resulting phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is accomplished by the very knowledge born of instruction, injunction (*niyoga*) is indeed useless.
Furthermore, regarding the injunction for the knowledge of Brahman and so forth, does it apply when Brahman is unknown or when it is known?
It cannot be the first, because it would be impossible; thus he says: "But [if it were] not made known.
He raises the second alternative with: "Now, [one might object]..."

He says "no," because once Brahman is known through instruction alone, the realization [of it] and the sublation of duality are established; thus, injunctions are useless, since what is already established cannot be brought about by an injunction.

Having stated the absence of the mandate (niyoga) due to the absence of such an object, he states its absence due to the absence of a person to be enjoined (niyojya), saying "and the person to be enjoined as well.
The meaning is: whether [the person] is included within the phenomenal world (prapañca) or is Brahman itself.
In the first case, because the living self would perish, an injunction would be impossible;
in the second case, there would be no person to be enjoined.
To the question, "What then is the status of the injunctive suffixes in relation to knowledge? he says: "The words such as 'to be seen' (draṣṭavya), etc."

One might object: "Why is the injunction for the performance of the means to that [knowledge] postulated, when one could simply abandon the knowledge derived from scripture? Anticipating this, he says, "Even for one who is oriented toward the object of knowledge," because knowledge is not something to be accomplished by human effort. Furthermore, the proponent of an injunction regarding knowledge must necessarily have the object of knowledge—Brahman—made known by the Vedāntas, since an injunction cannot be understood if its object is not cognized.
Thus, since knowledge arises through the Vedāntas themselves, the injunction is redundant; this is what he expresses with the words, "Therefore."
The meaning is that it refers to one who seeks knowledge.
Now, one might argue that an injunction is meaningful for the purpose of altering knowledge once it has arisen; to this he says "no," with the words "and not."

Now, one might object that even though the cognition "a woman is not fire" arises from the means of valid perception (pratyakṣa), it is seen to be altered by an injunction such as "one should meditate on her as fire. To this he says: "If [it were so]...
If a contrary cognition were something to be accomplished through effort (kṛtisādhya), it would simply be an action (kriyā).

If there were error even without an action, then, since knowledge is not established through an injunction in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the injunction regarding knowledge—which is dependent upon the reality of the object of that cognition—is false; this is the meaning. He states "moreover" (*kiñcānyat*) to show that there is another refutation for those who maintain the existence of injunctions within the Vedāntas.

Having raised the objection that the authority of the Vedāntic statement lies in its application to the identity of Brahman and the Self, he refutes it with the words beginning "now" (*atha*), arguing that because the purpose differs, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), and because the meanings are contradictory, there is a lack of authority.

Furthermore, Brahman is what is heard [in scripture], whereas an injunction (vidhi) is not heard in the Vedāntas; moreover, if one were to postulate such an injunction, it would follow that liberation is produced by ritual action, leading to the undesirable consequences of its being non-eternal and subject to degrees of excellence. Thus he says: "And if there were a focus on an injunction" (*niyogaparatāyām*).
He states the conclusion: "Therefore" (*ataśca*).
Now, as a bold argument (*prauḍhavāda*), he accepts the injunction for the sake of argument and then refutes its unity, saying: "Even if it were admitted" (*abhyupagamyamāne 'pi*).

A word expressing a distinct action is a different word, just as "he sacrifices" (*yajati*) and "he gives" (*dadāti*); likewise here, there is a difference of words between "one knows" (*veda*) and "one meditates" (*upāsīta*).

By these means of proof—the difference in form between the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) and the qualified (*saguṇa*), the difference in context (*prakaraṇa*), and the difference in fruit between liberation (*mukti*) and worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*)—the meaning is that there is a difference in the injunctions (*niyoga*) concerning the knowledge of the attributeless and the meditation on the qualified.
How then is there unity of injunction in sentences regarding subordinate and principal elements?

To this he replies: "Let there be a single injunction" (*prayāja*). The meaning is that because a single person desiring heaven has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to both the primary rite and its subsidiaries, and because the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) resulting from what is accomplished by them is one, there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*).
Likewise here, since the knowledge of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) and the qualified (*saguṇa*) Brahman share a single entitlement, let there be a single injunction (*niyogaikyam*).
"No," he says, "but not here.

Because seekers of liberation and those seeking worldly prosperity are distinct, and because it is impossible for two types of knowledge with mutually contradictory objects to stand in the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgin*), there is no unity of application (*niyoga*).
Nor should it be argued that the application of the knowledge of the attributeless (*nirguṇa-vidyā*) is one and the same as that which accepts the knowledge of the qualified (*saguṇa-vidyā*).
"Oh, how perverse is the wisdom of the Venerable One!
To claim that injunctions apply to knowledge that is fit for obstruction, while injunctions do not apply to that which is fit for injunction—

therefore, the conclusion that sentences concerning the qualified lead to a single syntactic unity with sentences concerning the unqualified by way of the dissolution of form is simply a false position."
However, their imagined form is the "goal" because prosperity is accomplished through its worship;
whereas statements concerning the qualityless (nirguṇa) have the ultimate reality as their objective. Thus, he concludes that our stated distinction alone is more sound: "Therefore... //21//
For [the scripture] negates the finitude of that which has been previously described; thereafter, it speaks further. (BS 3.2.22)

Having stated that Brahman is pure consciousness devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣacinmātratva*), the text declares its nature as Being (*sadrūpatva*) by establishing it as the ultimate limit of all negations: "For [the scripture] negates the finitude of what has been described, and thereafter it speaks of more. Having presented two groups—the three elements of earth, water, and fire as the "formed" (*mūrta*), and the pair of air and ether as the "formless" (*amūrta*)—it identifies the essence of the formless pair of elements as the "organ-essence" (*karaṇātmā*), namely Hiraṇyagarbha: "He who is this person in the solar orb, and he who is this [person] in the right eye..."
When it was said,

"A person in the state of deep sleep," its dream-forms consisting of latent impressions were described as diverse through similes such as: "It is like saffron-dyed cloth, like a white woolen garment, like a cochineal insect."
In this context, *māhārajana* refers to turmeric; cloth dyed with it is called *māhārajana*.
*Pāṇḍu* and so forth refer to white items such as woolen blankets (*kambala*).

However, some take the scriptural mention as an illustration [of the principle] that the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are formless (*amūrta*), whereas when they are "fivefold-composed" (*pañcīkṛta*), they become formed (*mūrta*). Thus, by stating that the essence of the formless exists [in them], the fact that the sense organs (*karaṇa*) are composed of all five elements (*pāñcabhautika*) is established.
They explain as follows:
"Now," that is, immediately after the description of the manifold (prapañca) consisting of the categories of existence;
"therefore," because the purpose is the negation of the aforementioned superimposition, the instruction is performed by means of the negation "not this, not this" (neti neti)—this is the meaning.
He states the meaning of the word "not" (neti) with the words "nahi" (for not).
The meaning is that because there is nothing other than this Self, it is called "not.
According to the established doctrine, the meaning of the Śruti is that the Supreme Brahman exists in order to refute [the view of] emptiness (śūnyatā).
Here, because the specific object to be negated is not perceived, he expresses doubt with the words "In that case, what is this... and so forth.
The meaning is that the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*) negates the entity presented by the word *iti* along with its form (*ākāra*).

When the word *iti* presents the general category of the object to be negated, there arises an expectation for its specific nature; [this is supplied] from the context as being the two forms and the Brahman possessing those forms (*rūpin*).

Having stated a doubt due to the appearance of the word "niṣedhya" (that which is to be negated), he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) through the connection of an objection that the previously mentioned Brahman devoid of attributes does not exist— beginning with the words "tatra prakṛtatve" [in that context, because it is the subject under discussion]. In the prima facie view, since the referent of the term *tat* (That) would be non-existent, the identity of the sentence-meaning cannot be established.
The result [of this] is that its establishment occurs within the final doctrine (siddhānta).

With the dissatisfaction that a universal negation is not tenable because no negation is observed without a substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), he states "or rather" (*athavā*) to mean that Brahman is negated within the phenomenal world (prapañca).
He then says "but the repetition" (*abhyāsas tu*) because there would be tautology of the two negative particles (*nakāra*) if only a single Brahman were negated.
He begins the established doctrine (siddhānta), which indeed deviates from the sūtra, with the word "evam" (thus).
To one who says that the consequence of emptiness (śūnyatā) is desired, he replies with "kiñcid dhi" (for something...).
The meaning is that "tat ca" refers to the negation.

The meaning is as follows: if there were no substrate remaining, the negation-statement would not constitute valid knowledge (*pramā*), because its cause—the form of that [substrate]—would be absent; for in the world, it is observed that a negation such as "this is not here" is always a cognition accompanied by a substrate. Furthermore, regarding the general rule (*utsarga*) that "whatever appears is real," the exception (*apavāda*) is the valid cognition of the substrate, which is the object of that appearance; through this, one determines that the prior appearance was an error, thereby subverting the existence of the object. However, if one does not accept the exception, the world-phenomenon (*prapañca*) would, by the force of the general rule, result in being real, and thus negation would be untenable; hence he says: "And if nothing remains... and so forth.

Having stated that the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) is not tenable because it is impossible to negate error without a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), he refutes another position of the opponent with the words "Nor [is it]... The sense is this: while the negation of duality—which is established by worldly means of knowledge (*laukikapramāṇa*)—is appropriate, as in the case of the conceit that the body is the self, the negation of Brahman, which is known through the authority of the Vedānta, is not. Regarding the claim that Brahman is fit for negation because it transcends speech and mind, he says: "By speech and mind..."

If it is asked, "If the statement regarding Brahman's transcendence of speech and so forth is not for the purpose of negation, then for what purpose was it stated?", he says: "For the sake of establishing...
He applies the Sūtra to the stated meaning with the words beginning "That which is this...
Since the two forms alone were introduced as the primary subject in the passage, "Verily, there are two forms of Brahman," the meaning is that the negation "not this" refers to those two forms.

One might object: "Is it not the case that Brahman is also mentioned here as the primary subject in the passage, 'The Person in the solar orb'? Anticipating this, [the author] states: "The Person is the subtle body (liṅgātman)," because of the scriptural statement regarding its being the essence of the formless (amūrtarasa), which indicates it is produced from the elements, and because of the scriptural statement regarding its dream-like nature. By saying "produced from that alone," the non-difference between the form and the bearer of the form is stated. Now, one might ask: "Why is the form consisting of latent impressions (vāsanāmaya) used as a point of comparison? Why could it not be the well-known [physical] form itself? To this he says: "Of the essence of the formless.
Since these two forms alone are the primary subjects under discussion, he states the conclusion: "Therefore... (tad).
The meaning is that [the world] is presented as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).

Nor can Brahman be negated on the grounds of its being primary in meaning, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of negating the king in the statement "the king has no servant. Furthermore, since Brahman is the object to be established here, there is no negation; thus he says: "And when [the world] has been elaborated... and so forth.
Now, one might object: "Since that which is negated in Brahman could still exist elsewhere, how can it be said to be merely imagined (kalpita)? To this he says: "Its locus is that" (tadāspadam).
The meaning is that what is negated in the material cause cannot exist elsewhere.
As for the claim that the negation of duality contradicts perception and other means of knowledge—
Regarding this, he says, "And it is logical.

For it was established in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* that the validity of perception and the other means of knowledge is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*) and not a revealer of ultimate reality (*tattvāvedaka*);
therefore, since there is a negation [of these means] from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no contradiction—this is the intended meaning.
[Objection: "Surely, since it is an entity (*vastu*), let there be a negation of Brahman as well, just as there is of duality.
[Reply: He says "not so" (*na tu*).
The meaning is that because Brahman is the witness (*sākṣin*) of both the existence and non-existence of duality, its negation is impossible.
The passage beginning with "na ca" has a clear meaning.
Regarding what was stated—that by means of two negations both form (*rūpa*) and the possessor of form (*rūpin*), as well as Brahman, are negated—he says: "And these two... [and so forth].

The principle that "there is a sequential correspondence between the number of subjects and predicates" is established by Pāṇini’s sūtra *yathāsaṅkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām*; therefore, the meaning here is that two prohibitions are enjoined with reference to the two forms [of Brahman]. Regarding the alternative view of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), he states the distinction—that through the negation of all perceivable things, the desire to know is stilled—by saying "enumerated," etc.
The meaning is that when one negates by specifying "it is neither the formed (mūrta) nor the formless (amūrta)," the desire to know does not cease.
He explains the remainder of the Sūtra with the words "for this reason also" (itaśca).

The meaning is that since negation would otherwise be untenable, it is understood that Brahman exists; furthermore, the Śruti declares directly that there is something beyond [the formed and the formless].
"And that" means the remaining Brahman;
the rest is clear. //22//
For it says that this is unmanifest. (BS 3.2.23)
He explains the Sūtra—"That which is not prohibited [from being perceived]"—in order to dispel the doubt that Brahman does not exist because it is ungraspable.
The meaning is that it is unmanifest and ungraspable by the senses due to the absence of form and other qualities, but not because of non-existence.
The grammatical construction is: "It is not grasped by other gods," that is, by other sense organs. //23//
Moreover, regarding the attainment [of the goal], it is established by both direct perception and inference. (BS 3.2.24)
Then, explaining the sūtra as an answer to the doubt of when [He] is to be grasped, he says: "And moreover, this...
The word "and" (api) has the sense of "but" (tu).
The meaning is that He is not grasped by the senses, but rather by means of *saṃrādhana*—that is, by a mind refined through the scriptures.

*Praṇidhāna* is the firm placement or fixing of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) within the mind through devotion and meditation; the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to recitation, salutation, and other such acts. *Svayambhū* is the Lord (*īśvara*).
He made his own sense-faculties turn away [from their objects] and, having done so, he pierced them—that is, he destroyed them.
For their destruction consists in their being created as apprehenders of non-existent objects; therefore, they were created by him in that manner.
The entire world perceives only the external object, not the inner Self.

However, a certain wise and intelligent person—whose vision is turned inward and whose senses are restrained—perceives the inner Self within the pure mind by means of the scripture; this is the meaning of being a seeker of liberation (*mokṣārthin*).
Thereafter, with a mind purified by action, meditating through the excellence of the quality of *sattva* known as knowledge, he perceives that partless [Self]; this is the meaning.
They are sleepless and free from darkness;
the cause for this is the mastery over breath and dedication to *prāṇāyāma*.
Those who are practicing are meditators; the Self attainable through yoga is the "Yoga-Self. //24//
And there is no difference [between the Lord and the individual soul], as in the case of light and so forth; and light [is manifested] in action through practice. (BsRp 3.2.25)

Just as light and other phenomena appear to differ according to their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) but not by themselves, so too the conscious self (*cidātman*), though luminous, appears to differ due to limiting adjuncts such as the act of meditation; yet in itself it is without distinction and of a single essence. This is established through the practice of the instruction "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). Such is the application of the Sūtra. //25//
Therefore, [the Self is] with the Infinite; for thus is the indicative mark. (BS 3.2.26)

The author of the Sūtras states that even from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the scriptural declaration of the fruit—the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman—the difference is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*): "Therefore, [the soul is] with the infinite" (Sūtra 2.3.26).
But because of the designation of both [aspects], it is like a serpent and its coils (ahikuṇḍalavat). (BS 3.2.27)
"Or [it is] like light and its substrate, because it is luminous.

(BBs 3.2.28) He states the connection between these two sūtras, which present the prima facie views regarding difference and non-difference, with the words "In that very same... Non-difference exists by virtue of being contained within it.

Just as there is difference in the state of a serpent known as a "coil" by virtue of its being coiled, so too there is non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) with respect to Brahman, while there is difference with respect to its nature as a jīva.

Alternatively, just as there is both difference and non-difference between the sun and its light based on the delimitation of the single attribute of being luminosity, so too difference and non-difference must be accepted for the individual soul and the Supreme Self through the single attribute of selfhood (ātmatva), on the strength of scriptural authority; such is the meaning of the two sūtras.
The state of being an earring is the state of having a circular shape;

the state of being curved is the state of having a bent shape; the state of being tall is the state of having the shape of a long staff; and "having an elevated face" is the meaning of the word "and so forth. // 27 // // 28 //
Or it is as before. (BBs 3.2.29)
And because of the prohibition [of such a position].
This is a *siddhāntasūtra*: "As before.

If one accepts both difference and non-difference through a distinction of properties (*dharmabheda*) or through a single property (*ekadharma*), then because difference would be real, there would be no cessation of it, just as with non-difference. If one accepts both difference and non-difference in one and the same thing, the very discourse on contradiction in the world would be destroyed.
Thus it should also be viewed;

therefore, it is established that Brahman, which is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca) and consists of the single essence of consciousness (cidekarasa), exists as the indicated meaning (lakṣya) of the word "That" (tat). // 29 // // 30 //
[The Brahman] is higher than that [the individual soul], because of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and distinction. (BS 3.2.31)
As for the claim that the Śrutis, such as "not this, not this" (neti neti), negate any entity other than Brahman,
that is incorrect;
he objects to this by stating "according to the view of others," on the grounds that the existence of other entities is indicated by Śrutis concerning the bridge (setu) and so forth.

Although the word "bridge" (*setu*) was explained as being used figuratively in the sense of a "supporter" in the *Dyubhvādyadhikaraṇa*, this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises from one who does not understand the resolution of the scriptural texts concerning measurement (*unmāna*) and so forth; for in that case, the texts on measurement and the like are taken in their primary sense, leading to the conclusion (*siddhānta*) that Brahman is dualistic. The distinction, however, is that in the final view, there is established the realization of the non-dual reality indicated by the term *tat* (That) as previously described.
Brahman is dual, because it is a bridge, like a worldly bridge.
He says "having crossed the bridge" because of the scriptural mention of having "crossed over.

According to the statement of physicians that "jāṅgala" is a place abounding in wind, *jāṅgala* refers to a region where wind is predominant; however, in this context, it should be understood as referring to the region itself.
The four quarters are the *kalā* [of the first foot] named "Possessing Light" (*prakāśavat*);
earth, intermediate space, heaven, and the ocean are the foot named "Endless" (*anantavat*);
fire, sun, moon, and lightning are the foot named "Luminous" (*jyotiṣmat*).
The name "possessing abodes" refers to the eye, ear, speech, and mind; "four-footed" means Brahman has four feet; "eight-hoofed" means its half-feet are eight;
and "sixteen-parted" means there are four parts (*kalā*) in each of the four feet—this is the meaning.
Just as sixteen *paṇas* of copper are known by the name *kārṣāpaṇa*, so too is Brahman of two-fold nature.
The meaning is "because it is limited.
And because it possesses a connection, he says "likewise, by way of connection," as in the case of a city.
"The other is immeasurable" means it is uncountable.
It should be understood that this is because there is a rule of limitation due to the smallness [of the eye] when compared to other points of contact (*anyasparśa*).
Furthermore, he says "and because it is designated as distinct, like a jar" (*bhedavyapadeśaśca*),
meaning that this [Self] residing in the eye is distinct from that [Self] residing in the sun.
Having explained the distinction [of the path] by way of its basis and its extension, he states it also by way of its limit: "And it has a limit" (sāvadhikam). //31//
But on account of similarity. (BS 3.2.32)
He explains the *siddhāntasūtra* with the words beginning "by the word 'tu' (*but*)":
"As for that which is other [than Brahman], is it beginningless or has it a beginning?

Not the first, because there is a lack of evidence and because an effect is non-different from Brahman and devoid of qualities"—having stated this, he says, "Nor is it the second, because of the determination of non-duality prior to creation," by the words "nor anything distinct from Brahman."
The sense is that the aforementioned inferences are sublated by scripture (*āgama*).
Having recalled what was stated, he declares the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reasons with the words beginning "nanu setu" (But [is it] by the scriptural mention of a 'bridge'...).
Does the establishment of the other [world] result from the scriptural mention of a 'bridge,' or rather from the implied meaning (*artha*)?
Having stated "not this," he raises a second doubt with the words "therein, in the other.
He says "nor indeed" because it is improper to subvert the scriptural teaching of non-duality by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being a "bridge.
Furthermore, he states that the indicative mark is unestablished with the words "moreover."
The intention is that the state of being a support (vidhārakatva) is indeed logical even with respect to a second [entity] that is merely imagined.
He states, "having crossed the bridge," to show that the reason [adduced for Brahman's non-difference], namely its state of having already crossed over, is also unestablished (asiddha). //32//
The term "for the sake of cognition" (buddhy-artha) is like [the term] "foot" (pāda). 3,2.33.
He states that its limited nature is also unestablished with the words "buddhyartha" (for the purpose of the intellect).

Just as speech, breath, sight, and hearing are the feet of the mind; and fire, wind, the sun, and the quarters are the feet of space—these being imagined for the sake of meditation—in the same way, this is the measurement of Brahman.
He provides a worldly illustration with the words "or else."
To the question, "Why should there not be conventional usage even without the postulation of quarters? he says: "Not so" (na hi).

Just as the quarter of a kārṣāpaṇa is postulated for the sake of conventional usage, the measurement of Brahman is postulated for the sake of the conventional usage of meditation by those of dull intellect; such is the meaning. //33//
[The difference in experience] is due to the difference in location, as in the case of light and so forth. (BS 3.2.34)
He states that the distinctions of relation and locus are merely imagined and do not establish the reality of a second [entity], beginning with the word "sthāna" (locus).

"Locus" refers to limiting adjuncts such as the intellect and so forth. When a single entity appears divided by its limiting adjuncts, the relation [of identity] is figuratively attributed to it once those adjuncts have ceased.

Just as the light of the sun and so forth, appearing divided by limiting adjuncts such as a finger, is figuratively attributed the relation of being a "great light" when separated from those adjuncts, so too, because of the difference between the two loci—the sun and the eye—the distinction of the Golden Person (*hiraṇmayapuruṣa*) is imagined. This is the meaning.
And because it is logical. (BS 3.2.35)
To the question, "Why should not the two primary types of relationship themselves be the distinct [meanings]? the Sūtra states: "And because it is logical" (upapatteśca) //35//.
Likewise, because there is a prohibition of others. (BsRp_3,2.7.36)

The connection of the individual soul with Brahman by way of its own essential nature consists in the cessation of difference; it is not a primary relation such as conjunction, because two distinct entities do not exist. Likewise, difference itself does not exist inherently, because of the scriptural teaching of oneness. This is the meaning.
By this [reasoning], its omnipresence is established on account of the words "extent" (*āyāma*) and so forth.
Now, one might object: "If there is no second [entity], does this not contradict the scriptural teaching of omnipresence? To this he says: "By this, its omnipresence [is established].
If the second were real, Brahman would be limited, like a bridge or similar things, according to the scripture: "That wherein one sees another—that is limited."

Furthermore, the meaning is that since it is impossible for the partless and unattached Brahman to have a connection with a real world-phenomenon (*prapañca*), there would be a contradiction for you alone with the scriptural texts concerning its omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*).
This is the logical principle (*nyāya*): the superimposed world is pervaded by its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) because it is superimposed, just as a snake [is pervaded] by a rope. //37//
The fruit [arises] from Him, because that is logical. (BS 3.2.38)
Having thus clarified the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) of that term, he states the literal meaning (vācyārtha): "The fruit [arises] from Him, because it is logical.
Because He is devoid of distinctions, His other nature—known as the cause of fruits—is such that the desired is happiness for gods and others, while the undesired is suffering for those in hell.

"Mixed" refers to that which has for its sphere (gocara) or basis (āśraya) the cycle of birth and death—the stream of births and deaths—that belongs to human beings; thus, it is "having the cycle of existence as its sphere.
Here, a doubt is raised—beginning with "What [is it]?"—because of the scriptural statements regarding both karma and the Lord as causes of the fruit.

In this context, the difference in results is as follows: in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the Lord—who is the giver of fruits and is denoted by the word "That" (*tatpada*)—is not established, the object of indication (*lakṣya*) is not established; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), that [Lord] is established.

As for the connection (*saṃgati*): since the prima facie view arises based on the previously stated attributelessness (*nirviśeṣatva*) [of Brahman], it argues that even the status of being the giver of fruits does not belong to the Lord.

Although the status of being the giver of fruits, like omnipresence, is established during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra-dashā*), nevertheless, [the opponent holds that] it is from karma alone [that results arise].

Thinking that this section (adhikaraṇa) is commenced for the purpose of determining the expressed meaning—which sustains the indicated meaning—by dispelling the doubt as to whether [the Veda] is the giver of fruits, he first states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "In that regard, first...
[He argues that] heaven and so forth must have a giver who is cognizant of specific places, times, and actions.
The logical argument is that [the action] is the fruit of the action, just like the fruit of service.
First, the action known as the performance of sacrifice and so forth is momentary; does it produce the fruit from its own destruction, or does it perish after having produced the fruit?
Or rather, is the accomplishment of the fruit from something previously non-existent?
He says "no" to the first case with the word "abhāvāt" (due to non-existence).
He raises the second possibility with "syāt" (it might be).

He refutes [the opponent's view] with the words "that too" (*tad api*) and so forth, on the grounds that there is no proof for the existence of heaven, pleasure, and so forth, which remain unmanifest from the moment the karma perishes.
He raises a third objection with the word "now" (*atha*):
does the *apūrva* (unseen force) act independently to bestow the fruit?
Or [is it] presided over by volition?
Regarding the first case, he says "that too" (tad api).

As for the second case, the point is that since a soul that is unperceived and lacks supernormal knowledge cannot logically be a presiding agent, the existence of God as the presiding agent is established.
He states that there is no such thing as the *apūrva* through a bold argument: "In its existence... [and so forth].
If it is argued that the permanent *apūrva* is established because momentary acts such as sacrifices cannot logically be the causes of heaven and other results as taught in scripture, we say: no.
The meaning is that the result is accomplished solely from the Lord (*Īśvara*), who is permanent and propitiated by those very actions.
The meaning is that the unprecedented (apūrva) is not established by mere reasoning alone. //38//
And because it is so stated in scripture. (BS 3.2.39)

If the existence of *apūrva* (unseen merit/demerit) is established by the scriptural and traditional texts cited under the sūtra "He possesses residual karma upon the exhaustion of [past] deeds"— namely, "Those who here have performed pleasant conduct," and so forth— then the author of the sūtras states "And because it is heard [in scripture]" (*śrutatvācca*) that the Lord's status as the bestower of fruits must likewise be accepted.
He is the "Eater of Food" (*annāda*), meaning he gives food completely to all living beings, and the "Giver of Wealth" (*vasudāna*), meaning the giver of riches.

Since karma or the *apūrva* is insentient and thus merely an instrument, it has been shown that the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the Lord alone is the independent bestower of results. //39//
Jaimini [maintains that] dharma [is the purpose of the Vedas], for that very reason.
Now he presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "dharma" and so on.
The scriptural injunction (*vidhiśruti*) has the injunction as its meaning;

the sacrifice is the object (*viṣaya*) of that injunctive sense (*liṅ-artha*), which consists of an impulsion (*preraṇā*). From the comprehension of that [sacrifice] as being [the object], it is understood that the sacrifice is the means to heaven.
The meaning is that if the sacrifice lacks the status of being a means to achieve the desired end, then instigation (preraṇā) would be untenable.
Having stated that the fruit of the action is established by way of the *apūrva*, he refutes the established position (*siddhānta*) with the words "But as for God" (*īśvarastu*).
Does God bestow the fruit independently of the action, or in dependence upon it?
The first [objection] says "of that which is non-variegated," and so forth.

Regarding the second [objection], the point is: since the fruit is established from the unseen merit (*apūrva*) alone—just as the act of wrapping occurs on a mat and such through the mere impression of wrapping—what is the need for God?

To this we reply: if pleasure and the like could arise simply from the perceived excellence of sandalwood, thorns, and so forth, then there would be no need for dharma and adharma; however, since there is a dependence upon those two by virtue of the authority of Śruti and Smṛti, what wrong has God done?
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the fruit [of action] arises from karma alone, independent of God. //40//
But Bādarāyaṇa holds the former view, because of the designation of a reason. (BS 3.2.41)
He provides the final conclusion: "But previously...

Since it is impossible for insentient karma to act of its own accord, and since the scriptural texts following the analogies of service and so forth are more authoritative, and because all Vedānta texts declare that the Lord is the cause of the world, the general meaning is that the accomplishment of results included within the world proceeds from karma presided over by the Lord. //41//

Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda.
Thus ends the second quarter (pāda) of the third chapter, titled "The Purification of the Meanings of the Words *tat* and *tvam*.
Now begins the third quarter of the third chapter:
[I bow] to Mārtaṇḍa for the destruction of darkness, and to Tilakasvāmin for my delight.
I bow down again and again to Vighneśa for the destruction of obstacles.
START BsRp_3,3.1.1ḥ:

*sarvavedāntapratyayaṃ codanādyaviśeṣāt* (BBs_3,3.1). Having determined the nature of Brahman, [the author] states the nature of the meditation that is the means for knowing it: "The cognition [of Brahman] is the same in all Vedāntas, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth."
He states the connection between the chapters with the words "it has been explained.
In the preceding chapter, the discrimination between the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam* was performed;

here, the fruit thereof—the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence—is determined by the sūtra "Bliss and so forth belong to the Principal," through the synthesis of the meaning expressed by the term *tat*, which was required and not yet repeated. Thus, there is a relationship of cause and effect (*phala-phalibhāva*).
Association:

It should be understood that the contemplation of the meaning of sentences concerning the qualities (*saguṇa*) is performed because it serves as a means to the knowledge of the qualityless (*nirguṇa*), by way of one-pointedness of mind for those who possess such knowledge.
Concordance.

Thinking that the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa-jñāna) has been described as being within the scope of an inquiry into difference and non-difference, he raises an objection with the word "nanu" (but/however).

The meaning is: an inquiry into the distinction between meditations (vidyā-bheda) would be appropriate if there were a distinction among the objects of knowledge (vedya-bheda); however, since the object of knowledge—Brahman—is one, there is no occasion for such an inquiry.
To the objection that even if Brahman is one, an inquiry might still occur due to a distinction in its attributes (dharma-bheda), he replies: "And because of its uniform nature" (ekarūpatvāt ca).
The meaning is that [Brahman] is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmatva*).
Since there might be a suspicion of difference because various modes could possibly exist even within a Brahman of a single form, he says "nor... and so forth.

Having stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) the impossibility of suspecting a difference in knowledge, he says "nor is this... and so forth, to show that the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—that there is no difference in knowledge because of the non-difference of the injunctions (*codanā*) and so on—is also untenable.
Having thus raised an objection regarding the commencement of the section, he provides the resolution: "That is being stated.

It should be understood that the investigation into difference and non-difference is conducted only with respect to meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇavidyā*); however, since unity is established in the case of the unqualified meditation (*nirguṇavidyā*), only the collection of qualities in the form of the literal meaning of the words is performed for the sake of determining the meaning of the sentence.

Thus, it will be stated in the sūtra "On account of the difference of words and so forth, they are manifold" (*nānāśabdādibhedāt*) that the Pañcāgni, Prāṇa, Dahara, Śāṇḍilya, Vaiśvānara, and other such meditations are mutually distinct.

In this case, however, since those [vidyās] are mutually distinct, a doubt arises as to whether they differ according to each Vedic branch (*śākhā*) or not, on account of differences in name and so forth, and because of the non-difference of the injunctions (*codanā*) and other factors.

The difference in result is that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), due to the difference of the vidyās, there is no combination of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*); whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), due to their non-difference, there is such combination. In the *Pūrvatantṛ*, the prima facie sūtra of the section concerning different branches states: "There is a difference of ritual action (*karmabheda*) in another branch because of differences in name, form, and specific duties; because of repetition; because of censure; because of incapacity; because of completion; because of statements regarding expiation; and because of the observation of something else."
It might be so.

In that regard, the reasons already mentioned—namely, name and so forth—are stated here for the purpose of distinguishing the Vidyās. For instance, in the passage, "Now this is the Jyotis; now this is the Sarvajyotis;

with this [sacrifice] involving a thousand-fold dakṣiṇā one should sacrifice," one might suspect that there is an injunction of the quality known as the "thousand-fold dakṣiṇā" by way of a restatement (anuvāda) of the previously mentioned Jyotiṣṭoma.

Since it is possible for the word *jyotis* to be the name of a distinct ritual action—and because it is therefore impossible for it to merely indicate the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, as well as because the word *atha* (now) marks a break in the context—it is established that a distinct ritual action with specific sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) is enjoined, separate from the *Jyotiṣṭoma*; thus, it is stated that a name serves as a differentiator of rituals.

By the phrase "in the case of *jyotis* and so forth," the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) is intended to include cases where a difference in ritual is understood from a difference in designation (*saṃjñā*), such as *ādhvaryavam* and *hautram*.
Heated milk solidified with curds is *āmikṣā*;

therein, the liquid portion in the form of water is the *vājina*. This is the distinction [between them] in the context of the Vaiśvadeva-āmikṣā sacrifice, as stated in the passage: "One pours curds into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas, and the *vājina* for the Vājins."

Having raised the objection that "vājibhyaḥ" (to the Vājins) might be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) for those already mentioned as the Viśvedevas, the Siddhāntin concludes that there is a difference between the two rites due to a difference in their essential character (*rūpa*), namely the substance and the deity. This is because it is impossible to refer back (*anuvāda*) to the Viśvedevas—who were mentioned as being subordinate to the *āmikṣā*—by means of the term "vājibhyaḥ. Furthermore, since the ritual act is already occupied by the *āmikṣā* prescribed at its origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), an injunction for a substance like *vājina* (curd-whey), which is not required, would be illogical. Therefore, the sacrifice with *vājina* and the deity Vājin is established as a distinct rite (*karmāntara*).
From the first word [of the sūtra], one should understand that a difference in sacrifice arises from a difference in substance, as in the case of "curds for Indra" and "milk for Indra.
Likewise here, there is a difference in knowledge (vidyā) between the Vājasaneyins and the Chāndogyas due to the difference in form, namely five fires versus six fires.

Similarly, there is a difference in the knowledge of the vital breaths (prāṇavidyā), because in the Chāndogya the speech and other organs are deficient of semen, whereas among the Vājasaneyins they are accompanied by it.
In the study of the *Kārīrī* texts, the Taittirīyakas have the specific duty (*dharma*) of eating on the ground, whereas others do not;

in the study of the fire-rituals (*agny-adhyayana*), some have the duty of fetching water for the sake of the teacher, while others do not; and in the study of the *Aśvamedha*, only some have the duty of bringing fodder for the horse, while others do not.
Furthermore, it is not logical that those very same rituals, such as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice and others, should sometimes depend on a specific merit (*dharma*) and sometimes not;

therefore, a difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*) is suspected in different recensional branches (*śākhā*) due to such a difference in merit. Likewise, in this case as well, because some alone observe a vow consisting of carrying a vessel of coals on the head during the study of the *Muṇḍaka*, while others do not, there would be a difference in knowledge (*vidyābheda*).
Repetition (*punarukti*) constitutes repetition (*abhyāsa*).

Just as the distinction between the *prayāja* offerings is stated through the repetition of the verb "he sacrifices" in the passage, "He sacrifices to the fuel-sticks; he sacrifices to Tanūnapāt," so too, from the repetition [of the same instruction] in another recensional branch (*śākhā*), there is a distinction between the meditations (*vidyā*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), censure and other such factors are included, as in the case of the pre-dawn oblation: "In the morning, they speak untruth who offer the *agnihotra* before sunrise."

Furthermore, there is a distinction [between the two views] because of the scriptural censure of the offering made after sunrise: "If one were to offer in the morning when the sun has risen, it would be just as if one were to bring food to a guest who has arrived at an empty dwelling";
for it is impossible for a single act to be performed both after sunrise and before sunrise.

Likewise, even from the performance of expiation for the transgression of the *uditānudita-homa* (the fire-oblation performed either after sunrise or before), a distinction in the *agnihotra* itself was suspected.
These instances of censure and expiation do not exist in the case of the Vedāntic knowledges, and thus they are not cited as examples.

Just as there is a distinction [of duties] due to the inability to know or perform a rite prescribed in all the Vedic branches (*śākhās*), so too there is a distinction between the various Vedāntic knowledges due to the inability to study and understand all the Vedāntas.

Just as it might be argued that the conclusion of all the Vedic branches (*śākhā*) is not stated to be uniform, but rather that the conclusion of a particular branch occurs at a particular point in a specific ritual act—
and thus, due to these differences in the statements of conclusion, a difference in ritual acts (*karmabheda*) is suspected for each branch— so too,
because one Vedānta text concludes with the all-pervasiveness of the syllable *Oṃ* while another concludes with something else, there would be a difference in the meditative knowledge (*vidyābheda*).

The reasons stated in the *pūrvapakṣa* sūtra—that "the perception of another purpose constitutes an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and that due to the difference in such passages there is a difference in knowledge (*vidyā*) just as there is a difference in ritual acts (*karman*)"—have been shown; some of these are employed here both in the *siddhānta* and in the *pūrvapakṣa*.

Likewise, [the six means of differentiating ritual acts]—difference of word (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), context (*prakriyā*), and name (*nāmadheya*)—are the factors that differentiate ritual acts.
