In that context, the triad of name, quality, and form has been explained. Just as a difference in ritual action (*karman*)—specifically the *bhāvanā* delimited by the meaning of the verbal root—is stated through differences in the verbal roots (*prakṛti*) such as "one should sacrifice," "one should give," and "one should offer oblations," so too here, a difference in knowledge (*vidyā*) arises from the difference in words such as "one knows" (*veda*) and "one meditates upon" (*upāsate*). Furthermore, just as there is a difference in ritual action due to number—as in "he offers three oblations"—there would likewise be a difference in the Saṃvarga-vidyā due to the number two, as in "Vāyu and Prāṇa."

In the context of the obligatory *agnihotra*, another *agnihotra* is heard of in a different section regarding the *kuṇḍapāyinām ayana* sacrifice, namely: "They perform the *agnihotra* for a month. Because it is situated in a different section, this *agnihotra* is a distinct ritual act;

likewise, here, due to the difference in sections within the various Vedāntas, there is a difference between the two [texts]. This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). He establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the word "evam" (thus).

The term *sarvavedāntapratyayāni* means those which are recognized by all Vedānta texts; the meaning is that they are enjoined by them. Since a difference among rites such as the Agnihotra would appear to arise for each branch (*śākhā*) due to the aforementioned names and so forth, there is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the section on different branches (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*), stated in the sūtra: "Or rather, it is one [rite], because there is no difference in connection, form, injunction, and name. In this context, *codanā* refers either to the injunctive word or to the effort enjoined.
He states the non-distinction between them with the words "just as in one [case]," etc.
The meaning is that because there is a unity of effort delimited by the oblation for the sake of a single element (dhātu), there is a unity of the effort of meditation.

Just as the knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇa-vidyā) characterized by qualities such as being the eldest is one and the same across all Vedic branches, so too the knowledge of the five fires (pañcāgni-vidyā) is one, due to the lack of distinction in its connection with the result and other factors.
Likewise, he states that the other [knowledge] is also distinct by saying, "In this way, [there are] five fires.
He refutes the reasons for the prima facie view with the words, "But those who...
It is not logical that there is a difference in ritual action based on names such as "The Kaṭhaka" and so forth.

Why? Because words such as *Kāṭhaka* and others do not denote an injunction (*codanā*), but rather function as names of texts; thus, they lack the status of denoting the ritual action itself. Therefore, even though there are differences between the textual branches (*śākhā*) that bear distinct names, the ritual action prescribed by them is one and the same. Even a slight difference in form does not contradict the unity of the action. Furthermore, specific properties (*dharma-viśeṣa*) are auxiliary to the study of the text, not auxiliary to the ritual action; therefore, they do not differentiate the action. As for the repetition [of mantras] across different branches, that is unestablished [as a fault].

Even the presence of censure (nindā) and the perception of different purposes (anyārthadarśana) do not constitute grounds for differentiation, because they merely serve as praise or injunctions for specific rites. Furthermore, even when one lacks the capacity to study multiple recensional branches (śākhās), it is possible to obtain from another branch whatever specific details required by one's own branch are not mentioned therein; thus, incapacity does not cause differentiation. Moreover, even in a single ritual act, expiation is possible for the omission of auxiliary parts (aṅgas). Likewise, differences in the statements regarding completion (samāpti) are also irrelevant. Thus, the meaning is that while the means of proof for the non-differentiation of the ritual act are powerful, the causes for differentiation have been refuted. //1//
If it is argued that [the Lord] is not [the cause] because of differences [in the effects], we say no; for even in a single [cause], such differences exist. (BS 3.2)

If it is argued that, by the very logic of different recensions (*śākhāntara*), the unity of the meditation (*vidyaikya*) is established just as there is unity of action (*karmaikyavat*), and thus repetition [of the teaching] is redundant, he says: "In this case also. The distinction lies in the fact that the form [of the meditation] is prescribed at the time of its origination (*utpattiśiṣṭatva*). There might be a difference in the meditations due to the difference in forms—such as the five fires (*pañcāgni*) and so on—found in the originative injunctions (*utpattividhi*) for the meditations, just as there is a difference in rituals due to the difference in forms such as *āmikṣā* and *vājina*; therefore, [the present passage] is not for the purpose of mere repetition, but rather for the purpose of dispelling such an additional doubt.
Anticipating the objection that this section (*adhikaraṇa*) involves a redundancy, he explains the doubt with the words beginning "It might be" (*syāt*).

It should be understood that because this is a separate treatise (*śāstra*), and because the principles of ritual action (*karman*) are difficult to apply to mental meditations (*mānasavidyā*) without a formal aphorism (*sūtra*), there is not even a scent of redundancy.

Now, one might argue: "The fire belonging to the final oblation (*antyeṣṭi*), which is the sixth [fire] mentioned by the followers of the *Vājasaneyi* (the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*) as if it were well-known for the purpose of cremating the deceased—that [fire] is to be incorporated into the *Chāndogya* [Upaniṣad]; thus, there is no difference in form (*rūpabheda*)."

Regarding this, he says: "And not here. Let it be that for the Vājasaneyins there is the insertion (*āvāpa*) of semen possessing the quality of procreation, and for the Chāndogyas its removal (*udvāpa*); what follows from that? To this he replies with "āvāpa... and so forth. Having conceded the absence of the sixth fire in the Chāndogya, he refutes [the objection] by stating "This is not so," etc., on the grounds that a minor difference in form does not contradict the identity of the knowledge (*vidyā*).
He abandons his initial position, stating: "It is also recited thus.
The meaning is that when one has departed from this world to another desired world after death, the kinsmen offer [the oblation] to Agni.

An objection is raised: "In the Chāndogya, only Agni is heard of, whereas by the Vājasaneyins, specific details such as the fuel (samit) and so forth are recited; thus, the difference in form remains as it was."
Regarding this, he says: "But the Vājasaneyins...

The meaning is that since the sixth fire and its specific details are merely restatements (anuvāda) and are therefore not objects of meditation, only the five fires are to be meditated upon in both [texts]; thus, there is no difference in form.
He further states, "Even though... to show that even if the sixth fire with its specific details were an object of meditation, there would still be no difference in form.

The meaning is that the fivefold nature of the five fires—such as the heavenly world and so forth—which are established by the very injunction for the attainment of the state of fire, is merely restated (anūdyate) as a matter of course; it is not enjoined as an object of meditation.

Furthermore, having stated that the Chāndogyas should incorporate the semen mentioned in the Vājasaneyaka branch, he says "nor [is there a difference] because of addition" (na cāvāpa), meaning that even in the absence of such incorporation, there is no difference in the knowledge (vidyā). //2//

For the same reason as for the private recitation of the Veda, and because of the qualification [for study] in the *Samācāra*, there is a restriction regarding that [recitation], just like the *Sava* sacrifice. (BBs 3.3.3)

Having stated thus that a difference in form does not constitute a difference in knowledge, he says "of the private recitation" (*svādhyāyasya*) to show that even a difference in ritual detail (*dharmaviśeṣa*) does not constitute a difference [in the knowledge].

The meaning is that the *śirovrata* (the head-vow), prescribed in the *sūtra* of the Ātharvaṇikas as a subsidiary part of their study—just like the *godāna* rite—is not a subsidiary part of the knowledge (*vidyā*).
He explains [the phrase] "and because of the context" (*adhikārāt*) with the words "not this... (*naitat*).

This is the subject at hand: the meaning is that the head-vow (*śirovrata*) is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the study of the *Muṇḍaka*, because of the scriptural statement, "A man who has not performed the head-vow does not study this [text].
Now, one might object: "But is it not the case that this vow is also heard of as being an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*)? [The author responds:
If there were only one single knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) across all recensional branches (*śākhā*), then the vow associated with that knowledge would also apply everywhere.
The meaning is that there is no connection [between the two], and thus there is a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*).

He refutes this by saying "No," on the grounds that the word "this" (*etad*)—referring to what is expressed in the present text—indicates that the term "knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*) pertains to the text concerning the manifestation of Brahman.
Regarding the rule that the "head-vow" (*śirovrata*) must be observed during the study of the *Muṇḍaka*, the phrase "as in the case of the *Sava*" is cited as an illustrative example.

The meaning is that all oblations are to be performed in that single fire which is prescribed by the Atharvans in their own Sūtra as being well-known under the designation of "the one seer" (ekarṣi). Thus it is restricted. //3//
And scripture also demonstrates this. (BBs 3.3.4)

Furthermore, the Sūtrakāra states, "And it shows," meaning that the Śruti demonstrates the identity of the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇabrahmavidyā*) through the identity of the object of knowledge (*vedyaikyena*); and because they are recited in proximity to that, he says that the identity of the knowledges of the qualified Brahman (*saguṇavidyā*) across all Vedic branches is also established. He says, "In the same way," meaning that it shows the one qualified [Brahman] to be the object of knowledge in the three Vedas as well.

Furthermore, he states that the reference to the categories mentioned in one branch [of the Veda] as established facts in another branch demonstrates the identity of the knowledge (*vidyaikya*), by means of the passage beginning with "Thus, a great terror...

When this person perceives even a slight interval—that is, a difference—within this non-dual reality, then for him there certainly arises the fear of *saṃsāra*; for to that wise man who perceives duality, that very Brahman becomes terrifying.
The meaning is: "of one who contemplates, 'I am indeed Brahman'.

He says "so it is" (*tathā*) to show that the meditation on [the sun] as being "a span in size" is presented as an established fact, thereby demonstrating the identity of this meditation with the Vaiśvānara-vidyā.

Furthermore, because terms such as *uktha* and others are perceived in all the Vedāntas, it is understood from this reason that those mentioned in one place are taken up for the purpose of meditation in another.

Therefore, he says "tathā" (likewise), meaning that because the meditations upon those [elements] are also based on the authority of all the Vedāntas, their identity is established for the most part, just as the identity of the knowledge of Brahman is established;
the sense is that there is an identity of the Uktha-vidyā and so forth. //4//
And [the meditation] is the same in the case of a common [object], because there is no difference in meaning, as in the case of supplementary injunctions (*vidhiśeṣa*). (BS 3.3.5)

He states the result of the inquiry into the unity of knowledge across all recensions with the words: "The combination. When there is a doubt as to whether the qualities heard in relation to an identical knowledge in different recensions are restricted to their respective texts, or whether those not heard in one place must be combined from other recensions—the conclusion is that even though the knowledge is one, the benefit of that knowledge is accomplished by the very qualities mentioned in each respective place.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the qualities are established according to the division of Vedic branches (*śākhābheda*); the consequence (*phala*) of this is that the inquiry into the unity of the knowledge under discussion would be fruitless.
He explains the aphorism as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words beginning "And when [the unity] is established," and so forth.
The meaning is that because qualities are inseparable from the possessor of qualities, this knowledge residing in one branch possesses the qualities of the knowledge mentioned in other branches,
since it is non-different from them— just like that [other] knowledge; thus, through this inference, the integration of qualities is established when there is unity of knowledge.

Regarding the inclusion of various auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) when the primary element (*pradhāna*) is one and the same, he provides an illustration with the phrase "like the remainder of an injunction" (*vidhiśeṣavat*). He states the very same point by way of contrast with the words "for if... (*yadi hīti*). Now, one might object: "Just as qualities (*guṇa*) restricted to the Āgneya sacrifice are extended to the Saura sacrifice—which is not different from it—why should qualities belonging to one meditation (*vidyā*) not likewise be extended to another meditation? To this, he replies: "In the archetype... (*prakṛtīti*).

The meaning is that while the attainment [of qualities] is appropriate in the case of a modification of the *prakṛti* (primordial nature), it is not so for the *vidyās* (meditative knowledges), because their relationship as *prakṛti* and *vikṛti* is not established. "Not thus" means that there is no non-inclusion of the qualities.
He avoids the redundancy of the subsequent sūtras with this sūtra by saying, "Of this very [sūtra]. //5//
If it is argued that there is a change [in the object] because of the word, we say no, because there is no distinction. (BS 3.3.6)

Previously, it was stated that the unity of knowledge (*vidyaikya*) follows as a general rule because there is no distinction in the injunctions and so forth; now, in order to state an exception (*apavāda*) to that, he says: "Otherwise-ness" (*anyathātva*).
Here, by the words beginning with "Vāja," he indicates the subject matter: the *Udgītha-brāhmaṇa* of the Vājasaneyins and the *Udgītha-adhyāya* of the Chandogas.
"Those gods"—the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) characterized by a sattvic disposition—"said to one another: 'Come now, in this sacrifice, by means of the Udgītha, [that is,] the office of the Udgātṛ...'"

"By means of this action, having transcended the Asuras—who consist of the activity of *rajas* and *tamas*—we shall attain the state of the gods. Having thus reached an agreement to determine the faultless performer of the *udgītha* as their object of worship, they first examined Speech (*vāk*). They said to her, "Perform for us the office of the *udgātṛ*. But she acted falsely; and likewise, through desire—that evil of the Asuras—the nose, the eye, the ear, and the mind were also overcome.
"Devoured" means having censured [the other organs], they determined that the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—which resides in the mouth (*āsanya*), that is, within the oral cavity—is the object of worship.

This means that when a battle consisting of mutual subjugation had commenced there, the gods, as before, brought forth the *udgītha*, thinking, "By means of this *udgītha*, let us conquer these Asuras.
He expresses the doubt through the measures of difference and non-difference with the word "there."

Here, according to the principle of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the preceding section, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because of the identity of the name "Udgītha-vidyā," there is identity of the meditations (*vidyaikyam*); the result of this view is the mutual combination of qualities.
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, despite the identity of the name, there is no such combination because of the refutation of the identity of the meditations.
Thus, it should be understood that wherever the prima facie view is based on a previous principle, the connection [to the present discussion] is one of exception (*apavādikī*).
He explains the portion of the Sūtra that addresses the doubt of the Siddhāntin: "But this is not tenable.

For the Vājasaneyins, the Prāṇa is to be meditated upon as the performer of the complete Udgītha rite, because of the word "Udgātṛ" (the singer), which denotes an agent; whereas for the Chāndogyas, the syllable *Oṃ*, which is a part of the Udgītha, is to be meditated upon as Prāṇa.

The meaning of the objection is this: since the text begins with "Oṃ—this syllable is the Udgītha" and then states "the vital breath (prāṇa) is the Udgītha," the word *udgītha* denotes the form of the ritual action; thus, because there is a difference between the agent and the object of meditation, the two meditations (*vidyā*) are distinct.
The phrase "as the Udgītha" means "as the syllable Oṃ."

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) refutes [the objection] by means of the principle already stated—that a slight difference in form does not contradict the identity of the knowledge—saying, "This is not so.

The intention regarding the "passing of the Asuras" is that the dialogue was for the purpose of conquering the Asuras; the meaning is that the scripture states in both places that just as a clod of earth is shattered upon hitting a stone, so too the Asuras who came to slay Prāṇa were themselves destroyed by his power.
Even if one were to admit a slight difference in form, it was stated that the knowledge is one; he says "vāk" (speech) to show that even this [difference] does not exist.
Since Prāṇa is heard of in both places as being the agent of the Udgītha, the agency heard of in one place is to be understood in both places—this is the meaning. //6//
Or rather, it is not so, because of the difference in context, as in the case of "the higher than the high" (parovarīyastva) and other such instances. (BBs 3.3.7)
He establishes the final conclusion—that there is no identity of knowledge due to the difference in many contradictory forms—with the words "or not.

He qualifies the Imperishable (akṣara) as "the Udgītha," meaning it is a constituent part thereof; that is, the syllable Om is the most excellent essence among the essences such as the earth and so forth.

Having stated the qualities—attainment and prosperity—the author introduces a narrative to establish the meditation on the syllable *oṃ* as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within that which possesses those qualities; thus he says, "The most flavorful," and so forth. Now, one might object: for the sake of syntactic unity with the words of Vāji, let the word *udgītha* appearing at the beginning of the Chāndogya refer to the entire division of the Sāman, and let it be explained that in the passage "the vital breath is the *udgītha*," the vital breath is to be meditated upon as the performer of the *udgītha*. To this, he replies: "In that case, if [it were] the *udgītha*... and so forth.

The meaning is that there would be two defects: first, the introduction [of the topic] would concern the meditation on the syllable *oṃ*, and second, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the agent in the word *udgītha*.

Now, one might object: even in the Siddhānta (the established conclusion), a figurative indication of a part must be accepted in that word; therefore, a figurative indication of the agent is better, as it is supported by another scriptural passage (*śruti*), and since the meditation on the agent-prāṇa is certain from the conclusion, it must also be certain from the introduction. To this, he says: "upakrama... (concerning the introduction).
For a commencement that is ambiguous is determined by the remainder of the passage;

just as in the case of "The gravel is anointed," where there is doubt regarding the substance used for anointing, the determination is made from the remainder, "Clarified butter is light. But here, in the commencement, the fact that the Imperishable (akṣara) is the object of meditation is already certain.

The meaning is that since the indication of a part (*avayava-lakṣaṇā*) for the word *udgītha*, which stands in grammatical apposition with that [prāṇa], is firmly established, the concluding statement "prāṇa is the udgītha" must be interpreted as having the same purpose as that [indication].

Thus, he says "vāja" etc., meaning that because the object of meditation is different—the syllable *oṃ* being taught as the object of worship in the Chāndogya, whereas in the other [text] it is prāṇa—there is a difference between the two meditations (*vidyā*).

He refutes the argument previously stated—that even in the Vājasaneyi-śruti there is identity of the object of worship because of the scriptural hearing of prāṇa’s nature as the udgītha—by saying "yad api" and so forth.

In this context, the meaning is that the *udgītha* is not mentioned as the object of meditation (*upāsya*), but rather as a quality (*guṇa*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is the object of meditation.

Furthermore, he states "the whole" (*sakala*) to show that there is a difference in the object of meditation: in the *Chāndogya*, the *udgītha* is the syllable *oṃ*, whereas here it is the *bhakti* (a portion of the chant).

Anticipating the objection that because the vital breath is insentient (*jaḍa*), it cannot be the *udgātṛ* (the chanter), but must be accepted by the Vājasaneyins as being merely the *udgītha*—thereby establishing identity—he says "and not" (*na ca*).
The meaning is that there is no impossibility [of the identity of the knowledge], because the Śruti states that "that Udgātṛ performed the office of the Udgātṛ with the prāṇa distinguished by speech.
Regarding the point stated—that the unity of the knowledge follows from the non-difference of the greater number of details—he says: "And not... (na ca).

The meaning is that since the difference in the nature of the internal objects of meditation is clear—namely, that in one case the *udgātṛ* (the breath) is to be meditated upon and in the other the syllable *oṃ*—it is not proper to assume identity of meditation based merely on the similarity of external explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
To show that identity of meaning does not follow from mere similarity of wording, he provides an illustration with the words "For instance":
"He indeed deprives him of progeny and cattle, and increases his rival, for whom the sacrificial offering has been set aside... [and so on].

"When the moon rises in the east, one should divide the rice grains into three parts: those that are of medium size, one should prepare from them a cake (*puroḍāśa*) on eight potsherds for Agni Dātṛ; those that are the largest, a pap (*caru*) of curd for Indra Pradātṛ; and those that are the smallest, a pap of boiled milk for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa"—this is the statement regarding the transgression [of the new-moon sacrifice].

The meaning of this is as follows: for that sacrificer who, on the fourteenth day itself, having mistaken it for the new moon (amāvāsyā), proceeds to perform the rites of the Darśa sacrifice, and for whom the oblation—consisting of rice, curd, and milk—has already been set aside (*nirupta*) beforehand, intended for the deities of the Darśa such as Agni and others, and yet the moon rises from behind him; for that sacrificer, due to the fault of the transgression of time, that very same [oblation] which was set aside...
The oblation diminishes offspring and the like, separates [the sacrificer] from his enemy, and increases that enemy, because the sacrificer is confused regarding the proper time.

Those rice-grains which have been divided into three parts—namely the middle portion and so forth—and have been set aside together with curds and other ingredients, one should divide them, separating them from Agni and the other deities; and having separated them, one should offer them to Agni and the others, who possess qualities such as being the giver and are non-different from the deities of the New Moon sacrifice. Thus, with curds...
The meaning is that one should prepare a *caru* of the coarsest rice in curd and a *caru* of the finest rice in boiled milk.

On the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) that, due to the lapse of time, a distinct ritual different from the *darśa*—in the form of an expiation involving other deities—is being enjoined here, [the siddhāntin replies]:

by restating the threefold division of the rice and so forth through the injunction "one should divide," it is established that within that very same [sacrifice], there is a separation of the oblation from its original deities.
In the case of the *darśa* rite, it was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is merely an injunction for the connection with another deity, and not a separate ritual act.

Likewise, in the sentence concerning the *abhyudaya*, because the undertaking is preceded by a lapse in the [proper] time, it is determined that within the *darśa* rite itself, there is a removal or separation of the oblation from its previous deities.

However, in the sentence regarding the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*), although it says, "Those which are the largest, one should offer them as a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni Sāṃnibhya... [the analysis continues].

The injunction— "One should offer those of medium size cooked in milk to Śipiviṣṭa-Viṣṇu, and those that are smallest as a *caru* to Indra the Bestower"— is identical in form to the sentence concerning the *abhyudaya* (the moon rising after the new moon).
Nevertheless, the rule "He who desires cattle should perform the *darśa* sacrifice on the new-moon day and then drive away the calves" refers to the obligatory (*nitya*) *darśa* rite.

The meaning is as follows: having completed [the previous rite], for the sake of the body [of the animal], because the procedure for "driving away the calf" (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) begins, there is indeed an injunction for a different sacrifice for one desiring cattle; thus, there is no identity of purpose with the *abhyudaya* passage. Likewise, in the present case as well, similarity of reference is not a cause for the identity of the knowledge (*vidyā*). The phrase "one should drive away the calves" means that one should lead them from the mother's location to another location.
He explains the illustration mentioned in the Sūtra with the words "like *parovarīyastva* and so forth.
The word *para* ends in the letter *s*; and because it is beyond (*para*) the other and more excellent (*varīyān*) than the excellent (*vara*), it is a single compound: *parovarīyān*.
The meaning is that the *udgītha* is so called because it is the support for the vision of the infinite Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is known as space (*ākāśa*).

The meaning is that, just as there is a difference between two meditations despite their similarity in being meditations on the *udgītha*—one as having the nature of space and the other as having the nature of the person with a golden beard—so too here there is a difference. //7//
If it is argued that [the self] exists because of its designation, that has already been addressed; however, even that [designation] does exist. (BBs 3.3.8)
Having set forth the identity of names as the seed of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), he refutes it with the words "saṃjñātaḥ" (from the name).

The meaning is that the multiplicity of meditations (vidyā) due to the difference in the forms of the objects of worship—which was previously stated—is supported by the literal words of the scripture (śruti) and is therefore strong; whereas a name is human-made (pauruṣeyī) and thus weak.
He states that identity of name is not invariably concomitant with identity of action, saying: "And there is...
He asks whether identity of name is entirely without authority everywhere, and answers: "But where...

In the absence of a subverting factor, even identity of name is a means of proof; for example, in the case of the Saṃvarga-vidyā, because of the identity of its name, there is identity of that vidyā across all recensions (śākhās).
The meaning is that the identity of the "Five-Fire" (pañcāgni) and other such meditations has been shown in the first sūtra. //8//
And because of pervasiveness, [the doctrine of the Lord] is consistent. (BS 2.2.38)
"And because of pervasion, [the relation] is consistent.
Having taken up the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as the subject, he states the doubt with the words "Om, this...
He explains the meanings of the terms such as "superimposition" (*adhyāsa*) and so forth with the passage beginning "Therein, superimposition... and so on.
Superimposition (adhyāsa) is the attribution of non-difference preceded by cognition; sublation (bādha) is negation (apavāda);
and unity is actual non-difference.

The distinction is that a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is that which differentiates. Previously, having taken for granted—as an established fact—the qualification of the syllable *oṃ* (the object of meditation) as being a part of the *udgītha*, which consists of the duties of the *udgātṛ* priest, the conclusion was reached that there is a difference in the meditations (*vidyā*) due to the difference in the objects of meditation. [Now], with the connection of an objection—that this is not tenable—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is set forth with the words "In that case" (*tatra*).

Considering that the result of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is the failure of the previously stated final position (*siddhānta*), while the result of the final position is its establishment, he explains the sūtra of the final position with the words beginning "the word *ca*," etc.
Having asserted the defectiveness of the three positions, he states the defect in the position of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) with the words "In that case, superimposition...

If the cognition of the *udgītha* were superimposed upon the syllable *oṃ*, there would have to be an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *udgītha*—which denotes that [sacrificial act]—in reference to the syllable *oṃ*, because [the word] would be intended to convey the quality of being the object of that cognition; furthermore, such a relationship is unestablished.
The meaning is that there would be the burden [of complexity] because the fruit of the meditation on the symbol (pratīkopāsti) would also have to be postulated.
He raises the objection that "the fruit need not be postulated" with the words "it is heard.
[He explains this with] "attainment and so forth."
The meaning is that the fruit mentioned in the scripture—"Oṃkāra is attainment, [it is] prosperity; he who meditates upon it attains his desires"—does not belong to superimposition (adhyāsa).

Having accepted the sublation of the cognition of one by the cognition of the other regarding the Udgītha and the syllable Oṃ, the futility of the cessation of the false cognition of the one was stated; now, however, he says "and never at any time" to show that there is no sublation because the cognition of either one is not erroneous.
If it were an error, it would cease; but since it does not cease, the meaning is that it is not an error.
Furthermore, he says "nor" (na ca) to show that the sublation of error occurs through a sentence that reveals reality, and this sentence is not one whose primary purport is [merely] reality.
He refutes the position that the words *oṃ* and *udgītha* are synonyms—like the words *ghaṭa* and *kumbha*—by saying "nor also" (nāpi).
He states that there is no synonymy either with the words "nor" (na ca).
Regarding the alternative view that the remaining [word] is a qualifier, he applies the Sūtra [with the word] "because of pervasion" (vyāpteḥ).

The meaning is as follows: when it is said, "One should meditate on the syllable Om," it would follow that the syllable Om—which pervades all the Vedas—is what is to be meditated upon here; therefore, the qualification "being a part of the Udgītha" is appropriate for the purpose of excluding that [over-extension].

In the case of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), a relationship consisting of the connection with the quality of being the object of that cognition would have to be postulated; thus, this would be a remote indication (*viprakṛṣṭā lakṣaṇā*). However, indication based on a part (*avayavalakṣaṇā*) is proximate, because of the relationship between a part and the whole, as seen in common usage such as "the cloth is burnt" when a part of the cloth is burnt. As for the word "Brahman" applied to names and so forth, one must resort to an indication based on the quality of being graspable by the cognition of Brahman due to the lack of any other alternative, since the meditation on the symbol (*pratīkopāsana*) is intended there.

In this case, however, if one were to assume that the injunction prescribes a meditation on the *pratīka* (the symbol), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) between enjoining the syllable *oṃ* as possessing qualities such as being the "attainer" (*āpti*) and enjoining the viewing of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within it.

Therefore, by setting aside the idea that the syllable *oṃ* pervades all the Vedas, it is established that the qualification is indeed appropriate for the purpose of enjoining the viewing of the vital breath within the syllable *oṃ*, because of the economy of conceptual construction (*kalpanālāghava*). //9//
Because there is no difference in all [the cases], these others are different from this. 3.3.10.
These others [the Vājins] are distinct because they are entirely non-different [from the rest].
To state their specific object of reference, he states the accepted meaning: "of the Vājins.
The quality of being a master of speech (*vāsiṣṭhatva*) belongs to the eloquent, as it is observed that they dwell in happiness.

The eye has the quality of being a foundation, because one who possesses sight perceives the foundation of the feet. The ear has the quality of excellence, because through hearing, there is the attainment of all objects. The mind has the quality of being an abode, because it serves as the locus for all objects of enjoyment by means of its various functions.
The meaning agreed upon by both recensions is that those qualities, having determined the preeminence of the vital breath (prāṇa), were surrendered to it by speech and the other organs.
He states the subject matter with the words "of others" and so forth;
the meaning is that the selection—that is, the determination—of the excellence of the highest good (niḥśreyasa) is being introduced.

The deities are speech and the others; "for their own excellence" means for their own preeminence. He states the doubt regarding this point—using the word "there"—because of the word "thus" and because of the recognition of the prāṇa as possessing the quality of excellence.
The non-inclusion or inclusion of these qualities constitutes the very result of the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) and the final (uttara-pakṣa) positions.

He presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of an analogy: "In that case, it follows... Just as the specific qualification of being the *udgītha* excludes the *oṃkāra*'s pervasion of all the Vedas, so too the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) excludes the qualities of other recensional branches (*śākhāntara*) by grasping only the qualities mentioned in the present context.

The meaning of the scriptural passage is as follows: just as the pre-eminence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) over speech and the other organs is established, so also one who, knowing this quality of pre-eminence, meditates upon it—having understood the pre-eminence in the vital breath—becomes pre-eminent himself.

Thus, since the identity of the knowledge (*vidyā*) is established by such similarity of type, it follows that the collection of qualities such as being the "best" (*vasiṣṭhatva*)—which is obtained through implication—is not grasped by the word *evaṃ* (thus), because [the word] relies solely on what is explicitly heard (*śruta*). To this, the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "They should be included. In the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa, the connection of the collection of qualities such as being the "best" with the knowledge of Breath (*prāṇavidyā*) is established by the word *evaṃ*. That very same knowledge is recognized (*pratyabhijñāyate*) in the Kauṣītaki Śruti.

Therefore, since qualities are inseparable from the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), even though they are obtained through implication, they are to be included together with the qualities explicitly mentioned, provided there is no contradiction with those explicit qualities.

He states "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) because the collection of qualities, consisting of both the heard [text] and the meaning, is referred to by the word "thus" (*evam*) found in the Kauṣītaki [Upaniṣad], since there is no distinction in their proximity to both the text and the meaning.
The Prāṇa situated in the Kauṣītaki Śruti possesses qualities such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhatva*).
It has been stated that because [the breath] is the best vital force (*prāṇa*),
just like the *prāṇa* mentioned in the Vāji-śruti, when there is an inference of unmentioned qualities, there is no abandonment of what is mentioned,
since there is no contradiction.
He clarifies this with the words "And this being so... [na caivaṃ sati].
He provides an illustration for the point that even qualities not specifically enumerated have indeed been heard [śrutā eva] with the words "For it is not... [nahi].
He states the conclusion with the words "Therefore... [tasmāt]. //10//
Bliss and other qualities belong to the Principal [Brahman]. (BS 3.3.11)
"Bliss and so forth belong to the principal [Brahman].
Because the object of knowledge, Brahman, is one and devoid of distinctions, he states the doubt: "There is a doubt regarding them.
In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), because there is no synthesis of the terms such as "Being" (satya) and so on, there is a failure to determine the meaning of the sentence.

In the Siddhānta, however, the result is the restriction [of attributes]. Since the vital breath (*prāṇa*) possesses specific qualities, the inclusion of attributes such as "being the most excellent" (*vasiṣṭhatva*) found in other recensions is appropriate; but since Brahman is devoid of specific qualities, its cognition is established by the words belonging to one's own recension alone, making the inclusion of words from other recensions redundant. Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is presented by way of a counter-example.
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "this" (*idam*).

The universals such as blissfulness (*ānandatva*), truthfulness (*satyatva*), and consciousnessness (*jñānatva*) are qualities superimposed upon Brahman; their "synthesis" (*upasaṃhāra*) across all Vedic branches means the utterance of the words expressing them—such as "bliss," "truth," "consciousness," and "infinite"—as a single syntactical unity, as in: "Brahman is bliss, truth, consciousness, and infinite."
"Purity, non-duality, and Self"—these words in grammatical apposition, by abandoning contradictory attributes, point toward a single, indivisible manifestation that serves as the substrate of all.
Nor should it be argued that another word is redundant since the indicated object is established by a single word alone; [for this is not the case].
Because there is no contradiction in a single word, figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) does not apply;

even though figurative indication may apply to both words, nevertheless, when it is said "Brahman is bliss," although the delusion regarding suffering and meagerness is dispelled, a misconception regarding non-existence, insentience, and so forth might still arise. Therefore, for the purpose of dispelling that, words such as "Being" and "Knowledge" must be employed.
Nor should it be argued that because error has no limit, the sentence would remain incomplete;

for when there is the perception of the specific reality—"I am Brahman, whose nature is existence-consciousness-bliss, devoid of all attributes, non-dual, and free from conceptual construction"—all error is dispelled.
The sense is that as many words as are required to bring about that perception of the specific reality, so many words should be employed. //11//
The state of having "Pleasure as the head" and so forth is not attained [by the individual soul], for increase and decrease exist only where there is difference. (BS 3.3.12)

If it is argued that because of the identity with Brahman, attributes such as bliss and so forth must be attained everywhere, then there would also be the attainment of attributes belonging to the knowledge of Saguna-Brahma; in order to dispel this doubt, he explains the Sutra: "The dear," etc. The pleasure from seeing a son is "dear" (*priya*); the joy derived from news of him and so forth is "delight" (*moda*); and when there is an excellence of that knowledge, there is "great delight" (*pramoda*).

Attributes characterized by such gradations do not apply to the non-dual object of knowledge, because those which are not the very nature of Brahman are of no use for the realization of Brahman—this is the sense.
He states that their status as Brahman and as Dharma is unestablished with the words "And these are not...
Anticipating the objection that they might nevertheless be attained since they serve as means for directing the mind toward Brahman, he says "Even so...
The meaning is that because these [means] are themselves unknowable, there can be no attainment of them within Brahman, which is the object of knowledge.

To the question, "For what purpose, then, is the Sūtra? he says: "The qualities of Brahman" (*brahmadharmān*). He states the result of this hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvācintā*) with the words "And he" (*sa ca*).

The meaning is that the Sūtra should be explained as follows: since external objects are of no use regarding the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), they are not attained; therefore, by the logic of this principle, qualities such as "having all desires" (*saṃyadvāmatva*) and so forth are not attained.

Anticipating the objection that even if knowledge (*jñāna*) is not employed, there might still be attainment through other forms of knowledge (*vidyā*) because those attributes (*dharma*) are employed in meditation (*dhyāna*) due to the identity with the Brahman to be meditated upon, he says: "For in them...
The meaning is that for those attributes which are subordinate to the injunctions for meditation, their application is determined according to the specific injunction. //12//
But the others [the fires] are [to be established] because of the commonality of purpose. (BS 3.3.13)

He states "But the others," etc., to show the distinction between bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth from attributes such as "the gathering of all desires" (*saṃyadvāma*), on the grounds that [the former] are useful for knowledge.
It is thus established that the five terms—*satya*, *jñāna*, *ānanda*, *ātman*, and *brahman*—are to be combined everywhere. //13//
[The meditation on the individual self as Brahman] is for the purpose of higher contemplation, because there is no other purpose [for such meditation]. (BS 3.3.14)
He states the doubt—using the word "therein"—because it cannot be determined whether there is a difference or non-difference of sentences for the purpose of meditation.
In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there is a difference of meditations due to the difference of sentences;
in the final conclusion (siddhānta), there is unity of meditation due to the unity of the sentence. This is the result [of the discussion].

In the preceding section, it was stated that qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*), which are of the very nature of Brahman and are to be combined [in meditation], serve as means to the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman. Here, however, it is stated that even that which is not of the nature of Brahman—namely, the orientation toward wealth and so forth, which is not to be combined—serves as a means to that same fruit. Thus, the connection (*saṅgati*) lies in the fact that they share a single fruit. Furthermore, because there is a difference between the meanings and so forth—which are to be established as something new (*apūrva*) by virtue of being qualified by their respective orientations—and the resulting distinct sentences, there is a division of the text (*vākya-bheda*).
"There is no fault"—this is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Having proposed a conclusion not explicitly stated in the sūtra, he explains the reason given in the sūtra: "The person alone.

The meaning is that since [the person] possesses fruit and is something not previously established [by other means], the person alone is to be understood as the primary object of exposition; whereas the fact that the purpose, the means, and so forth are subordinate is stated because they exist for the sake of that [person].

Furthermore, the Veda—by means of the indicative mark of the negation of what is beyond ("There is nothing higher than Puruṣa; that is the ultimate limit") and by the indicative mark of being the terminus for the sublation of everything else—demonstrates its intent (tātparya) regarding Puruṣa and shows that the statement of the superiority of each subsequent entity over each preceding one is for that purpose. Thus he says: "Moreover" (apica).

The mention of the objects and so forth here is for the sake of meditation; since they have no inherent purpose other than to facilitate the vision of the Puruṣa preceded by meditation upon each of those [objects], he applies the sūtra with the words: "For the sake of meditation" (ādhyānāya). //14//
And because of the word "Self. (BS 3.3.15)
He states that by means of such marks as "selfhood" (ātmatva), it is the Puruṣa alone that is to be established, saying: "And because of the word 'Self'.

Furthermore, since there is consistency between the opening and the conclusion—namely, "That is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu" and "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa"—and since it is certain that the entire passage forms a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatva) directed toward a single Puruṣa who possesses an established fruit, one must not resort to the assumption of a split in the sentence (vākyabheda) or a plurality of fruits.
It is not tenable [to say] "because of respect," as he says: "Moreover" (api ca). //15//
The Self is grasped [as the object of meditation], as in other cases, because of what follows. (BS 3.3.16)
The grasping of a self;
that which blinks and moves;
it is called "water" by the world.
Ambhas is heaven;
Marīcis is the intermediate world;
Mara is the world of mortals.
"Water" means the world of Pātāla.
Since the word "Self" (ātman) is used for both Brahman and the Sūtra-Ātman, he states the doubt with the words "In that regard.

Here, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), because the passage is intent upon the meditation on the Sūtra, there is no inclusion (anupasaṃhāra) of the attributes of the Supreme Brahman, such as bliss and so forth, in the Aitareyaka.
In the Siddhānta, the result is that there is a synthesis because [the passage] has Brahman as its ultimate purport.

It was stated that, due to the contingency of a difference from the *puruṣa*-passage, sentences concerning objects and so forth do not have the function of establishing those objects; likewise here too, due to the contingency of a difference from the preceding *Prajāpati*-passage—namely, "The gods are the semen of Prajāpati"—there is a [contingency of difference] for the sentence beginning with "Verily, the Self... (*ātmā vai*).
He presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of the example that [the passage] does not have Brahman as its ultimate purport, beginning with the words "not the Supreme Self" and so forth;
the meaning is that the intention of the sentence is seen to lie in Prajāpati.

Having raised this prima facie view, he refutes it by stating that the syntactical connection of the sentence does not reside in Prajāpati because of the indicative mark (liṅga) of being the creator of the worlds, beginning with the word "but surely" (nanu).
Since the worlds themselves are the great elements, he says "and the worlds.
Because the word "world" (loka) is not conventionally established in the sense of the great elements, the worlds are indeed composed of derived matter (bhautika).
And because of the etymological derivation, he says "and likewise."

Having stated in the Sūtra, "The waters, the rays, the death," the Śruti itself explains: that world which is beyond the sky, above the sky, established in heaven, and pervaded by the water of the moon—that is "water";
the intermediate space is "the rays";
and the earth is "death."
"That which is below is water.

[The opponent objects: "But surely even the creation of the world must proceed from the Lord alone? [The author replies: "No," he says—"In the world..."—meaning having the form of a person, i.e., human in shape.
The meaning is that the Self, as Hiraṇyagarbha, created everything down to the smallest ant;
"of beings" means of the worlds.
He states that Prajāpati is the creator of the world also on account of the context, saying "the Aitareyins also [state this]. "Retas" means the effect.
He applies the marks of Brahman to Prajāpati with the words beginning "the word 'Self' also," and so forth.
Furthermore, having created living beings, the Creator of the world brought a cow for their enjoyment and likewise brought a horse;
yet they were not satisfied with the acquisition of the cow and horse. Then, when a human body was brought, they said, "We are satisfied.
He states that this worldly transaction is a mark [of the status] of Prajāpati as the Creator of the world, by saying "apica" (moreover).

The author establishes the final conclusion—that the Supreme Self (paramātman) is to be understood—on the grounds that the word "Self" (ātman) has its primary meaning in the conscious Self (cidātman), that there is no sublation in accepting this primary sense, and that it is consistent with the subsequent mention of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) and so forth; thus he says, "This being the case...
The intention is that the scriptural passage stating that [the Self] created the worlds preceded by the creation of the great elements (mahābhūta) is to be explained in this manner. //16//
If it is argued that [the self exists] because of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), [we reply: it would be so because of the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). (BS 3.3.17)
Having restated the seed of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he refutes it with the words "because of the connection" (*anvayāt*). The sense is that,

since the identity [of the Self and Brahman] is ascertained through the scriptural mentions of "Self" (*ātman*) and "Brahman" found in the opening and concluding passages— namely, "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" and "Brahman is consciousness"—
and since the marks such as "entering" (*praveśa*) override marks such as being the creator of the world, the Inner Self (*pratyag-brahman*) is what must be understood.
He is the Supreme Lord.

Having split open this very boundary—the parting of the hair at the crown of the head—and having made an aperture, He entered through this gateway called the *brahmarandhra*, distinguished by His *liṅga*; this is the meaning.
If speech and the other organs had performed their respective functions without Me, [the result would have been different].

Then, having at that time investigated the meaning of the term "thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*)—asking "Who am I?"—he himself perceived this very Self, which had been purified, as Brahman, the most pervasive (*tatamaṃ vyāptatamam*).
The elision of the letter *t* [in *tatamaṃ*] is a Vedic archaism.

The compound *prajñānetram* means that whose guide (*netram*) is consciousness (*prajñā*), that is to say, that which is governed by the conscious Self (*cidātman*). The word *netram* is derived from the root *nī*, meaning "that by which one is led," hence it signifies a controller or regulator.

Considering that the synthesis of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) is not clear in the previous explanation and thus lacks connection to the section (*pāda*), he states another interpretation, beginning with "others. *Udarka* means conclusion.
He expresses doubt regarding the word "Being" (*sat*) because it is common to both the Self (*ātman*) and the non-Self (*anātman*), saying "therein."

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because there is a difference—namely, that in the *Chāndogya* there is the meditation on the attainment of the identity of Brahman and the Self within the generality of Being (*sattāsāmānya*), whereas in the *Vājaśruti* it is the knowledge of the attributeless (*nirguṇavidyā*)—there is no mutual combination of qualities.
In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, because the knowledge of the attributeless is one and the same in both places, there is a combination; such is the difference in result.

The summary of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: since the word "Being" (*sat*) denotes the universal (*jāti*) of existence because the potency of words is grasped with respect to universals, the opening statement is of certain meaning; therefore, by the force of the opening statement—which has not yet encountered any contradiction—the teaching of identity must be interpreted as being intended for the sake of meditative identification (*saṃpatti*). In the previous case, because the sentences formed a single unit, the unity of the meditation was asserted after abandoning the focus on the meanings [of the individual terms] and so forth. Here, however, because there is a difference in the opening statements—since the words "Being" (*sat*) and "Self" (*ātman*) denote the universal and the self respectively—and thus a difference in the sentences, there is a difference in the meditations (*vidyābheda*).
Thus is the connection with the counter-example.

Furthermore, the word *ātman* does not denote a genus (*jāti*), because there is no genus due to the identity of the individual self (*ātmavyakti*); rather, it denotes the reality that is the innermost of all.

It should be understood that even if [the word] denotes an imagined genus (*kalpitajāti*), the difference in the initial statement (*upakrama*) is indeed clear, because of the distinction between existence (*sattā*) and the self-nature (*ātmatva*).
He establishes the final conclusion with the words "In that way" (*tathā*) and so forth,
[stating] "because of the connection with the initial statement."
The meaning is that the conclusion depends upon the introduction.
And that restriction is appropriate only when the Self is grasped by means of the word "Being" (sat); thus he says, "And that.
The restriction is that "Being is one alone."

"By this living self"—this refers to the reference to the individual soul (jīva) by means of the word "self," with the True Deity as the agent. The statement that "during deep sleep, the individual soul becomes united with Being" is the explanation.
"Please, venerable sir, instruct me further"—this is the request for further instruction.
By the word *sat*, that which is the substratum of existence (*sattāśraya*) is expressed, not mere genus (*jāti*) alone, because it ends with the suffix *śatṛ*, which denotes an agent.

Thus, since the opening statement mentions the generality of the substratum of existence, when the expectation arises as to what that substratum is, it is determined from the remainder of the sentence to be the Self; this is what [the author] states with the words "and not... (*na ca*).

It was stated [by some] assuming that the word *sat* is common to both the Self and the non-Self; however, even that is not so. Just like the word *ātman*, the word *sat* denotes an individual (*vyakti*), and that individual is none other than the conscious Self (*cidātman*) which is incapable of sublation. Thus, there is no discrepancy between the introductory passages of the Vājasaneyins and the Chandogas. Having accepted the discrepancy regarding the word *sat*, he says: "In the Vājasaneyaka passage... [etc.], explaining that in the Vājasaneyaka statement, the referent of *tvam* culminates in the referent of *tat* as the indicated object (*lakṣya*), whereas in the Chandogya statement...

However, since it is the teaching of that [object]—extending even to the meaning of "Thou"—it follows that although there is a difference in method, the unity of the knowledge (vidyā) results from the unity of the sentence-meaning;
thus he concludes with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). //17//
Because of the mention of what is to be done, there is something not previously known. (BS 3.3.18)
"Because it explains what is already known, it does not convey something new.

Thus questioned by Prāṇa, "What is my food? What is my clothing?", Vāk and the others replied, "Whatever exists here, down to dogs and even worms—that is your food; water is your clothing. This refers to that which is consumed by all living beings.
The meaning is that the practitioner should contemplate as follows: "Whatever food is well-known, down to that of dogs and so forth, that is your food, O Prāṇa; water is your clothing.
Having thus stated the common scriptural teaching in both recensions, he speaks of the difference in the specific scriptural teachings with the words "And immediately after... and so on.

Therefore, because water is the garment of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), learned scholars (*śrotriya*) who are eating—that is, performing the act of eating—do this: namely, they sip water both before and after the meal. This means that by means of water, they clothe or cover the vital breath.

The sense is that one should perform the meditation on non-nakedness (*anagnatādhyāna*), which consists of contemplating the state of water being the garment of the vital breath, in relation to the waters connected with the preceding and succeeding sips.

Therefore, for that reason—the meaning of which has already been stated—since the ancient wise ones sipped water both before and after eating, thinking that by that sipping they were making this very breath of theirs "anagna" (un-naked, i.e., covered), therefore a contemporary practitioner who knows this should also do likewise; such is the meaning of the Vājin-śruti.
Here, because both [the actions] are unprecedented (*apūrva*), he raises a doubt: "What then? etc.

Just as there is a determination of a doubtful initial statement by means of the remainder of the sentence, so too, when there is doubt regarding whether the word "ācāmantī" (they should sip water) is an injunction, its status as an injunction is determined by the remainder of the sentence "ācāmet" (one should sip). With this analogy as the point of connection, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "What, then...
The connection to the chapter (*pāda*) should be understood as arising from the investigation into the injunctions for the subsidiary parts of meditation (*upāsana*), which is a means to knowledge.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the conclusion is that a previously unestablished act of sipping water (*ācamana*) is enjoined as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) and must therefore be integrated elsewhere.

In the final view (*siddhānta*), the distinction is that because it is not something to be enjoined, there is no integration as an auxiliary. Alternatively, fearing that enjoining both would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), he states another position with the words "Or rather" (*athavā*).
"This rinsing of the mouth is indeed praiseworthy, because by means of it they consider the vital breath (prāṇa) to be unclothed"—this is the praise.
He establishes the final conclusion according to the principle that "that which is not well-known is to be enjoined by way of restating what is already known": "In this manner.
The meaning is: *prāyatya* is the state (*bhāva*) of one who is purified (*prayata*), that is, the state of being endowed with effort; [the compound] means "for the sake of that purity."

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: since the act of rinsing the mouth (ācamana) is already established as a subsidiary element of all ritual acts prescribed for the purpose of purification by means of Smṛti, this [Vedic] text merely restates that ācamana and enjoins the previously unknown meditation on non-nakedness (*anagnatādhyāna*) itself. One might raise the objection: "Is it not the case that the Smṛti-based ācamana is not being restated by this Śruti, but rather that what is enjoined by this Śruti is being restated by the Smṛti? [The author] refutes this with "No," because there is no relationship of source and derivative between these two—the Śruti and the Smṛti—due to their having different subjects.
The Smṛti passage beginning with "A twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet)" has its root-status refuted by accepting it as an injunction for a different kind of ācamana;
now, [the author] states that this injunction is not established at all, saying: "And this is not a Śruti.
"For this very reason" means: precisely because there is no injunction for such ācamana.

He states with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) that the resolve known as meditation (*adhyāna*), which consists in [viewing] water as the clothing of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is enjoined as an ancillary part of the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*).
By the words "and itself," he means that this is because it is something not previously established (*apūrvatva*).

Anticipating the objection that it is contradictory for the sipping of water (*ācamana*), which is prescribed for the purpose of purification, to serve the purpose of clothing the vital breath, he says: "And this being so... (*na caivaṃ sati*).
The meaning is that it is unproven that the sipping of water (ācamana) has clothing as its purpose.

Furthermore, just as in the preceding passage the meditation on food was prescribed as an ancillary to the vital breath (prāṇa), so here the meditation on clothing is prescribed in relation to the waters; otherwise, if this were merely a rule for sipping water, there would be an inconsistency—meditation being enjoined previously and a ritual action subsequently. Thus he says, "Moreover" (api ca).

The meaning is that because there is no word [in the text] saying "one should eat," and because it is impossible for a human householder to eat all kinds of food such as dog-meat, there is no injunction of action in the preceding sentence.
Furthermore, he says "Moreover" (apica) to show that the sipping of water (ācamana) is not to be enjoined here.

He raises an objection—starting with "But surely" (nanu)—that even the mental visualization of clothing (*vāsastvadhyāna*) in the passage "they consider it not naked" cannot be enjoined, on account of the equality of the fault [of redundancy].

The meaning of the resolution is as follows: since it would be futile for both to be mere restatements (*anuvāda*), one must necessarily be a restatement and the other the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*). And that which is to be enjoined is the meditation on the garment (*vāsodhyāna*) alone, because it describes the effect of the garment—namely, freedom from nakedness—and because it is something not previously established (*apūrva*). The phrase "as before" means that it is already established by traditional scripture (*smṛti*).

"One should sip water" (*ācāmet*) is not an injunction (*vidhi*), but rather a restatement (*anuvāda*), just as in the statement "Viṣṇu is to be worshipped with a portion of the *aṃśu*. To this point, he states the indicative mark (*liṅga*): "For this very reason" (*ata eva*). The meaning is that since the sentence "One who knows thus, about to eat, should sip water; having eaten, one should sip water" is not an injunction, the fact that the Kāṇvas do not recite it serves as the indicative mark.

He refutes the opinion of some who claim that by the force of the reading, there is an injunction for sipping water (*ācamana*) in the Mādhyandina school and an injunction for meditation (*dhyāna*) in the Kāṇva school: "Even he who... (verse 18).
And likewise, [the self] is the same because of its non-differentiation. (BBs 3.3.19)
And because it is thus non-different from the Samāna [breath],
it is seen by Śāṇḍilya and marked with his name;
the meaning is that it exists subtly within the heart, like a grain of rice or similar seed.
He states the doubt based on repetition and recognition with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
The non-inclusion and inclusion of qualities are the results of the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final (*uttarapakṣa*) positions respectively.
In the preceding case, the injunction for meditating on the state of being unclothed was stated as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the already established practice of sipping water (*ācamana*).

But here, within a single recension (*śākhā*), because there is no certainty as to which of two statements situated in distant locations is the injunction (*vidhi*) and which is the restatement (*anuvāda*), he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by way of a counter-example, stating: "What, then, [is the case]?
As for what was further stated:

Anticipating the objection that there is no pervasion (vyāpti) because this would be contradicted in the case of the Prāṇa-vidyā, the Pañcāgni-vidyā, and others—where the same teaching occurs across different branches of the Veda—it is stated that "repetition" is not established when the branches differ; thus he says: "In the case of different [branches]...

Anticipating the objection that just as in the Agnihotra passage there is an injunction for the rite, while in the passage "He offers with curd" there is an injunction for an accessory (guṇa), so too here it may be the same, and there is no difference in the knowledge (vidyā)—he says: "And here there is not one [single thing]."

The repetition of qualities already mentioned would be redundant; therefore, the sense is that there is a difference in knowledge (*vidyā*) due to this repetition, just as there is a difference between the *prayāja* offerings.

[The opponent argues: "The mention of qualities already stated is not redundant, because it serves to recognize the non-difference of the object of meditation (*upāsya*) as characterized by certain specific qualities. Thus, he applies the *siddhānta-sūtra*—that because of the non-difference in the form of the object of meditation, there is unity of knowledge even within the same recensional branch (*śākhā*), just as in different branches—by saying "just as" (*yathā*).
The "ca" (and) in the Sūtra has been explained as having the sense of "also.

Since it is determined that where many qualities are heard, there is an injunction of the principal [act] in one place and an injunction of qualities by reference to that [principal act] elsewhere, the intention is that while the Agnirahasya constitutes the injunction of the principal, the subsequent [passages] constitute the injunction of qualities. //19//
Because of this connection, it is likewise in other cases as well. (BBs 3.3.20)
The same connection applies elsewhere as well.

Having introduced the Brahman known as Hiraṇyagarbha— which consists of the three existent elements (sat-bhūta-traya), namely earth, air, and ether, and which consists of the true, unperceived elemental self— ...

That which was stated as the Truth is that very one who is yonder Āditya; [it is taught] that it is not merely the orb, but rather the Person consisting of instruments (karaṇātman) located in that place, who, when considered from the perspective of the self (adhyātma), resides in the place of the eye. Having thus instructed [this], and having described his body in the form of the Vyāhṛtis—“Bhūḥ is his head, Bhuvaḥ is his arms, Svaḥ is his feet”—two Upaniṣads, i.e., secret names of the deity, are taught.
The name of that [Self] residing in the solar orb is "Day" (ahar) because of its luminosity; the name of that [same Self] residing in the eye is "I" (aham) because of its inwardness.

Regarding these two names as the objects of inquiry, a doubt is raised—expressed by the word "tatra"—because of the oneness of the named Brahman known as Truth, despite the mention of different locations.

In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there is the performance of both names at each respective location; in the established conclusion (siddhānta), the result is the performance of only one name according to the scriptural text.
He explains the *pūrvapakṣa* sūtra by way of an analogy with the word "just as":
"Just as it was stated that there is a combination [of details] due to the unity of the knowledge (*vidyā*), so too in other cases there ought to be a combination of a single knowledge.
The meaning is this: since there is no difference in the opening statement—"Brahman is Truth"—these two, the person in the eye and the person in the sun, are established in one another.

Because the rays of the sun are established in the eye, and the eye is established in the sun—this reciprocal textual arrangement (*vyatiṣaktapāṭha*), meaning a reading of mutual connection, establishes the identity of the two Upaniṣadic teachings.
To the question, "Even if the teaching is one and the same, what would follow from that?", he says: "How so?
He removes the doubt that even if the teaching is one, there might be no commingling of the two Upaniṣads due to the difference in their locations, by means of an illustration: "For whoever... (20).
Or rather, it is not so, because there is a distinction. (BS 3.3.21)
Because the names are distinct, a confusion of names is not appropriate;

thus, it might be argued that the one residing in the eye possesses the name "Day" because it is the True Brahman, just like the one residing in the sun. To this, he applies the sūtra of the established conclusion:
"No. The meaning is that the two names are connected with [the objects] as qualified by their respective forms, meditations, and locations.

The sense is that the inference—based on the concluding portion which intends to connect the names with the two persons referred to by the word *tat* and qualified by their respective proximate positions through the two sentences "His secret name is Ahar" and "His secret name is Aham"—is sublated.

Anticipating the objection that there might be a confusion of names because the substrata (the persons) are one and the same, [the author] states the restriction of the names based on the difference between the persons as qualified by the difference in their positions, beginning with the words "But surely... (*nanu*).
He provides an example regarding a qualified relation with the words "it exists" (*asti*).

Since a counter-example possesses a relation in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), he states that there is no example for the qualified object under discussion with the words "in a village" (*grāme*) etc. //21//
And scripture also demonstrates this. (BS 3.3.22)
He states that "and it shows" because the transfer [of qualities] is the indicative mark for the determination of the names already mentioned;

for if the combination were established solely by the identity of the knowledge (vidyā), the transfer would be redundant. Therefore, it is established that even within a single knowledge, there is no combination of the qualities mentioned in different locations without the transfer. //22//
Furthermore,
from this [same source], there is also the collection of materials, as well as the pervasion of heaven. (BS 3.3.23)
And because of the accumulation, the shining, and the pervading;
those for which Brahman is the eldest cause are "brahmajyeṣṭhāni," where the elision [of the suffix] is Vedic.
The heroic deeds (*vīryāṇi*) are specific acts of prowess, such as the creation of space and so forth; and those heroic deeds were accumulated and brought to fulfillment without obstacle,
because there was no one to create obstacles for the work of the Universal Controller.
And that [Brahman] is the eldest; even before the emergence of the gods and others from Agni, it pervaded the sky—that is to say, heaven—meaning it is eternally all-pervasive.
The qualities "being first of all" and "being beyond rivalry" are the attributes to be understood from the word *prabhṛti* (beginning with) in the supplementary portion of the sentence.
The term *khileṣu* means in those passages which are devoid of injunctions and prohibitions.
He states the doubt arising from the connection with Brahman and the appearance of a difference in the meditations (vidyās) with the words: "In those [meditations]...

The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that because the glories of Brahman taught as unconnected [passages] are recognized through their connection with Brahman in all meditations on Brahman, they should be combined.
He states the established conclusion (siddhānta) with the words: "The [glories] such as being 'collected'..."

The construction of the Sūtra is as follows: "Accumulation (*saṃbhṛti*) and pervasion of heaven (*dyuvyāpti*)—that [pair] also is not to be combined everywhere, because of the connection with specific limiting factors, just as in the case of the two Upaniṣads.

When it has been stated that there is no attainment [of these qualities] in those meditations associated with the specific internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), because there is no reason for the recognition of the divine manifestations (*ādhidaivika-vibhūti*), the author raises an objection regarding the reason: "But in these...

The meaning of the objection is that there is an attainment of "accumulation" and so forth in those respective meditations either due to the commonality of being divine or due to the commonality of being devoid of the specific internal bases.

The two reasons stated do not bring about the acquisition of qualities, because it would follow that there is a mutual commingling of qualities between the *śāṇḍilya*, *dahara*, and other such meditations on the divine (ādhidaivika), as well as with the meditation on the "abode-less" (*āyatanahīna*).

Therefore, he refutes this with the words "True indeed," etc., [arguing] that the cause for the acquisition of qualities is the identity of the object of meditation characterized by several common attributes, which brings about the unity of the meditation; since that is absent here, there is no such acquisition.

This is like the distinction between two names based on their specific locations, or the distinction between Brahman qualified by the qualities of the *saṃbhṛti* and so forth, and Brahman qualified by the qualities mentioned in the *śāṇḍilya* and other meditations.

Because of the mutual difference in form, there is no synthesis (upasaṃhāra) of the Saṃbhṛti and other meditations; since this [present case] is an extension of the logic already stated, it does not require [further discussion of] connection and so forth.

Just as in the case of a single Udgītha, the meditation on qualities such as "being higher than the high" differs from the meditation on qualities such as "having golden hair," so too, even though the Brahman is one, the distinction between different meditations is possible. Therefore, he says, "like the 'higher than the high' and so forth," meaning that the recognition of Brahman does not necessitate the inclusion of all its qualities.
Therefore, it is established that this is an injunction for another knowledge distinguished by qualities such as the accumulation [of merit] and so forth. //23//
And because the other [details] are not mentioned, as in the case of the Puruṣa-vidyā. (BS 3.3.24)

He speaks of the Puruṣavidyā, the knowledge found in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, beginning with the words "There is [a man]": "Man, indeed, is the sacrifice. His twenty-four years constitute the morning libation (prātaḥsavana); his forty-four years constitute the midday libation (mādhyandinasavana); and his forty-eight years constitute the third libation (tṛtīyasavana). This is for the purpose of establishing a similarity with the well-known ritual sacrifice.
The three pressings have been conceived:

"When he is hungry, when he thirsts, and when he does not find delight—these are the consecrations (*dīkṣā*). Then, when he eats, when he drinks, and when he finds delight—these are the *upasads*. Then, when he laughs, when he eats solid food, and when he engages in sexual intercourse—these are the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns. And then...

Whatever penance, charity, and so forth [are performed], that is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); death itself is the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). "May my vital breaths, in the form of Vasu and the others, extend these three pressings (savana) for as long as life lasts"—this is the prayer. The application of the three mantras—"Thou art imperishable," "Thou art unshakable," and "Thou art sharpened vital breath"—shows that the fruit is a lifespan of one hundred and sixteen years.
He states the Puruṣavidyā from another branch for the sake of resolving this doubt: "The Taittirīyakas," and so forth.

Here, a doubt is raised by the phrase "of the knower of the sacrifice" (*viduṣo yajñasya*), because it is uncertain whether the two genitive cases are in apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or not (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). He says "therein" (*tatra*) to indicate that the very result [of this discussion] is whether there is a synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) or no synthesis of these elements.

In the preceding case, it was stated that there is a difference between the two meditations (*vidyā*) because there is no recognition of common, unique qualities in the *saṃbhṛti* and other passages. Here, however, by way of a counter-example, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that there is identity of meditation because of the recognition of the identity of form as a "human sacrifice" (*puruṣayajña*), characterized by the unique quality of death as the final bath (*avabhṛtha*). To this, the author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "They are not to be combined."
