For one who knows this, the sacrifice is as follows: the self is the sacrificer, faith is the wife, the body is the fuel, the chest is the altar, the hair is the sacrificial grass, the head is the Veda, the heart is the sacrificial post, desire is the clarified butter, anger is the victim, austerity is the fire, self-restraint is the pacifier, the sacrificial fee is speech, the Hotṛ priest is the out-breath, the Udgātṛ priest is the in-breath, the Adhvaryu priest is the eye, and the Brahman priest is the mind; [this is not so] because of the great difference in their respective characteristics.
The meaning is that there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) based on identity of form.
The grammatical connection is: "The Veda is the handful of *kuśa* grass; tranquility is the restraint; and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) [is the third].
Furthermore, in the *Chāndogya*, there is the conceptualization of the three divisions of life as being the three *savana*s (pressings).

But here, he points out the dissimilarity by saying "yad api" (even that which), meaning "at the time of evening and so forth. Since there is also a semblance of similarity in the Taittirīya Śruti—"That which is death is the final bath (avabhṛtha); that which one enjoys is the Upasads"—he says "yad api kiñcit" (whatever little...).
The meaning is that this semblance of similarity, like the four-footedness common to both elephants and camels, is not a cause for identity.
Furthermore, he states another point of dissimilarity: "And not [so]," because in the *Chāndogya* the identity of the person and the sacrifice is heard, whereas here there is a distinction.

Although the genitive case in both instances is appropriate for grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) according to the principle of the "chief of the Niṣādas" (*niṣādasthapati*), nevertheless, due to the cumbersome assumption of an unestablished identity and because of the statement of their difference—"the Self of the sacrifice"—as well as the contradiction of one and the same thing being both the sacrifice and the sacrificer, [the phrase refers to] that sacrifice which is well-known to belong to the knower of the Self.
It is indeed proper that there be a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (vaiyadhikaraṇya).

Furthermore, when there is a syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) perceived through the injunction of the perfection of the constituent parts by means of the limbs belonging to the knower—following upon the restatement of the qualified object, which is the sacrifice related to the knower—then for you who maintain that the qualified object and the constituent parts have separate injunctions, the fault of syntactical split (vākyabheda) would arise; such is the meaning.

Furthermore, after teaching renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) with the words "Moreover, apart from truth and so forth, there is renunciation and what else," and then teaching the knowledge of the Self that is to be accomplished through renunciation in the preceding *Prājāpatya-anuvāka*— namely, "Having known this Self as 'all this world by means of all,' the wise man does not again enter into death"—
the subsequent *anuvāka* follows by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that very knowledge of the Self, for the purpose of its glorification, with the words "For him who knows thus."
The completion of the sacrifice is performed as a subsidiary part of that [meditation], because of the scriptural statement regarding the identity of the fruit;
however, for the Chandogas, it is an injunction for an independent meditation. He states this with the words, "Moreover, together with renunciation.
He states the result of this reflection with the words, "Therefore... (24).
Because there is a difference in meaning regarding the act of piercing (*vedha*) and so forth. (BBs 3.3.25)

Because of the difference in purpose, such as piercing and so forth, the performer of the malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) prays to the deity: "All this," etc. O Deity, pierce—that is, tear apart—all the limbs of my enemy; specifically, split his heart, rend the *dhamanīs* (arteries) and *sirās* (veins), and utterly destroy his head on all sides.
The meaning is: "O God Savitṛ, let my enemy be thus divided and disunited in three ways;
impel the sacrifice and its lord—that is, bring them to completion."
The meaning is: "You are blue like an emerald, like that Indra who possesses the white horse Uccaiḥśravas; may you be *śam*, a bringer of happiness, to us.
The Agniṣṭoma is indeed Brahman itself; the day on which it is performed is also Brahman. Therefore, that which is to be accomplished on this day [is Brahman].
The construction of the sentence is as follows: those who perform [the rites] by means of Brahman as their instrument reach Brahman, and they, in due course, attain immortality.
He states a doubt regarding the mantras and so forth—whether they are supplementary to the respective Vidyās of the Upaniṣads—based on the presence or absence of evidence: "Is it...?
The result [of the inquiry] is as before.
One might object: "But surely there is no inclusion [of these elements], because there is no evidence that they are subordinate to those [vidyās]. To this, he replies:
"Certainly. Mantras and so forth are subordinate to their respective vidyās because they are in proximity to vidyās that possess fruit, just like the Puruṣamedha sacrifice found in the Taittirīyaka;
thus, the application of the illustrative example is consistent.

Regarding the Siddhāntin’s position, he states the subverting argument that the proximity [of the mantra] would otherwise be purposeless with the words "na hi" (for not). The purposefulness of the proximity consists in its making known the status of mantras and so forth—which lack an explicit fruit—as being subsidiary to that which possesses a fruit. Since this is possible, it is not reasonable to resort to that proximity as being devoid of meaning; this is the sense.
Alternatively, if the reading is "na" (not), the meaning is: it is not reasonable to resort to that [proximity] for such a purpose without a reason, i.e., "akasmāt."

One might object: "But surely, since mantras lack the capacity to reveal a meaning inherent in the knowledge (vidyā), they cannot be subordinate to that knowledge. This is raised with the word "nanu" (but surely). He replies: "And how so?"—meaning that by the sentence, "They proceed with the Pravargya rite prior to the Upasads," the subordination of the Pravargya to the sacrifice is heard; and since the Agniṣṭoma and other rites have heaven and the like as their purpose according to their respective scriptural injunctions, they do not have knowledge as their purpose. Thus he says: "And how so?"
He states that "this is not so" because mantras possess the capacity to illuminate the heart, the channels (*nāḍī*), and so forth, which are associated with the *vidyās*.
He says "and it is seen" because the employment of mantras in meditations (*upāsti*) is not observed anywhere else;

for instance, in the *Chāndogya*, a meditation on the three worlds as the hair of the body is taught for the sake of a son's long life, and this is the mantra of supplication used by the father therein.

In that context, he utters the son’s name three times with the words "by this one"; the meaning is: "Together with this son, I attain both this world and the other world through the word *bhūḥ*, and may there be no separation from my son.

He provides an illustration for the point that even those ritual acts which are enjoined elsewhere by specific scriptural statements are not precluded from being employed in connection with the meditations (*vidyās*) due to their proximity—namely, the Vājapeya sacrifice.

This refers to the case of the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, which, although enjoined for the fruit of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) by the statement, "One desiring spiritual luster should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," [is also employed in other contexts].

The meaning is that there is no contradiction, just as in the case of the Bṛhaspatisava, where the sentence located within the context of the Vājapeya—"Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava"—enjoins it as a subsequent subsidiary (uttarāṅga) of the Vājapeya.
Even though a single sentence effects both the recognition of the Bṛhaspatisava situated in another context and the injunction of its status as a subsidiary; [there is no conflict].

Furthermore, it is improper to perform [both] because it would entail the fault of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*); therefore, as in the case of the *māsāgnihotra*, a distinct ritual action called the *bṛhaspatisava* is enjoined as a subsidiary (*aṅga*).
Thus, there is no "application of what has already been applied" (*viniyuktasya viniyoga*), as established in the two systems of Bhaṭṭa and Guru.

Moreover, just as in the context of the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice, the obligatory *agnihotra* is recognized by its name in the statement, "Restraining his speech, he performs this *agnihotra* for that night."

Just as in the case of a modified sacrifice (vikṛti) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, where in a single sentence— "he offers the two ājyabhāgas"— there is recognition of the two ājyabhāgas established in the archetype (prakṛti) by means of the word, and their injunction by means of the sentence, why should it not be the same here, where there is recognition of the Bṛhaspatisava by means of the word and its status as an auxiliary (aṅga) is enjoined by means of the sentence?

Nor should it be argued that a noun (*nāmapada*) is incapable of recognizing an established action because it is dependent on a verb (*ākhyāta*) that prescribes the meaning of something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

For even if an already established thing is to be performed again as a subordinate part (*aṅga*), it can once more become something to be accomplished; thus, it is logical for the verb itself—though its status would otherwise be established—to be dependent on the noun which conveys a well-known meaning.

Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, the *kuṇḍapāyinām ayana* sacrifice would likewise enjoin the permanent *agnihotra* merely as a subordinate part; for such a consequence is actually desired.
Nor is there any contradiction with the earlier treatise (*pūrvatantra*), because the later treatise (*uttaratantra*) is more authoritative,
and because the earlier treatise is concerned with the distinction between independent and dependent meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Therefore, the intention of the venerable Bhagavatpāda is that the single verbal root-meaning named *bṛhaspati*, although already enjoined for the sake of Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*), is also enjoined as a subsidiary element of the *vājapeya* sacrifice.

Furthermore, there is a universally accepted example of that which is enjoined for one purpose being enjoined for another: the use of *khadira* wood and so forth, which, though enjoined for a sacrifice, is also enjoined for results such as vigor (*vīrya*).

Likewise, it might be argued that mantras and ritual acts, though enjoined elsewhere, are subordinate to knowledge (*vidyā*). Having reached this position, the author establishes the final conclusion with the words "Not these" (*naiṣām*) and so forth.

Even though there is a connection of the heart and other parts with the knowledges, because the meanings such as "piercing" (*vedha*) have no connection [with them], the entire meaning of the mantras is connected only to rites like malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), due to the proximity (*saṃnidhi*)—which is stronger than [any other factor]—being indicated by signs (*liṅga*) such as the piercing and so forth. Thus, the mantras [belong] only to the malevolent magic and the like.
The meaning is *viniyoga* (application).
From the sentence, "O God Savitṛ, impel [the sacrifice]," one sprinkles water around the fire from left to right; thus there is a connection with the sprinkling of water around the fire.
Furthermore, from the sentence, "He offers the Sāvitra oblation before the rite, offering at each pressing," there is a connection with that specific rite, the Vājapeya.
Regarding the phrase "of this mantra," he says: "tadviśeṣa" (its specific [details]).
He extends the stated reasoning to passages such as "the white horse" (Śvetāśvatara) and so forth by saying: "evamanyeṣām" (so too for others).
"Other means of knowledge" refers to context and the like.

Now, it was argued that even for those [mantras] employed elsewhere by means of *liṅga* (indicative power) and so forth, there may also be an application within the meditations (*vidyā*) by means of proximity (*saṃnidhi*), since there is no contradiction;
to this, he says: "For [proximity] is weak. This refers to a conflict between two [means of proof] when they have the same object (*samavāya*).
The weakness of another [word] is due to remoteness from the meaning;
the sense is that, in conveying its own meaning, the other word functions with an intervening step.
This is the intention: since that which has been employed in one place is rendered free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*), its employment elsewhere is indeed contradictory;

however, when the two means of proof (*pramāṇa*) that employ it are of equal strength, it is impossible to abandon the employment by either one. Therefore, as a last resort, the employment of what has already been employed is accepted by generating an expectancy, as in the cases: "The sacrificial post is made of *khadira* wood" and "For one desiring vigor, [the post] is made of *khadira* wood."

By the two sentences, "one should make [the post]" and "[one desiring vigor] should make it of khadira wood]," the quality of being made of *khadira* wood—which was already enjoined for the sacrifice—is further enjoined for the fruit of vigor.

However, where there is an inequality between the two means of proof (*pramāṇa*), such application is not accepted, because the application by the weaker means of proof is sublated by the stronger one.

For example, in the case of the verse beginning "Never art thou barren," the injunction "one worships the *gārhapatya* fire with this verse addressed to Indra" is established by the direct statement (*śruti*) of the instrumental case-ending, which is independent of anything else.

The status of being subsidiary to Indra, which is suggested by the *liṅga*—defined as the capacity to manifest Indra—is set aside by the status of being subsidiary to the *gārhapatya* fire, as made known by the [injunctive] remainder.
For *liṅga* does not directly indicate subsidiarity; rather, it merely manifests Indra.
By means of this *liṅga*, an implied *śruti* must be inferred, stating: "By this mantra, Indra is to be worshipped."

Since the cognition of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) arises through that [indirect means], the indicative mark (*liṅga*), which indicates subsidiarity with an intervening scriptural statement (*śruti*), is immediately sublated by the scriptural statement that directly conveys its own meaning.

Likewise, syntactical connection (*vākya*) is sublated by the indicative mark, as in the case of the two parts of the mantra: "I prepare this seat for you; I fashion it with a stream of ghee," and "Sit upon it, O essence of rice, being well-disposed, and take your stand in immortality. Here, each part [of the mantra] individually...

When there is an application through the medium of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*)— by means of the indicative power (*liṅga*) consisting in the capacity to manifest that [specific act]— in the case of the preparation of the seat and the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*),

the perceived syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is sublated; for even in the entire mantra, there exists the capacity to manifest the preparation of the seat as well as the capacity to manifest the placing of the sacrificial cake.

Furthermore, having postulated the indicative power (*liṅga*), there is a conceptualization of the direct statement (*śruti*); thus, in both cases, when the application of the entire mantra is understood, there is a greater distance from the single intervening direct statement in the case of the indicative power that has been postulated, because it is separated by both the indicative power and the direct statement.
Nor should it be argued that the capacity (*sāmarthya*) need not be postulated.

Because that which lacks capacity cannot be employed [in a function], for this very reason the capacity in the form of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is postulated for the word *gaṅgā* in its employment for the cognition of the "bank. Likewise, context (*prakaraṇa*) is sublated by syntactical connection (*vākya*), just as the twelve *upasad* rites mentioned in the context of the *sāhna* sacrifice are displaced from their status as subsidiaries of the *sāhna*—which would have been obtained through context—by the sentence "twelve [are for] the *ahīna*," which makes known their status as subsidiaries of the *ahīna*. Context, which consists of the primary rite's expectancy for its subsidiaries, is [sublated] by syntactical connection, capacity, and direct statement (*śruti*) regarding the unity of the sentence between the subsidiary and the primary.

Because when there is a cognition of the application for its own purpose through what is being postulated, both the capacity of the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) are weaker than the postulating sentence due to the intervention;
likewise, proximity (*saṃnidhi*) is sublated by context (*prakaraṇa*).
For example, [the rule] obtained through the reading in proximity to the specific Soma sacrifice called the *Abhiṣecanīya*, which is included within the context of the *Rājasūya*.

In the case of the narrative of Śunaḥśepa and others, the status of being subsidiary to the *Abhiṣecanīya* rite is set aside, and their status as subsidiary to the entire *Rājasūya* is established; this is because proximity (*saṃnidhi*) is weaker than a context (*prakaraṇa*) already established [by other means], since proximity functions as a creator of a context. In the same way, proximity overrides name (*samākhyā*). For instance, in the section named *Pauroḍāśika*, mantras for the rites of the *Āgneya*-cake and others are recited in sequence; therein—
In the proximity of the *sānnāyya* offerings consisting of curd and milk, the mantra "Be purified for the divine rite" is recited; there,

although the status of this mantra as a subsidiary to the purification of the *puroḍāśa* vessels would be established by the force of its name (*samākhyā*), that is set aside by proximity (*saṃnidhi*) and it is brought to the status of being a subsidiary to the purification of the *sānnāyya* vessels.

The section pertaining to the *puroḍāśa* is called *pauroḍāśika*; thus, although the human designation (*pauruṣasamākhyā*) indicates a general connection between the mantra contained within that section and the *puroḍāśa*, it is weaker because it depends on factors such as proximity (*saṃnidhi*) when it must indicate the specific application (*viniyoga*) consisting of the relationship between the subsidiary (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*).
Therefore, when there is such a conflict, the direct statement (*śruti*) is indeed the sublater, while the designation is merely the sublated.

However, regarding the four intermediate [means of proof], the meaning of the *Śrutiliṅga* Sūtra is that the preceding one sublates the succeeding one and the succeeding one sublates the preceding one.

Therefore, it is established that mantras already employed elsewhere by means of *liṅga* (indicative power) and so forth cannot be employed in the *vidyās* by means of the weaker *saṃnidhi* (proximity). The same applies to ritual actions (*karma*).
The meaning is that there is no evidence whatsoever for the idea that ritual actions assist knowledge (*vidyā*) or that they share a single fruit with them.
The phrase "apica" (furthermore) expresses this same point.
[An objection: "In that case, what is the status of the recitation of sentences such as 'piercing' (*vedha*) alongside the Upaniṣads? To this, he replies: "araṇya... (in the forest).
Therefore, it is established that rites involving mantras such as piercing (vedha) and the like are not to be combined with the meditative knowledges (vidyās). //25//

But in the case of loss, because the word "taking up" (*upāyana*) is supplementary [to it], it is like the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the hymns of praise, and the singing; this has been stated. (BS 3.3.26)
Regarding the removal [of impurities], it has been said:

"Just as a horse becomes stainless by casting off its old, dust-covered hair, so too shall I, having shaken off evil and being one whose self is perfected— that is, whose mind is made stainless— become clear, like the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu."

The meaning is that, having shaken off— that is, cast off— the body and being liberated from the identification with the body, he "comes toward" (abhisambhavāmi) the uncreated, immutable world whose essence is Brahman as his own inner self (pratyaktvena).
The meaning is that the knower is just like rivers which, upon reaching the ocean, abandon their names and forms.
The meaning is that, upon the death of that wise one, he abandons his inheritance— his wealth— and by means of that power of knowledge, he casts off both his good and evil deeds.

Acquisition (*upāyana*) is the taking [of something], because it is preceded by relinquishment; since taking is impossible for two things that have not been relinquished, relinquishment follows by implication.

However, where relinquishment alone is explicitly heard in the text, a doubt arises as to whether the coexistence of relinquishment and acquisition is necessary or not; thus he says, "But where... and so forth.

In this context, the result is that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) the excellence of the praise is not established, whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) it is established. Although in the *Tāṇḍya* and *Atharvaṇa* Śrutis—which concern knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-vidyā*)—only the abandonment of karma is heard and not its "attainment" (*upāyana*), one might raise the objection that since "attainment" is heard in the *Kauṣītaki* Śruti regarding the knowledge of the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahma-vidyā*) seated upon the couch, it should be integrated here as well. Anticipating this, [the author] says:

He states that there is no synthesis because of the difference between the meditations (*vidyā*), using the phrase "in another meditation" (*vidyāntara*). Furthermore, just as it was stated that there is no synthesis in the meditations because the ritual acts of mantras are not mandatory, so too, since abandonment is possible even without the acquisition [of specific qualities], acquisition is not mandatory; thus, by way of analogy, the conclusion follows that there is no attainment.
He establishes the conclusion with the words "But in the case of abandonment," and so forth.
The meaning of the Sūtra is that because the word "appropriation" (upāyana) is supplementary, it requires the word "abandonment" (hāna).
The intention is that, based on the analogy of the horse's hair, since the merit and demerit shaken off require a location elsewhere, their appropriation by others must be stated.

Regarding the rule that there is no combination of qualities when there is a difference in the Vidyās, he says "yaducyate" (as for what is said), meaning that this is established as pertaining to the domain of ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) and not to the domain of praise (*stuti*). [An objection: But if praise is accomplished even by means of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the abandonment of what was heard, for what purpose is the explanatory passage concerning the taking up (*upāyana*) brought in?

Regarding this, he says: "for the sake of attaining the excellence of praise. Now, one might object: "The connection of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) with an injunction (*vidhi*) is well-known, but not its connection with another explanatory passage"; therefore, he says: "and it is well-known. The meaning is: "from this world, the earth."
Because the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons are treated as one, there are five seasons.
Regarding the conceptualization of the sacrifice as a person, it is stated in the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa* that "there are two Triṣṭubh verses for the sake of [endowing him with] sense organs.
In response to the inquiry as to how the Triṣṭubh—being merely a meter—can be conceived of as a sense organ, the meaning is that this Yajurvedic statement is cited in corroboration.

[Objection: Since merit and demerit are formless, their material cause (upādāna) is impossible; therefore, there can be no "taking along" (anupasaṃhāra). To this he says: "And because it is for the purpose of praising knowledge. The meaning is that the word "they attain" (upayanti) expresses that the fruit of those two [merit and demerit] residing in the knower is obtained by others through the power of knowledge. [Objection: But how can the fruit of actions residing in one person be transferred to another?
If it is argued that [the result occurs] by the force of the scriptural statement, we say no; for it is not heard that they "attain the fruit.
Nor should it be said that it is here as in the case of the merit from a *śrāddha* performed by a son accruing to the ancestors.

According to the maxim that "the fruit belongs to him for whose sake an action was performed," although an action performed with the intent of satisfying the ancestors has a result residing in a different locus (the ancestors), it is impossible for a wise person at the time of performing the rite to have a result in a different locus that was not intended.

Furthermore, since the action ceases to exist upon the fall of the body of the wise person, the result would accrue to one who serves the wise person throughout their life or to one who hates them; therefore, he says: "one should not be overly attached."

The meaning is as follows: through service to or hatred of a wise person, merits and demerits equal to those residing in the wise person arise for the servant and the hater respectively; since the acceptance of these [merits and demerits] by the wise person occurs as their fruit, there is no insistence on this point because the resolution is easily obtained.
He states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that the "gift" (*upāyana*) and so forth are merely praises: "upāyana... etc.

If the intention were to discuss the *upāyana* (the taking up [of qualities]), the author of the Sūtras would have mentioned the *upāyana* alone in the summary; therefore, by mentioning that [the *upāyana*] in connection with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), he indicates that it is a matter of praise (*stuti*).
To the question, "What is the relevance of a discussion on praise within this chapter (*pāda*) which consists of an inquiry into knowledge (*vidyā*)? he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He provides an illustrative example for the principle that a specific detail found in one Vedic branch (*śākhā*) should be adopted in another branch as well: "The *kuśa*-grass," etc. (*kuśādi*).
The *kuśās* are wooden sticks used by the *udgātṛ* priests for counting the hymns (*stotra*).

"O *kuśās*, you are of the forest (*vānaspatyāḥ*); 'forest-plant' (*vanaspati*) refers to a great tree standing in the forest, and you originate from that. Being such as you are, protect me—save me! This is the prayer of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

In this context, because of the feminine designation "tāḥ" (they) and because of the commentary stating "audumbarīḥ," it should be understood that the word *kuśa* has a feminine gender when referring to the small sticks (*śalākā*), but not when referring to the *darbha* grass itself, according to the grammatical rule: "the word *kuśa* is not feminine.
He explains the example from the Vedic meters with the words "yathā ca" (and just as).

The meters consist of nine syllables; some belong to the Asuras and others to the Devas. Regarding the rule "they praise with these meters," since no specific distinction is initially established, the meaning is that a specific one is adopted based on the statement of Paiṅgi. He explains the praise with the words "just as":

when there is an inquiry among the Chandogas and others as to when the chant belonging to the *ṣoḍaśin* cup—an auxiliary of the *Atirātra* sacrifice—should take place, a specific time is determined by the Vedic text of the Ṛgveda, which states, "The *ṣoḍaśin* chant occurs when the sun has entered the moment of rising."
This is the meaning.
Those who study the *ṛc* verses are called *ārcas*.
He analyzes the "singing along" (*upagāna*) with the words "just as."

The meaning is that, because of the general scriptural statement "the officiating priests (ṛtvij) sing along," and because of another scriptural statement "the Adhvaryu does not sing along," one concludes the specific point that the officiating priests other than the Adhvaryu are the ones who sing along.
Now, why is it accepted that even sentences such as those concerning the *kuśa* grass have a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) with another specific scriptural statement?
To this he says: "For [it is] produced by another scriptural statement... and so forth.

When there is a possibility of a single unified statement (*ekavākyatā*) between the general rule and the specific rule, it is not proper to create a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) and thereby assume an option (*vikalpa*)—such as "the Adhvaryu both sings along and does not sing along"—based on the prohibition "not the Adhvaryu" and the non-specific scriptural injunction; for an option is resorted to only as a last resort (*agatyā*), as in the case of *vrīhi* and *yava* grains. This is the meaning.
The assumption of an alternative option is improper because it is vitiated by eight defects.

To explain: if one relies on the statement regarding rice (*vrīhi*), then there is the abandonment of the accepted authority of the statement regarding barley (*yava*), and the acceptance of its unaccepted lack of authority; [and similarly for the other case].

If one were to rely on the barley injunction at one time, there would be four defects in that single barley injunction: the abandonment of its established authority and the acceptance of its lack of authority, as well as the acceptance of its lack of authority and the abandonment of that same lack of authority.

Similarly, there are four defects in the rice injunction as well. Thus, in order to avoid such faulty alternatives, Jaimini maintains that even two scriptural texts from different recensions (śākhās) form a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatā); as it has been said: "Tad uktam."

In the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "One who is not initiated does not offer oblations," while elsewhere it is heard: "One should offer the Agnihotra as long as one lives. In that case, if the sentence regarding the non-initiated were a prohibition of the oblation, then because it would serve the purpose of the sacrifice, the prohibition would have to be performed; yet, by the injunction to perform it throughout one's life, the oblation would have to be performed—thus there would be an option (vikalpa) between the two.

And that would be improper; rather, since the sentence concerning the initiated (*nadīkṣita*) is supplementary to the sentence concerning lifelong [observance], the negative particle (*na*) must serve to exclude the other, acting as an indicator for "other than the initiated," and not as a prohibition of the oblation.

Therefore, the meaning of the Siddhānta-sūtra of the *Adīkṣitādhikaraṇa* is that there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) stating: "Hence, one who is not initiated should offer oblations for as long as he lives.

Here, the venerable Bhagavatpāda recited the sūtra itself; however, the commentators (Miśras) stated that the Siddhānta-sūtra of the *Paryudāsādhikaraṇa*—"But it should be a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), because an option (*vikalpa*) is improper; it should be a part of the injunctions"—is what was recited here by implication (*arthataḥ*).
That is to be considered:

for the meaning of the Sūtra is that it is heard [in scripture] that "the phrase *yeyajāmahe* must be employed in every sacrifice," and it is also heard that "one does not perform the *yeyajāmahe* in the *anuyāja* offerings."

In that case, even though the negative particle (*na*) functions as a prohibition, there would arise an option—namely, "it should be employed" versus "it should not be employed"—just as there is an option regarding the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup in the *atirātra* sacrifice. However, because such an option is improper due to the lack of distinction in their sacrificial nature (*yajñatva*) among the *anuyāja* offerings, the sentence concerning the *anuyājas* cannot be a mere part of the injunction for the *ye-yajāmahe* formula;
rather, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), it must be understood as a supplementary portion (*śeṣa*) of that injunctive statement. This is the meaning.
And thus, there is a single syntactical unity (ekavākyatā) to the effect that the phrase "yeyajāmahe" is to be employed in sacrifices other than the *anuyāja*s.
He states another interpretation with the words "or else":
in the previous [section], having taken for granted that "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*) means the abandonment of karma, the inclusion of the "attaining" (*upāyana*) was stated.
The distinction here is that it is that very [shaking] which is being established as the probandum.
He states a doubt because the definition is identical in both cases, asking: "What?
For in the case of shaking, two results are observed regarding horse-hair and the like: falling away from its previous nature and transfer elsewhere.
In this regard, the meaning of the doubt is whether what is indicated is a "shaking off" (*saṃkrānti*) or rather a "falling away" (*cyuti*).
In that context, it is generally agreed by all that the primary meaning of the word "shaking" (*vidhūnana*) is "trembling.
However, that [trembling] is not possible for merit and demerit, as they are formless.

Therefore, the "shaking" (*cālana*) of those two refers to their inherent nature—their capacity to bestow fruits—and their "falling away" (*cyuti*) from that due to the obstruction caused by knowledge (*vidyā*). This is what is to be understood; it is not a literal "loss," because it is impossible for those two, being formless, to migrate elsewhere, and because they would otherwise depend on something else.
This is the meaning of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "It is indeed in the case of loss."
If mere falling away (cyuti) were the intended meaning, then the expression "they go toward" (upayanti) would be inconsistent.

Nor should it be argued that there is no impossibility because, while in some instances where the word *upāyana* (approaching) occurs in proximity to the root *dhū* (to shake), abandonment (*hāni*) is indicated, yet in other cases—such as with a learned servant—the root *dhū* alone indicates the transfer of equal karma to another. For [in those cases], it is not abandonment that is indicated.

The sense is that even for the root *dhū* alone, since its primary meaning is impossible [in this context], it is more appropriate for it to indicate elsewhere through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) the abandonment (*hāni*) which has already entered the mind. Having raised the objection that because "taking up" (*upāyana*) is not the primary meaning, it cannot serve as the basis for indicating "abandonment" anywhere, he refutes it with the words "Even though... and so forth, showing that taking up—which consists in the acceptance of merit and demerit by way of their fruits—is logically untenable without abandonment, and thus serves to determine the secondary indication.

Just as elsewhere the mention of being made of udumbara wood and so forth serves as a determiner for the *kuśa* grass and other items, so too this "taking up" (*upāyana*) serves as a determiner that "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*) signifies abandonment; thus he says: "In some places also.
Why is "shaking off" not said to be primary? To that he replies: "And not..."

Nevertheless, raising the doubt as to how "abandonment" (hāna) is indicated [by implication], he says "and the horse" (*aśvaśca*), meaning that it is through the primary connection (*mukhya-sambandha*).

Having stated the two forms of the seed of indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—namely, impossibility (*anupapatti*) and connection (*sambandha*)—he points out the indicative word (*lakṣaka-pada*) with the words "like a horse" (*aśva iva*).

The meaning is that the word "having shaken off" (*vidhūya*) signifies abandonment (*hāna*) in its ultimate sense within the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and thus it indicates abandonment in the case of the subject under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*) as well.

Alternatively, let it be that [the root *dhū*] expresses only "abandoning" (*hāna*). Nor is there a contradiction with the Dhātupāṭha, which states "dhūñ means trembling," because that [entry] is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*); thus he says "aneka... (in the verse). The meaning is that the Jaimini-sūtra, which was previously cited and explained, establishes that the "taking up" (*upāyana*) found in another recension serves to determine that "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*) is indeed "abandoning. Thus, since it is established that "shaking off" is "abandoning," it is proven that the "taking up" is to be combined with the mere "abandoning. //26//
Because there is nothing further to be crossed in the hereafter, so it is with others. (BS 3.3.27)
"In the next world" means in another life;
"on the way" means on the middle path.

Relying on the previously mentioned fact that "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*) signifies "abandoning" (*hāna*), and noting the scriptural statement that this abandonment occurs immediately after crossing the river—as well as the scriptural statement in passages such as "like the hairs of a horse" that it occurs prior to the casting off of the body—the author states the doubt: "Now, what... and so forth.

In the passage, "In the middle of the path to the world of Brahman, he crosses the river named Virajā; by that, he shakes off his good and evil deeds," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the destruction of karma occurs at the halfway point. This is because the use of the pronoun *tat* (by that) in the revealed text (*śruti*) refers to the immediately preceding act of crossing the river, thereby identifying that very act as the cause of the abandonment of karma. However, in that prima facie view, it remains unestablished that knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cause of the destruction of karma.
Considering that this is established in the final doctrine (siddhānta), he establishes the conclusion: "In the state beyond" (sāṃparāya).
This means prior to death.

The meaning is that since there is no fruit for one who has departed—that is, one who is dead—for some time while karma still exists, and because entry onto the path of the gods is impossible [at that stage], exhaustion occurs at the very beginning.
He says "contrary to knowledge" because knowledge, which is the cause of destruction, is non-existent midway on the path.
However, the reading immediately following the crossing of the river must be rejected, as it contradicts the meaning; thus he says "therefore."
The sense is that by the pronoun "that" (tat), the very knowledge under discussion is expressed. //27//
According to one's preference, because there is no contradiction between the two. (BBs 3.3.28)

Furthermore, since the performance of knowledge according to one's will (*chandataḥ*) is impossible for one who has died, the causal relationship between the two—the exhaustion of knowledge and the exhaustion of karma—as heard in scripture would be contradicted.

Moreover, according to the principle that "when the complete cause exists, there is no delay in the effect," you would incur a contradiction with scriptural passages such as the *Tāṇḍya*, whereas in our position there is no contradiction; thus he says, "according to one's will" (*chandataḥ*).

Therefore, since the abandonment of karma is the fruit of knowledge, it is established that the mention of the "taking up" (*upāyana*) in the case of mere abandonment is for the purpose of praising knowledge. //28//
The purposefulness of the journey is established in both ways; otherwise, there would be a contradiction. (BS 3.3.29)

Regarding the purposefulness of the path (*gati*): in some instances, the path is heard of in connection with knowledge possessing qualities (*saguṇavidyā*), but it is not heard of in connection with knowledge devoid of qualities (*nirguṇavidyā*). Since the path is mentioned in proximity to the "forsaking" (*hāna*) [of the body] and yet appears unnecessary there, a doubt arises. Based on the connection with the preceding illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntasaṃgati*), he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "Just as...
The meaning is that, because the path is heard of in some places just like the "taking up" (*upāyana*), it should be included everywhere.
In this regard, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) holds that even for those who know the attributeless (nirguṇa), there is a requirement for a path for the sake of liberation;
however, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that there is no such requirement.

The established conclusion is that there can be no synthesis [of paths], because it would contradict scriptural authority supported by logic, namely that a path is required only for the attainment of an object separated by space and other factors.
Stainless and unattached, Brahman is equanimity. //29//
[The mind] has arisen [in a new state], because its characteristic object is perceived, as in the world. (BBs 3.3.30)

[Objection: In that case, would not the path be useless even for the knowledge with attributes (*saguṇavidyā*)? To this he says: "It is appropriate. That [attainment] is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), i.e., the cause, of the object; thus, it is "that which has that as its characteristic" (*tallakṣaṇārtha*). //30//
There is no restriction regarding all [the powers], for there is no contradiction with scripture and inference. (BBs 3.3.31)
There is no restriction regarding all [meditations].

Here too, since the subject matter is specifically the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-mārga*), a doubt arises because of the mention of specific meditations (*vidyā*) in certain contexts and because there are also general scriptural statements. Regarding this, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "What, then, [is the case]? Since a distinction exists between the presence and absence of the path in meditations on the qualified (*saguṇa*) and unqualified (*nirguṇa*) Brahman, it follows by way of analogy that there is likewise a restriction among the qualified meditations. In response to this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) refutes that restriction; thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the path, but rather non-restriction (*aniyama*).
The result applies in both cases.
Having stated the context regarding the restrictive rule (*niyama*), he states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for [avoiding] redundancy with the words "furthermore" (*api ca*).
The meaning is that if the path already mentioned in one place were to apply elsewhere as well, the repetition would be useless.
He establishes the conclusion with the words "of all [the meditations].
"Exaltation" refers to the world of Brahmā.
He says "this is not so" to show that there is no fault in the subordination of the specific context by means of scriptural statements and other evidence that lack qualification.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: among those authorized for that [path], those who thus know the five fires, and those who in the forest worship with "faith and austerity"—that is, they meditate on Brahman characterized by faith and austerity—they attain the light (*arciṣam abhisambhavanti*). Now, one might object: since only faith and austerity are mentioned in the scripture, would not the journey via the light and so forth belong only to them, and not to those whose practice consists of the Vaiśvānara-vidyā and other such meditations? This is the doubt expressed by the words "But how? He resolves this with "This is no fault," because the path of the ignorant is prohibited; therefore, by the terms "faith" and "austerity," what is indicated is the knowledge of Brahman which is accomplished through them.
That is the station of the Brahma-world;
"gone beyond" means turned away,
insofar as the defects of desire and anger do not exist there.
The meaning is that those who perform mere ritual acts (*kevalakarmin*) and even ascetics (*tapasvin*) who lack knowledge do not go [by this path].

He states a sentence free from the defect of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*): "But the Vājasaneyins... Furthermore, because scripture declares a downward course for those who have fallen away from both paths characterized by knowledge and action, he says: "Now, as for those two... [to show] that those who meditate on Vaiśvānara and others attain the path beginning with light (*arcis*).

The *daṇḍaśūka* is a snake. Furthermore, having stated without distinction that those who have departed [from the body] proceed by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*)—in the Smṛti passage: "Fire, light, the day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice; departing there, the people who know Brahman go to Brahman"—[the author] says "Smṛti" to indicate that they attain that [Brahman].
The bright path consists of the route beginning with light (arcis) and so forth; the dark path consists of the route beginning with smoke (dhūma) and so forth;
[these pertain] to the world subject to knowledge and action.
[The two paths] are considered eternal and constant.
Among them, by one [path], which is white, one goes to Brahman from which there is no return; by the other, having gone to heaven, one returns again—this is the meaning.
He refutes the fault of tautology with the words "as for that which... (yatpunar).

In each of those instances, there is the hearing of the path for the purpose of daily reflection on the path, since it is understood through the context that meditation on the path is a constituent part of knowledge (*vidyā*).
And so the author of the Sūtras will state: "And because of the application of recollection of the course [of transmigration] remaining from that."

The meaning is that this repetition is for the purpose of making it known that those who have not heard of the path obtain the path even without meditating upon the path, through the power of their knowledge (*vidyā*).
Therefore, it is established that in all meditations (*upāsanā*) where the symbols (*pratīka*) differ, there is the attainment of the world of light (*arcis*) and so forth. //31//
The persistence of those who hold office lasts as long as their office endures.

The established conclusion is that, as long as there is a specific office or qualification (*adhikāra*), the journey [of the soul] is purposeless in the case of knowledge devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa-vidyā*) because its fruit is liberation;
however, in all cases of knowledge with attributes (*saguṇa-vidyā*), it is purposeful because its fruit is the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*).
That [objection] is not tenable;

for since even those who possess knowledge of reality are seen to take rebirth in the Itihāsas and other texts, it follows that knowledge does not have liberation as its fruit—this is the connection [of the objection] arising from such a challenge.
The observation of rebirth among the knowers of reality is shown in the Bhāṣya to be a seed of doubt.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the scriptural texts concerning liberation through knowledge are merely praises of knowledge and thus knowledge lacks liberation as its fruit, the result [of the inquiry] is the inclusion of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-mārga*) because there is no distinction in their having the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) as their fruit;
whereas in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the distinction is that the aforementioned systematic arrangement is established. This is also the case in the Śruti.
In the mantra "medhātithermeṣa," the birth of Indra as a ram is perceived;
the meaning is that the *arthavāda* of the *Bahvṛcas* has this sense: that Vasiṣṭha was born as the son of Urvaśī.
The term "occasional" (*pākṣika*) is used in a superficial sense.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that [knowledge] is indeed not a cause [of liberation].
He establishes the final position (*siddhānta*) with the words "But those..."—that knowledge is not a non-cause of liberation.
In the established order of the world, "authority" (*adhikāra*) refers to ownership.
As long as there exists the *prārabdha* karma that brings about [the body], for that duration those who hold office remain in the state of *jīvanmukti*;
upon the exhaustion of *prārabdha*, due to the absence of obstacles, *videhakaivalya* (liberation while bodiless) occurs. Regarding this, he states the proof with the word "atha" (*atha*).
"Then" (*atha*) means immediately after the exhaustion of *prārabdha*.
Thereafter, having risen— meaning having emerged and abandoned the body— he becomes distinct, absolute, and of the very nature of Brahman.
Being alone and without a second,
he abides in the intermediate state, which is his own indifferent (udāsīna) essential nature.
Now, one might ask: "If even the wise undergo another birth, how can there be liberation? To this he says: "That which has once set in motion.
If the wise were subject to another birth dependent on karma other than that which has already begun (prārabdha), then there would be no liberation through knowledge;
but this is not the case.

However, they exhaust the *prārabdha* karma—which has arisen once for the sake of the fruits of many births—and even while taking birth, they do not grieve due to the power of the yoga of knowledge; the meaning is that upon the completion of the *prārabdha*, they are liberated.
The reason why the next birth of the knowers is dependent on the *prārabdha* caused by their previous birth is their state of having unimpaired memory (*aluptasmṛtitva*).
For there is a pervasion (vyāpti) such that whoever possesses another birth dependent on other karma while being endowed with the memory of past births is one whose memory has been lost; thus,
in the case of the knowers (jñānins), due to the absence of the pervader, the absence of the qualified pervaded is established.

[Objection: "But surely their lack of lost memory is established otherwise by virtue of their being rememberers of past births (jātismara). To this he says: "And these [are] not... The meaning is that since they possess the qualifying attribute of not being rememberers of past births, the absence of the qualified entity (the specific state) is established simply due to the absence of the qualificand. Those who lack recognition of their previous bodies, who are dependent on others, and who possess self-conceit are the rememberers of past births.
However, there is a distinction: those who hold office retain their former names, yet they are independent and free from ego-inflation.
Therefore, the meaning is that he engaged in *vyudya*—that is, he carried out a debate—with Janaka.
For one who possesses knowledge (*vidvas*), there is no bondage because there is an absence of karma other than that which has already begun (*prārabdha*).

He establishes the point that the scriptural statements regarding liberation through knowledge—supported by the principle that "in the absence of the cause, there is an absence of the effect"—are not merely figurative praise, with the passage beginning "If indeed [knowledge] has been employed," and so forth.
He also provides a logical argument for the meaning stated in the Śruti and Smṛti, beginning with "Nor is it ignorance.

[An objection is raised: "If the destruction of karma, which is its effect, occurs because the afflictions (*kleśa*) are burnt away by knowledge (*vidyā*), then how can there be the continued existence of *prārabdha* (karma already set in motion)?"
Regarding this, he says: "of that whose fruit has already begun" (*pravṛttaphalasya*).

The sense is that, because scripture declares that for the knower [liberation] lasts until the fall of the body, and because of actual experience, it is established that knowledge—which removes a portion of the ignorance that veils [the Self]—lacks the capacity to remove that portion of ignorance which is conducive to the persistence of the distractions of *prārabdha* (commenced karma); therefore, the exhaustion of *prārabdha* occurs through experience alone.

Anticipating the question of how those who possess knowledge can hold an office, he says, "And in other cases of knowledge," [meaning] that it is due to the power of worship and other practices performed prior to the attainment of knowledge;
"pratisaṃcara" refers to the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*),
and "of the Supreme" refers to Hiraṇyagarbha.
The meaning is that at the conclusion of their qualification, those who have directly realized the Self are liberated.

Anticipating the doubt that even the fruit, which is the state of becoming Brahman, might be something yet to be produced, [the author] states "not so" (na hi), citing the sublation by the scriptural text "That thou art" (tat tvam asi).
Therefore, it is established that in the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman, there is no inclusion of the path (mārga). //32//

But there is a restriction of the meditations on the syllables [of "Om"] because of the commonality and the presence of that [state], as in the case of the *aupasada* [offerings]; this has been explained. (BS 3.3.33)
Regarding "akṣaradhiyām" (of the cognitions of the Imperishable): here, the subject matter consists of the negative words that establish the Imperishable Brahman.
He states the doubt—using the words "tāsām" (of these)—based on whether or not it is possible for as many [negations] as are heard in each instance to negate all duality without exception.

Just as in the case of the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa-vidyā), there is no synthesis [of meditative elements] because the path is not required, so too, since the negations heard in one's own recension can— by way of implication— negate all dualities, there is no need for the words of negation found in other recensions; thus, based on this analogy, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) holds that there is no synthesis, with the result being simplicity (lāghava).
In our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, the result is the absence of these two defects.
To explain: if the negation of what is not heard is indicated by the words that are heard, then there is the defect of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*);

if it is not so indicated, then because the negation of all duality would not be established, there would be the defect of the absence of a cognition of the non-differentiated (*nirviśeṣa*). This is the distinction.

The construction of the sūtra is as follows: "akṣaradharmī" refers to the substratum that is the Imperishable; "akṣaradhiyaḥ" refers to the cognitions that negate duality; "taddhetavaḥ śabdāḥ" means the words that are the causes of those cognitions; and "tāsām avarodhaḥ" means their inclusion or synthesis.

If it is argued that because the subordinate Brahman exists in all recensions (śākhās) and because the knowledge of Him is uniform, there should be a synthesis of the remaining [details], then—since the same logic applies—the problem of redundancy remains. To this, he says: "for the sake of elaboration" (*prapañcārtham*).
Thus:

"Since [attributes] such as bliss constitute the essential nature [of Brahman], let there be their subsumption; however, since negations are not the Self and are infinite, there can be no subsumption. In response to this objection regarding the scope [of the rules of subsumption], [the reply is:

although they are not the Self, because they serve the purpose of bringing about the knowledge of the undifferentiated Brahman, their inclusion is established by virtue of being negations of ignorance and its products.

The meaning is that it is appropriate to consider the subsumption (upasaṃhāra) of words expressing prohibitions— which are established by their state of being independent, not coarse, and not minute— through syntactic unity with the prohibitory sentences heard elsewhere.
He explains the illustrative example for the connection of supplements (śeṣa) heard in one place with a primary element (śeṣin) situated elsewhere, saying "just as" (yathā).

Having begun with the statement, "Jamadagni, desiring prosperity, performed a sacrifice with the four-night rite," the *jāmadagnya*—the *ahīna* (non-soma) four-night sacrifice performed by Jamadagni—is prescribed. In that context, the *Taittirīyaka* ordains the *iṣṭis* (sacrificial offerings) accomplished by means of sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), stating: "In this [rite], the *upasads* consist of sacrificial cakes.

Since these are to be performed by the *adhvaryu*, and because the mantras originating from the Sāmaveda are to be employed therein, the meaning is that their performance is by the *adhvaryu* alone, not by the *udgātṛ*.
The meaning of the mantra for addressing Agni is that the *hotṛ*-offering and the ritual action of the fire belong to you alone.

The injunction of origin (*utpattividhi*) is secondary because it depends upon a result; the injunction of application (*viniyogavidhi*) regarding the result of what has been originated is primary because it possesses fruit.
Likewise, since mantras originate in the *Udgātṛ-veda*, their performance is by the *Udgātṛ*.

The meaning of Jaimini’s sūtra is as follows: regarding the conflict between a subordinate and a primary element when there is a contradiction—such as the performance being prescribed by the *adhvaryu* through the rules of application (*viniyoga*)—the primary element, being more powerful, takes precedence; thus, the mantra, which constitutes the Veda, is to be employed by the *adhvaryu*, because its origin is for the purpose of application.

Although, according to the *Śābara-bhāṣya*, because the *Vāravantīya* and other *sāmans* originate in the *Sāmaveda* with the high pitch (*uccaiḥ-svaraka*), they are [recited] loudly as an auxiliary to the fire-installation (*ādhāna*).
Regarding the application of accents, in the passage "He who, knowing thus, sings the Vāravantīya, sings the Yajñāyajñīya,

sings the Vāmadevya," the low (upāṃśu) accent of the Yajurvedic [Sāmans] is to be employed by virtue of the applicatory injunction (viniyoga-vidhi) belonging to the Yajurveda at the time of the fire-consecration (ādhāna).

When there is a conflict between a subordinate quality and the primary [textual source], since the originative injunction (utpatti-vidhi) is for the purpose of the applicatory injunction, the Sāmans are connected with the accent of the Yajurveda through the force of that primary applicatory injunction.
Thus the Sūtra has been explained;
nevertheless, because the principle is the same, the mantras of the *aupasada* [offering] are cited as being within the scope of the Sūtra, so there is no contradiction. //33//
On account of the mention of this much [in the Upanishads]. (BS 3.3.34)

Because of this repeated instruction, and because there is a difference in the manner of presentation in both mantras as well as the appearance of the identity of the object to be known, he states the doubt: "What is it here?
In the passage concerning the drinking of the *ṛta*, qualities are heard [stated] such as, "The imperishable Brahman which is supreme."

In the case of the *Suparṇa* passages, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that attributes such as "not eating" and so forth are not to be combined with one another; however, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), because the meaning of the sentences is one insofar as they describe the nature of Brahman, there is a combination—this is the distinction.
Let it be granted, then, that there is a combination of the cognitions of the Imperishable (*akṣara*) due to the unity of the object of knowledge.
But here, because of the difference in the objects of knowledge (*vedya*), there is no combination; this constitutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by way of a counter-example.
If it is argued that this has already been refuted in the section concerning qualities (*guṇādhikaraṇa*), we reply: true.

However, in order to maintain the primary sense of the word "drinking," the two who drink—the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*)—must be understood as the substrates of the act of drinking, both by their own nature and through figurative attribution. As for the "two birds" (*suparṇau*), since there is a suspicion that they might refer to the individual soul and the Lord (or the individual soul and the limiting adjunct of ignorance), we must consider that in both mantras, due to the commonality of the dual number, there is a recognition of two identical entities characterized by innate duality; this is because there is no sublation [of this recognition] and it is supported by the context and other factors. Thus, referring back to the individual soul, [the passage points toward] the non-transmigrating Brahman.
The intention is that this aphorism is for the purpose of explaining the purport of the two mantras in detail. //34//
It is internal to the self, like the collection of living beings. (BBs 3.35)
Just as in the case of the multitude of living beings within [the body],
a pot or similar object is immediate through being an object of consciousness,
whereas Brahman is immediate by virtue of not being an object at all.
The ablative case is used in the sense of the nominative.
Here, in the Śruti, the attribute of the self— immediacy— is predicated of Brahman,
and the attribute of Brahman— being the innermost of all— is predicated of the self.
Therefore, it should be understood that their identity has been firmly established.

In response to Uṣasta’s question, "Explain that to me," Yājñavalkya set forth the witness of seeing and so forth as the impeller of the vital breaths and other functions. Likewise, in response to Kahola’s question, "Explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all," he set forth the one who transcends hunger and other such needs.

In that regard, although there is a doubt concerning both Brāhmaṇas because of the question, the repetition, and the recognition of being "innermost to all," let there be identity of knowledge (vidyaikya) in the case of the two mantras due to the identity of the object to be known;
however, here, even though the objects to be known in the two Brāhmaṇas are identical, there is a difference in knowledge due to repetition,
just as there is a difference in the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) due to the repetition of the act of sacrificing— this is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by way of a counter-example.

In this regard, the distinction is that there is no mutual application of attributes (*dharmopasaṃhāra*) [in the case of the Smṛti], whereas in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is such application. First of all, it is established that the two [texts concerning] Brahman refer to one and the same reality, because it is impossible for both to be internal to everything (*sarvāntaratva*).
And thus, because the object of knowledge is one, there is no dispute regarding the unity of the Nirguṇa-vidyā. //35//
If it is argued that otherwise the distinction [between the two states] would be untenable, we say no; for it is like other [types of] instruction (upadeśa). (BS 3.3.36)

If it is argued that otherwise there would be no justification for the repetition [of the teaching] given the unity of the knowledge (*vidyaikya*), it is replied: that repetition alone serves to differentiate actions which is purposeless; however, in this case, since the repetition has another established purpose—namely, to state the specific quality of the Self described in the *Uṣasta-brāhmaṇa* as being beyond hunger and so forth—it does not differentiate the knowledge. This is the collective meaning. //36//
There is an interchange [of qualities], for they distinguish [the one] as being like the other. (BS 3.3.37)
There is a reciprocal interchange. "Reciprocal interchange" (vyatihāra) refers to the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara),
because that is what is heard in the scripture.

Furthermore, according to the maxim that "a vision directed toward the superior bears fruit when applied to the inferior," one must indeed cultivate the notion of the Lord's identity with the individual soul (jīva) even when doubt exists, based on the aforementioned reasoning. The scriptural passage concerning mutual exchange (*vyatihāra*), however, is established as being otherwise explained—as a mere repetition intended to strengthen that very notion—just like the case of repeated study (*abhyāsa*). This constitutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by way of illustration. In this regard, the distinction is that simplicity (*lāghava*) is the result for the prima facie view, whereas for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the meaningfulness of the scripture (*śrutyarthavattva*) is the result.
The meaning is that since the realization of oneness is already accomplished by the single utterance "I am thou," the statement "Thou art I" would be redundant.
He recalls the aforementioned objection with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Reasoning has scope only when there is a matter in doubt.
But here, because it is so heard in scripture, their mutual identity is to be meditated upon;

for even if the nature of being the individual self (*jīvātmatva*) is superimposed upon Brahman for the sake of meditation—just like its being composed of mind (*manomayatva*) and so forth—there is no possibility of any resulting inferiority. Thus he resolves the objection with the words: "This is not a fault."

He raises an objection, saying "But if this is so," [thinking]: "By abandoning the notion of inferiority toward Brahman and meditating on identity with the individual soul (jīva), exactly what I have stated follows.

He replies: "We do not [say that]. He explains: "The twofold nature of cognition is stated by us even though it was not mentioned by you; furthermore, this sentence is primarily intended for meditation, while the identity is established because it does not contradict other means of valid knowledge.
He concludes: "Therefore, this exchange [of attributes] is to be combined in the meditations involving the grasping of the 'I' (ahaṅgrahopāsti). //37//
For that [meditation] itself consists of truth and the other [qualities]. (38)
For that very [Brahman] is indeed "Satya" (Truth) and so forth.

The meaning is that whichever qualified seeker worships this Brahman— known as Hiraṇyagarbha— which is vast, all-pervasive, worthy of worship, the first-born among material beings, and which consists of "Sat" (Being) and "Tyat" (That), i.e., Satya (Truth)— the conquest of the worlds is the fruit for him.
The name "Satyam" consists of three syllables: *sa*, *ti*, and *yam*.

Among these, the first and last syllables are truth (*satyam*), while the middle syllable is untruth (*anṛtam*). Because it is enclosed on both sides by truth, it becomes essentially truth itself. Thus, the meditation on the syllables of the name is taught as an ancillary part of the knowledge of Truth (*satyavidyā*).

That which was previously introduced as being called the "Heart" (hṛdaya) and now described as possessing qualities such as being a Yakṣa and so forth—that very Puruṣa who is in the solar orb and in the eye—has as its fruit the destruction of evil through the knowledge of his two names, "Ahar" and "Aham. This is the meaning.

Here, [the author] states a doubt, beginning with the word "tatra," because a difference in fruits is heard between the preceding and following sentences, and because there is a reference back to the subject under discussion.

The result is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is a performance [of rituals] through the systematic arrangement of qualities (*guṇa-vyavasthayā*), whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is unity of performance.

Just as a duality of views was stated regarding the individual self (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) due to the differences in scriptural passages concerning their mutual identity, [so too is the case here].

Thus, by means of an illustration, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that there is a difference in knowledge (*vidyābhedah*) due to the difference in the mention of fruits: "Two" [is the word used].
It is improper to draw out only the qualified Brahman (*viśeṣya-brahmamātrākarṣaṇam*);

for by means of the pronouns "that which" (*yat-tat*), Brahman as previously described with its specific qualities is drawn forth, since there is an injunction of qualities such as being located in the sun and the eye.
And thus, he establishes the final conclusion—that the unity of the knowledge is established from the statement itself—by saying, "It is one alone.
He says, "Not so," because it is not like the case of the Dahara and Śāṇḍilya knowledges where there is merely a recognition of the oneness of Brahman;
rather, there are other reasons, such as the difference in context and so forth.

Thus, even when there is a difference in the meditative knowledge (*vidyā*), this knowledge of the identity of the object of worship (*upāsya*) would exist; however, here, since both possibilities are present, a doubt arises as to whether the *vidyās* are identical or distinct. The literal meaning is that, because of the knowledge of the identity of the form of the object of worship—expressed by the word "truth" (*satyam*)—there is a determination of the identity of the *vidyā*. In the absence of a cause for sublation, the general rule (*utsarga*) that the *vidyās* are identical due to the identity of form is established; nor is there a sublation of this rule on account of a difference in results. He states, beginning with "But as for... (*yat punar...*), that a difference in results is not established, because the mention of results regarding a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) is merely scriptural assertion (*śrutimātra*).

Furthermore, in cases where a fruit such as "desiring this" (*evaṅkāma*) is heard in connection with the primary injunction itself, the expectation for a fruit on the part of the subsidiaries is satisfied by the fruit of the primary rite alone; thus, the mention of a fruit in relation to a subsidiary is merely a eulogy (*stuti*).

Here, however, having accepted that the fruit of "conquering the worlds" belongs to the primary injunction of knowledge—namely, "one knows Brahman as the Truth born first"—we have stated that the mention of a fruit for the subsidiary consisting of names and forms is a eulogy.

In reality, however, since even in the primary injunction there is no mention of the word "desiring such" (*evam-kāma*), and a fruit must therefore be postulated according to the *Rātrisatra* principle, any fruit whatsoever that is heard—whether in the primary rite or its subsidiary—is equally "heard" (scripturally established).

Thus, by the logic of the *Jāteṣṭi* fruit, the distinction of having multiple fruits for a single primary rite through their combination is not established; this is what [the author] states with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).
He applies the Sūtra with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He sets forth and refutes the explanation of certain partial interpreters (*ekadeśin*) with the words "Some people" (*kecit*), and so on.

Regarding the view that there is a meditation on the golden person (*hiraṇyamaya-puruṣa*) upon the *udgītha*—which is an auxiliary to the ritual—in the *Chāndogya*, he states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this with the word "Therein" (*tatra*).
When the earth and fire are seen as the Self, the *Ṛk* and *Sāman* become its vocal qualities (*geṣṇau*).

Therefore, because the *Ṛk* and *Sāman* are its vocal qualities, the meaning of the scripture is that the Udgātṛ priest who knows "the Puruṣa is the Udgītha" is capable of accomplishing the fruit of the ritual action.
But the knowledge of Truth (satyavidyā) does not depend on being a subsidiary part of ritual action; thus he says, "Not so.

The meaning is that because the independent Hiraṇyagarbha-vidyā is distinct from the vidyās concerning the subsidiaries [of ritual], there is no combination of qualities [from one to the other]. //38//
Desire and so forth [are the cause] elsewhere; in that case, it is from the abodes and so forth. (BBs 3.39)

Regarding the qualities such as "having true desires" and "mastery" mentioned in the scriptures concerning knowledge with attributes (*saguṇa-vidyā*) and knowledge without attributes (*nirguṇa-vidyā*):

since there is doubt as to whether these qualities should be combined across the two or not— based on whether their combination yields a fruit or not— it follows that because the knowledge [of Brahman] is one, there should be a commingling of qualities.

Even here, since there is a distinction between the two knowledges (*vidyā*) based on the difference between their qualified (*saguṇa*) and unqualified (*nirguṇa*) forms, and since there is no fruit for the combination of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) in the knowledge of the unqualified, it follows—having reached this preliminary conclusion—that there is no combination. To this, the author establishes the final position (*siddhānta*) with the words beginning "In that regard, this... [and so forth]. Even though the difference between the knowledges is thus clear, how can there be a combination of qualities?
Regarding this, he says: "But [the qualities] of those possessing qualities.

Even though the qualities of those situated in different levels of ignorance differ, their synthesis in a state devoid of qualities is appropriate for the purpose of praise, as they reside within the intellect through the similarity of their bases (*āyatana*) and so forth;
for there is a desire for the excellence of the praise of knowledge.

Because it is appropriate to perform praise by means of qualities seen in any [text] whatsoever; even though the qualities residing in the Nirguṇa are indeed already included within Satyakāma and others residing in the Saguṇa, nevertheless, the statement regarding their combination (upasaṃhāra) is not redundant. This is because, by dispelling the doubt that the qualities heard in one place might be meditated upon elsewhere merely as a matter of praising the Nirguṇa, it serves to strengthen the fact of their inclusion. Thus, there is no fault. //39//
There is no omission [of the practice] due to reverence. (BBs 3.3.40)
"There is no omission [of the rite] due to its being performed with reverence.
Here, by means of the words "yat" (which) and "agnihotra," he states the doubt: "In this regard, the following is to be considered.

The connection to the chapter (*pāda*) is established because the discussion of the Prāṇāgnihotra—which is a subsidiary part of the knowledge (*vidyā*)—is undertaken as a duty to be performed prior to the feeding of guests by one who worships Vaiśvānara.

The distinction is that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), even when the meal is omitted, the Prāṇāgnihotra is to be performed with another substance, whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is omitted.

Now, one might argue: by the word "whatever" (*yat*) in the phrase "whatever food," the food implied by the act of eating is restated; then, by the injunction of connection with the oblation in the phrase "that which is to be offered," if the implied eating is omitted, the oblation dependent upon that implied food must also be omitted.

Thus the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) raises an objection with the words "tadyat" (as for that...). He refutes it with the sūtra of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), using the analogy: "Even when the meditation on the qualities of the qualityless [Brahman] is omitted, the praise is still accomplished through respect for the Prāṇāgnihotra, just as the stability of qualities intended for praise remains even when the actual eating is omitted. He begins this response with the words "evam prāpte" (this being the case).
"Thus, that [is done]" means that, having not performed the *prāṇāgnihotra* oneself, one performs it for the sake of guests.
Having recalled what was previously stated, he provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "But surely," etc.

Just as in the case of the *māsāgnihotra* occurring within the *kuṇḍapāyin-satra*, because of the word *agnihotra*—which here denotes the obligatory *agnihotra* figuratively—the attributes of the obligatory *agnihotra* [are extended].

Just as there is the acquisition of milk and other substances [in the Agnihotra], so too here, in the case of the *prāṇāhutis*, since milk and other substances are acquired by default due to the application of the term "Agnihotra," an exception is made by the rule prescribing food (*bhakta*) for the purpose of eating.

Therefore, because the rule regarding food serves as an exception, even if eating is omitted— and thus the subordinate quality (*guṇa*) known as "food" is omitted— there is no omission of the primary Agnihotra itself.

The meaning of "it follows" (*prāptam*) is that, in the absence of an exception (*apavāda*), its accomplishment is possible through the milk and other ingredients obtained by the general rule (*utsarga*).
This refers to the Jaimini-sūtra: "When a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is omitted, the primary element (*mukhya*) is not [omitted].
In the context of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), there are the *pavamāneṣṭi* offerings; therein it is stated: "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla-puroḍāśa*) to Agni Pavamāna."

The meaning is as follows: "offering" (nirvāpa) is heard as a subordinate element [of the ritual], as in the injunction, "one should offer the oblations in the *agnihotrahavaṇī*. This [use of the vessel] is obtained through the extension (*atideśa*) of the *agnihotrahavaṇī* prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) known as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
Since there is no *agnihotra* at the time of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), although that [vessel], being a subordinate factor, is omitted, the primary act of offering is not omitted.

Since rites such as those that have been commenced must necessarily be performed, when the prescribed substance is unavailable, the rite must be performed even with a substitute substance; this is the principle of substitution (pratinidhi-nyāya). //40//
Because of the scriptural statement regarding that [attainment] when it has arrived. (BS 3.3.41)
He establishes the conclusion: "Because, when it has arrived, there is an injunction for that.
