He raises the doubt as to how the nature [of Brahman] established starting from the *janmādi-sūtra* could not exist, saying: "But surely" (*nanu*). He replies: "True," meaning that the knowledge of the true nature [of Brahman] is the fruit of the Vedāntas, and its firmness is achieved through an inquiry into whether it serves the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*) or the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). //2//
Because we observe [the Buddha's] conduct. (BBs 3.4.3)

He states that the observation of the ritual conduct of those who know Brahman is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that knowledge of Brahman has ritual action as its constituent part: "Ācāra... etc.
The meaning is that he performed a sacrifice (*īje*).

Addressing the Brāhmaṇas with the words "O venerable sirs" (*bhagavantaḥ*), the King of Kekaya, a knower of Brahman, says: "I am about to sacrifice, I am going to perform a sacrifice; may the venerable ones dwell here. This is the meaning.
The phrase "in those other than [this]" means "in those whose intent is the injunction for knowledge.

Having obtained the knowledge that is the means to liberation, which requires little effort, they should not perform ritual action, which requires great effort; regarding this, he provides an illustration with the word "akva," meaning "nearby."
Even if the reading is "arka," the meaning remains exactly this. //3//
Because of that scriptural statement. (BS 3.4.4)

He states that there is also a scriptural mention in the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) to show that knowledge of Brahman is an auxiliary part of ritual action, saying: "Because of that scriptural statement" (Sūtra 4).
Because of the act of simultaneous grasping. (BBs 3.4.5)
He states another inferential mark with the word "samit":
the meaning is that knowledge and action follow him as he goes to the other world. //5//
Because there is an injunction for that which possesses it. (BBs 3.4.6)

Performing the duty consisting of service to the guru, having studied the Veda according to the rules during the remaining time after [the period of study], and immediately thereafter— meaning, from the family or house of the teacher, that is, from the state of studentship (brahmacarya)— having performed the formal return ceremony (abhisamāvartana), he remains established in the household life (gārhasthya) within his family; performing daily the study of his own Veda (svādhyāya) in a pure place, and practicing other obligatory duties (nitya-dharma) such as [the five great sacrifices], he [attains] the world of Brahman (brahmaloka).
The meaning of the Vedic text is that [one] attains [the fruit].
Just as threshing extends only until the removal of the husks, so too does study extend until the comprehension of the meaning.

This is established in the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā (Pūrvatantra) because, since the visible fruit known as the comprehension of meaning is possible, it is improper for study to have an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose.
And therefore, since even the *Brahma* [Veda] is the meaning of the Vedas, the injunction for ritual action belongs to one who possesses the knowledge of that; such is the meaning. //6//
And because of the restrictive rule. (BBs 3.4.7)
He states that even the lifelong observance of ritual action (*karmaniyama*) is a sign here, saying "and because of the observance" (*niyamācca*).
While performing actions in this body, one should desire to live for a hundred years; thus, while you live as a performer of action, O man, evil action does not cling to you.
There is no way other than through this [observance of] action.
The meaning is that there is no higher good without action (*karman*).
"Ending with old age and death" means having old age and death as its limit. //7//
But because of the teaching of something additional, Bādarāyaṇa holds this [view], for that is seen [in scripture]. (BS 3.4.8)

He establishes the final position—that the knowledge of reality is not an auxiliary part of ritual action—on the grounds that there is no remaining portion of ritual action for a superior agent who is a non-transmigrating Self; this is indicated by the word "superior" (*adhika*).
From the supplementary statement "of this great one," it follows that the Self to be seen, which is indicated by what is dear, is indeed the Supreme Self.
Furthermore, he who impels the vital breaths and so forth is also the Supreme Self alone, based on the supplementary statement concerning the transcendence of hunger and other such needs.

Likewise, the "Person in the eye" (*akṣipuruṣa*) is also the Supreme (*para*), because of the complementary passage stating that he is the "supreme light" (*paraṃ jyotiḥ*). Thus, there is no contradiction in accepting that the reference back to the individual soul (*jīva-anukarṣaṇa*) is intended to indicate non-difference. To the question, "How can this be? For if there is non-difference, it contradicts the soul's status as a transmigrating being," he says: "belonging to the Supreme Lord" (*pārameśvaram*).

The reason previously stated—that knowledge is an auxiliary to ritual action because, while not itself a fruit, it serves as a support for what remains of the ritual—is unestablished (*asiddha*); such is the sense. //8//
But the scriptural evidence is equal on both sides. (BS 3.4.9)
[The practice of renunciation] is not universal.

(BBs 3.4.10) Since those who know Brahman are seen to possess renunciation just as they possess action, the author states "But it is the same" (tulyaṃ tu) to show that their characteristic mark consisting of the performance of action is established otherwise—as being for the sake of maintaining the world order.
Furthermore, he states "Moreover" (api ca) to show that he who possesses action is not a knower of Brahman.
If it be argued that, in that case, the Vaiśvānara-vidyā would be a constituent part of ritual action (karma), he says: "But not...

The point is this: even though action is performed by those who know Brahman for the sake of maintaining the world, it does not constitute [true] karma, because they lack the sense of personal agency (abhimāna) and thus have no [binding] qualification for such action. // 9 // // 10 //
The division is like that of a hundred. BBs 3.4.11.

Having accepted that the statement regarding "taking hold" (*samanvārambha*) refers to one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*), the author of the Sūtras stated the distinction that knowledge takes hold of another seeker of liberation as one who is already liberated. However, in reality, that is not the case; thus he says: "And this statement regarding taking hold is not [to be taken literally]. In that context, regarding the transmigrating soul, he explains the meaning of the terms "knowledge" and so forth in the passage beginning with "that [knowledge] takes hold of him," which merely restates what is already established. He says: "In that [context]."
The knowledge of the Udgītha and so forth is prescribed, while that consisting of meditating on a naked woman and the like is prohibited. //11//
[The entitlement belongs] to one who possesses merely the study [of the Veda]. (BBs 3.4.12)

"Because there is no distinction" (nāviśeṣāt). Regarding the phrase "and this which," the word "has been stated" is to be supplied as the ellipsis; the meaning is "because of ignorance," that is, because of being devoid of knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas.
He says, "This is not a fault," [meaning] that the word "only" (mātra) excludes knowledge of the self, but does not exclude knowledge of ritual action. // 12 // // 13 //
Or rather, it is an approval for the sake of praise. (BsRp_3,4.1.14)

It has been stated that the injunction regarding ritual rules (*niyamavākya*) is intended for the ignorant, or else it is for the purpose of praising the knowledge of the wise; this is expressed by the words "praises" (*stutayaḥ*).

Thus, even when it says "perform action," it means that for you, O man, there is no transmigration through action other than the state of Brahman attained through knowledge—that is to say, there is no such thing as worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) by means of action.
For action does not defile [the knower].
The meaning is that it does not lead to the application of a new form; this is the intention of the Śruti. //14//
And some [hold] that it is by one's own will. (BBs 3.4.15)

He states that knowledge (*vidyā*) has independent fruit because it is characterized by the renunciation of progeny, ritual action, and means of action according to one's own will—this is expressed by the word "kāma" (desire).

The meaning is: for us, those for whom this very Brahman is the immediate Self (*ātman*), this alone is the world and the human goal (*puruṣārtha*); having reflected, "What shall we do with progeny and the rest?", they abandoned ritual action. Now, an objection is raised: is it not improper to say that the fruit of knowledge is "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*), since, like the fruit of action, it is unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*)? To this he replies: "anubhava" (experience). //15//
And the sublation [of the world]. (BsRp_3,4.1.16)

Knowledge is not only not a constituent part of ritual action because it serves no useful purpose for it, but also because it destroys ritual action; thus he says: "And [because of] its sublation" (1.1.16).
And [the same applies] to those whose semen is drawn up (ūrdhvaretas), for there is a scriptural statement to that effect. (BBs 3.4.17)

Furthermore, he states—beginning with the word "ūrdhva"—that the knowledge of the reality of action (*karmatattvajñāna*) and action itself do not stand in a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhūta*), because they reside in different classes of qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*), just like the Rājasūya and the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifices.

The meaning is that there are three divisions of dharma consisting primarily of ritual action corresponding to the [first] three stages of life (*āśrama*), while the fourth is "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*).

This is according to the Vedic revelation: "By means of celibate studentship one pays the debt to the sages, by sacrifice to the gods, and by progeny to the ancestors; thus one becomes free from debt."

Nor should one entertain the doubt that renunciation belongs only to one who has already entered the householder stage and discharged the three debts, based on the Smṛti passage: "Having paid off the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation; but he who pursues liberation without having paid them off goes downward. For this is refuted by the contradiction of such statements with the injunctions of Śruti and Smṛti which state, "One may renounce even from the stage of studentship," and "One should desire the second stage [of life] and dwell in it"; thus, it is understood that those Śruti and Smṛti passages containing explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) refer to those who lack dispassion. This is what he states with the words: "pratipanna... (having entered...).
"Therefore" means because of being established in renunciation (saṃnyāsa). //17//
Jaimini maintains that there is a reference [to the soul], because it is not an injunction; for [the scripture] indeed refutes [such an injunction]. (BS 3.4.18)

He raises the objection that "there is no renunciation" with the words, "Jaimini [holds] that there is a reference [to it]. Regarding the question of whether the life of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya), designated by the term *ūrdhvaretas*, is to be practiced or not, a doubt arises based on whether its source is valid or erroneous; he states that it is not to be practiced because its source is erroneous, saying, "The three. The plural number is used in view of the internal subdivisions of the stages of life (*āśrama*).
Accordingly, the *Kāṇvāyana-smṛti* is cited here according to its meaning:
"The *gāyatra*, the *brāhma*, the *prājāpatya*, and the *bṛhat*—thus the student (*brahmacārī*) is of four kinds.
Among these, he who, after the initiation (*upanayana*), for three nights eats neither pungent nor salty food and studies the *Gāyatrī*, is the *gāyatra*.
He who practices celibacy until the completion of his Vedic studies is a Brāhma;
he who always approaches his own wife only during her fertile period and avoids the wives of others is a Prājāpatya;
likewise, a student (brahmacārī) who performs the Vedic vows for one year is a Prājāpatya.
One who dwells in the teacher’s house until death is called a *naiṣṭhika* or a *bṛhat*.
The householder (*gṛhastha*) is also of four kinds: the *vārtāka*, the *yāyāvara*, the *śālīna*, and the *ghorasaṃnyāsika*.

Among these, the one whose livelihood is *vārtāka* is one who lives by the occupations of Vaiśyas and others, such as agriculture and cattle-rearing, and is devoted to the constant performance of ritual duties.
A *yāyāvara* is one who lives by begging, being averse to officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts;
a *śālīna*, however, is devoted to the six duties and subsists by officiating at sacrifices and other such means while accumulating wealth.
One who performs his daily rites with water that has been drawn and purified, who lives by the practice of *uñcha* (gleaning), and resides in a village, is called a *ghorasaṃnyāsika*.

Because he is averse to violence, the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) is also of four kinds: the *vaikhānasa*, the *audumbara*, the *vālakhilya*, and the *phenapa*. Among these, one who performs the *agnihotra* and other rites using uncultivated plants that ripen spontaneously and grow outside the village is called a *vaikhānasa*.
He who, rising early in the morning, looks toward whichever direction and is devoted to ritual action using *udumbara*, *badarī*, *nīvāra*, and *śyāmāka* grains from that region, is an *audumbara*.

He who wears matted hair and bark garments, having gathered eight handfuls for his morning sustenance, eats what he has collected during the four-month period, and renounces all flowers and fruits at the end of the month of Kārtika, is a *vālakhilya*.
Those who subsist on withered leaves and fruits, dwelling anywhere at all and devoted to ritual action, are the *phenapas*.
Likewise, there are four kinds of wandering mendicants (*parivrājakas*): the *kuṭīcakas*, the *bahūdakas*, the *haṃsas*, and the *paramahaṃsas*.
Among them, the *kuṭīcakas* are those who carry three staffs (*tridaṇḍins*) and wander for alms within the houses of their own sons.

The *bahūdakas*, however, are also *tridaṇḍins* who wear a water-strainer (*śikya*), a water-purifier (*pavitra*), sandals, a seat, a topknot (*śikhā*), a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), a loincloth (*kaupīna*), and saffron-colored robes (*kāṣāya*); wandering to various holy sites (*tīrthas*) and begging for alms, they seek [realization of] the Self.

The *haṃsas*, however, carry a single staff, wear the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) except for the topknot (*śikhā*), hold a sling and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in their hands, reside in a village for only one night, and are devoted to the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances.
The *paramahaṃsas*, on the other hand, carry a single staff, have shaven heads, do not wear the sacred thread, have abandoned all ritual actions, and are established in the Self (*ātman*).

Regarding this, the difference in the result is that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is absent, the independent fruit of knowledge is not established; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), because it exists, that [fruit] is established.

The meaning is that one who emaciates the aggregates (*skandhas*), the stages of life (*āśramas*), and the self (*ātman*)—that is, the body—within the family home of the teacher is a *naiṣṭhika*. It has been stated that in the passage concerning the aggregates (*skandha-śruti*), the stages of life are not enjoined, but rather the state of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) is restated as the fourth. To this, an objection is raised: "But even in the case of a reference (*parāmarśa*... He accepts the cognition [of the stages of life] based on the preceding statement required for the restatement: "True."

One might argue that the direct perception of the scriptural statement regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) itself should be the original injunction (*purovāda*), and not a restatement (*anuvāda*); to this, he says: "Smṛti.
Let this very scripture be the source for those two [the Smṛti and the Purāṇa] as well, because there is parsimony in postulating only the injunction when the scripture is already established.

If this were merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), there would be the complexity of postulating two things: first, the scriptural injunction regarding the stages of life (*āśrama*) for those with and without sacred fires (*sāgnika* and *anagnika*) as its source (*mūla*), and second, the injunction itself therein; therefore, he says "and thus" (*ataśca*).
Because they are based on the Smṛti, the stages of life that are not contradicted by the direct Vedic injunctions concerning lifelong ritual duties (*karma*) are to be accepted.

However, the contradictory stages of life involving no sacred fires are to be disregarded, or else they are to be practiced by those such as the blind who are ineligible for [Vedic] rituals—this is the meaning.
The sense is that, because it would contradict the scriptural injunction [that one should remain a householder] "as long as life lasts," the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) must be abandoned.

Having raised the objection that—since there is no difference in their being merely restated (*anuvādya*) in the *skandha-śruti*—the other stages of life should be practiced just like the householder's stage, he replies with the words beginning "nanu" etc., stating that while its practice follows from its being based on scripture (*śrautatva*), the others do not because they lack a scriptural basis; therefore, this passage concerning the "aggregates" (*skandha*) is intended solely as a praise (*stuti*) of being "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃsthata*).
The meaning is that the phrase "and likewise those who... implies the completion of the sentence: "they proceed toward the flame" (*arciṣam abhisaṃbhavanti*).

He states that "because the word *skandha* is not conventionally established (*arūḍha*) in reference to the stages of life (*āśrama*), there is no injunction regarding the stages of life here" by saying "and it is doubtful.
If one then asks, "In that case, is 'they go forth' (*pravrajanti*) an injunction for the stages of life? he replies with "so [it says] 'this'.

The meaning is that this is a statement of praise (*stuti*) based on a description of the present state, intended to show that the world of the Self (*ātmaloka*) is so great that people perform even the difficult practice of renunciation (*pravrajyā*) for its sake.

Now, having set aside the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), he states that this scriptural passage is considered under the assumption that it does not exist, beginning with the words "nanu" and so forth. //18//
Bādarāyaṇa maintains that [the meditation] is to be performed, because of the scriptural statement regarding equality. (BS 3.4.19)

The author establishes the final position (*siddhānta*) that the other stages of life (*āśrama*), which are prescribed in other Vedic texts, are merely restated (*anūdyante*) within this passage—just like the householder’s stage (*gārhasthya*)—because they are subject to restatement in this very statement; thus he concludes: "It is to be performed.
He provides an example where a restatement is preceded by an injunction: "And as...

In the sentence, "The *nivīta* [wearing of the sacred thread] is for men, the *prācīnāvīta* for the ancestors, and the *upavīta* for the gods," the *upavīta* is enjoined for rites dedicated to the gods.
Two things are restated for the purpose of praising that [renunciation]:

because the *nivīta* (the sacred thread worn over the right shoulder), known as the "binding of cloth on half the body," is already established in human activities due to its practical convenience; and because the *prācīnāvīta* (the sacred thread worn over the left shoulder) is also already established in ancestral rites (*pitrya-karma*) by virtue of other injunctions.

Furthermore, he states that the injunction for wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) is found directly in another passage through its association with the things to be enjoined: "In this very way... and so forth.
The phrase "of this" refers to the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*).
The meaning is that because it is mentioned alongside enjoined acts such as the study of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*), the state of wandering mendicancy itself is also enjoined.
He states that there is a similar scriptural declaration even in another passage with the words "and he who."

The phrase "of this" refers to the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). The meaning is that because the forest-dweller is mentioned together with the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), which is itself an injunction, that [knowledge] must also be an injunction. He states, beginning with "As for what was said," etc., to show that the word *skandha* is determined to refer to the stages of life (*āśrama*) based on the fact that the number three is heard in the text and cannot otherwise be accounted for.
"Distinct in their origination" means that they have arisen separately, such as "one should sacrifice," "one should study," and "one should give. //19//
Or rather, it is an injunction, like the rule for wearing [the sacred thread]. (BBs 3.4.20)

Having accepted that the mention of the "stages of life" (*skandha*) is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*), it was stated that the stages of life must be practiced by assuming another injunction (*vidhi*).
Now, he says "or rather, an injunction" (*vidhir vā*), meaning that the status of that very [mention] as an injunction should be assumed due to parsimony (*lāghava*).
The intention is that since the scriptural texts such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) refer to those who lack dispassion (*avirakta*), they do not constitute a sublation of parsimony.

This single statement appears to be intended solely for the praise of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) by means of censuring the other three stages of life (*āśrama*) due to their yielding meager fruits. In this regard, one raises the objection: "But surely..."—for it is improper to enjoin the stages of life here, as they have not been previously established by another injunction and thus cannot be the subject of a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

He says, beginning with "It is true," that it is better to assume a distinction between the injunctions for the stages of life (*āśrama*) because they are not previously established (*apūrva*), rather than the fault of [interpreting them as] praise (*stuti*).
He provides an illustration for assuming such a distinction by breaking up the perceived unity of the sentence with the phrase "like the *dhāraṇa*.
This refers to when the oblation (*havis*) placed in the *sruc* ladle during the Great Ancestral Sacrifice (*mahāpitṛyajña*) and the *Pretāgnihotra* is being carried toward the *āhavanīya* fire.

The meaning is that although the phrase "for above" (*upari hi*) appears to form a single syntactical unit with the statement enjoining the holding of the fuel-stick below the oblation— namely, "he should run after [the oblation] while holding a fuel-stick below it"— nevertheless, because this is a new injunction regarding the holding of the fuel-stick above the handle of the *sruk* ladle during a *daiva* (divine) *homa*,
there is a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), as stated by the teacher Jaimini in the third chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*].

Thus, the position that four stages of life (āśrama) are prescribed has been stated. Now, he states another position—that by way of restating the three stages of life, only the state of wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) is prescribed—beginning with the words "yadāpi" and so forth.

Anticipating the objection as to how the prescription of wandering mendicancy follows from the prescription of being firmly established in Brahman (brahmasaṃsthatā), he investigates this with the words "sā ca" and so forth.

One might object: "Since the statement 'there are three' does not include the four stages of life (āśrama), this inquiry is groundless. Anticipating this, one may doubt whether the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) is referred to in that passage or not; regarding the first alternative, the author states the prima facie position: "If [it were so]," etc. One might ask: "Why could one who is not in any stage of life (anāśramin) not be 'established in Brahman' (brahmasaṃstha)? To this he replies: "In the state of being without an āśrama," etc.
The sense is that there is a prohibition stating, "One who is without an āśrama should not remain [so]."
In the second [verse], he states the attainment of the perfected ones (siddhas) with the word "atha.
Having thus expressed doubt through the presence or absence of such reflection, he presents the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) with the word "tatra":
for it is well known that for one dwelling in the forest, asceticism (tapas) such as the *kṛcchra* penance is unique [to that state].
Therefore, it is improper to include both [asceticism and learning] by means of that single word "tapas," because there is no established renown for a mendicant being an ascetic (*tapasvin*).

And thus, by means of the unique dharma such as sacrifice and so forth, just like the three stages of life beginning with the householder, the fourth stage—whose primary characteristic is devotion to Brahman—is understood by the very term *brahmasaṃstha*.

And he establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that this [fourth stage] is enjoined along with the state of being established in Brahman on the strength of the praise [of the text], starting with the words "That is incorrect" (*tadayuktam*).

Furthermore, because of the separate designation, he states with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*) that the one established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃstha*) is distinct from the previously mentioned practitioners of the stages of life.
Nor should it be argued that those very same persons could attain "abiding in Brahman" (brahmasaṃsthā) through a difference in their stages of life;

for even with a difference in time, as long as there is dullness of intellect, or as long as there is the performance of ritual action accompanied by an abundance of [worldly] wisdom, it is impossible for those whose minds are distracted to abide in Brahman.
And since the abandonment of action belongs only to the wandering mendicant (parivrāj), our desired conclusion—that he alone is one who abides in Brahman—is established. This is the intended meaning.

In order to clarify this very point, he raises an objection with the words, "But how [is this so]? Although the term *brahmasaṃstha* is not conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsāśrama*), it nevertheless brings that very stage to mind through its etymological connection (*yoga*). He states, "To this it is replied," because the etymological meaning is not applicable in the other stages of life.

Regarding the point that for one who has renounced all actions, there is nothing further to be performed beyond being firmly established in Brahman as the meaning of the *praṇava*, he states the authoritative proof with the words "And so" (*tathā ca*).
He provides the reason for praising renunciation (*nyāsa*) or *saṃnyāsa* as Brahman with the words "For Brahman...

(*brahmā hi*). Since Hiraṇyagarbha is well-known as the Supreme (*para*), renunciation is praised as being the Supreme by virtue of its identity with Brahman; having thus praised it, he censures those ritual acts with the words "those... (*tāni*).
Therefore, the meaning is that *nyāsa* (renunciation) alone is superior because it is the liberator through the gateway of knowledge.

For the sake of that [knowledge], those whose minds are fixed on Brahman, who have become one with It, whose nature is Brahman, who are established in It, who are intent upon hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, who are devoted to that, and who seek Brahman—meaning, those who are free from desire—are called "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*).

Thus, since the word *brahmasaṃstha* denotes an *āśrama* (stage of life) where knowledge is predominant, the injunction is transformed as follows: "One who desires immortality should practice that *āśrama*."

Therefore, he concludes that there is no fault of the knowledge being purposeless with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). Now, he sets aside the hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvācintā*) with the words "anapekṣya" (without regard for). The intention is that this inquiry was conducted by taking up the scriptural mention of the aggregates (*skandha*) for the sake of clarifying the understanding of the student.
"Or else otherwise" (yadivetarathā) means:

if detachment should arise for one who remains in the state of a religious student (brahmacarya) due to the ripening of previously performed merit. Regarding the claim that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) concerns those such as the blind who are ineligible for ritual action, he says "and not so" (na ca) to refute it.
The sense is that there is no reason for the contraction of the general scriptural statement.
Regarding the word "separately" (pṛthak),
the word "of renunciation" (saṃnyāsasya) is to be supplied as the remainder.
The sequence of the construction is as follows: one who has observed vows (*vratī*), meaning one who has fulfilled Vedic vows such as the *godāna* and others;

a *snātaka*, meaning one who has returned from the teacher’s house (*gurukula*) after the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) but has not yet entered the householder stage and continues to serve his teacher; a *vidhura*, meaning one whose sacred fires have been extinguished; and an *anagnika*, meaning one who has not yet taken up the sacred fires—one such as these may renounce (*pravrajeta*).

He states [the following] beginning with "Brahman" (*brahma*) to show that renunciation is appropriate for those who, while possessing all their limbs, are somehow disqualified from ritual action (*karman*); however, those with deficient limbs, such as the blind and so forth, do not possess the qualification for renunciation which is centered on knowledge (*jñāna*).

The meaning is that there is no qualification for the blind, the lame, the mute, the deaf, and others, because knowledge does not arise without the practice of moving about purified by right views, hearing [the scriptures], and so forth; and also because of the indicative mark of the prayer for the integrity of the limbs: "May my body be most excellent, may my tongue be most sweet, and may I hear much with my two ears."
"And that" means that renunciation is an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of Brahman;
"for the sake of becoming Brahman" means, in short, for the sake of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman. //20//

If it is argued that [the passage] is merely a statement of praise because of its connection [to another injunction], we say no, because it conveys something not previously known (*apūrvatva*). (BS 3.4.21)
This is merely a praise:
among the seven essences—earth, water, herbs, man, speech, Ṛk, and Sāman—the eighth, the syllable *oṃ* which is a part of the Udgītha, is the "most excellent essence" (*rasatama*).
Because it is a symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it is the "supreme half" (*parārdhya*) of the Supreme Brahman; that is to say, it is worthy of being its very abode.
Regarding these scriptural passages, he states a doubt—asking "What [is it]?"—because they mention specific parts of the body and because their meaning is not something previously established.

Just as renunciation (pārivrājya) is to be practiced because of the scriptural statement of its similarity to the stage of the householder which is to be practiced, so too these scriptural passages must be for the purpose of praise, due to their similarity to scriptural passages praising the *juhū* ladle and other such items; thus he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by stating, "They are for the purpose of praise."
"This very earth is the *juhū*," thus it is praised;
"the tortoise situated upon the altar is the sun," and "the *āhavanīya* fire is the heavenly world"— such is the praise.
The meaning is that there is praise of the *udgītha* and so forth by means of qualities such as being the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*).

The author establishes the final position (*siddhānta*)—that the postulation of an injunction is preferable to [interpreting the passage as] mere praise—because it results in the attainment of performance [of the rite], whereas praise does not: "For [it is] not praise...
One should understand that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the result is non-performance, while in the final position, the result is performance.
To the question, "Why might they not have purposefulness by way of being commendatory (stāvakatvena)? he says: "Of the injunctive [passage].

It is appropriate that passages such as "This indeed is the juhū ladle" have purposefulness by way of being commendatory, because they reside within the context of injunctions for the juhū and other implements which possess results; however, since passages such as "the most flavorful" (rasatama) do not reside within the context of injunctions for the auxiliaries of a sacrifice, it is more appropriate that they enjoin meditations on the apūrva which possesses results, just like the scriptural texts concerning other sacrifices—this is the intended meaning. //21//
And [the suffix *yañ* is applied] after a word expressing a state (*bhāva*). (Pāṇini 3.4.22)

Furthermore, as for the statement "what is to be enjoined here?"—this was said by way of a hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvācintā*); in reality, however, it is not to be enjoined because it is already established. This is what he states with the word "bhāva" (existence). Nor is it correct to say that the scriptural passages concerning "the most flavorful" (*rasatama*) and so forth merely serve to praise the injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*). The sense is that since it is possible for them to provide the object required by the injunction, they cannot be construed as mere praise (*stuti*).

One might ask: since forms such as the optative (*liṅ*) are used even in expressions of prayer, such as "May the God do what I desire," how can it be determined that words like *upāsīta* ("one should meditate") have the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*)? To this he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*).

This [optative] suffix and so forth, by way of general rule (*utsarga*), would invariably be the indicator (*jñāpaka*)—that is, the definition—of the injunction known as "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) within the Vedas. However, when there is a sublater (*bādhaka*) such as a specific accompanying word (*upapada*), it has another purpose; this is the meaning.
This is what he says with the words "liṅ-ādi" (the optative suffix, etc.).

Furthermore, one should not be deluded into thinking that because the word "fifth" is mentioned in the verse, only five words possess the character of an injunction (*vidhi*), and not [words such as] "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) and so forth. For, by taking *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*—which denote action in general—as examples, it is intended to show that all optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others, when colored by any verbal root, possess the character of an injunction. The mention of the "fifth" word, however, is for the purpose of completing the meter with respect to what has already been stated.

Just as in the expression "death runs as the fifth," although only the verbal root *ḍukṛñ* (to do/make) expresses the general action termed *bhāvanā*— which is denoted by the word "action" (*karaṇa*)— because its meaning is "doing," whereas the other two roots, *bhū* (to be) and *as* (to be), have been stated to have different meanings, namely "existence" and "becoming" respectively; nevertheless, [this applies] to the "becoming" known as birth and to its fruit, which is existence (*astitva*).

Furthermore, because that which resides in the person to be prompted (the *prayojya*) is pervaded by the *bhāvanā*—which consists of the activity of the prompter (*prayojaka*)—there is a conventional usage of those two [roots and suffixes] as denoting action in general.

In this regard, in the expression "one should do" (*kuryāt*), the *bhāvanā*, which is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), is restated by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), just as in the usage "two," the meaning of the root, namely duality, is restated by the suffix.
Likewise, by the optative suffix (*liṅ*), the injunction known as the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is made known for that [action].
But since the agent is implied by that [efficient force], the efficient force (bhāvanā) with an implied agent has been illustrated.
Likewise, in the case of "it should be done" (kriyeta), the meanings of the stem and the suffix have also been explained;
since the object is here primarily implied, the efficient force with an implied object has been illustrated.
The Mīmāṃsaka position is that because finite verbs (ākhyāta) lack the capacity to denote the agent and other factors of action (kāraka), the agent and the object are merely implied (ākṣepa).
In the expression "it must be done" (*kartavyam*), the object factor (*karmakāraka*) is expressed by the kṛtya suffix;
the distinction is that while the object is subordinate, the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is expressed by the verbal root (*prakṛti*).

Likewise, one should provide examples such as "he becomes a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍī bhavet*), "he is being made a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍinā bhūyate*), and "he must become a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍinā bhavitavyam*). Similarly, examples for the root *as* (to be) should also be seen as: "he would be" (*syāt*), "he is being" (*bhūyeta*), and "he must be" (*bhavitavyam*); this is because the substitute *bhū* takes the place of *as*.

By means of verbal suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like, which are colored by these three roots, a single injunction (*vidhi*)—consisting in the nature of being the means for achieving a desired end—is expressed as residing in the *bhāvanā* that is itself colored by the meanings of all the roots.

Although there is a difference among the roots, the suffixes, and the grammatical factors (*kāraka*) such as the agent, there is no difference in the injunction; this is shown by providing three examples for each root so that it may be understood. Thus everything is clear.
Having thus explained in the Sūtra that "the *bhāva* is the injunction," he explains that "by the word *ca* (and), the result [is also denoted]," stating: "in each respective section."
The meaning is that this priest-officiant is capable of accomplishing the fruit through the singing of the *kāmāgāna*.

In this way, if even the meditations (*vidyā*) based on the subordinate parts (*aṅga*) possess independent fruits, what need is there to mention the independence of the meditation on the Self (*ātman*), which is not a subordinate part?

"If it be argued that they are for the purpose of the *pāriplava* [narrative recitation], we say no, because of the specific qualification. (BS 3.4.23)
The term *pāriplava* refers to discursive narratives.

In the context of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, it is prescribed that one should "recite the *pāriplava* for the king surrounded by his sons and others," which consists of the telling of various kinds of stories.

Thus, because the stories found in the Vedānta share the common nature of being narratives and because they are situated in proximity to meditations (*vidyā*), a doubt arises—hence the question: "What [is the case]?"

Previously, it was stated that the *vidhi* (injunction) is superior to the praise (*stuti*) because of the attainment of performance; likewise, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the narratives do not serve as praise for knowledge because of the attainment of the *pāriplava* performance. Regarding this, he states the result [of the prima facie view] with the words "And therefore" (*tataśca*).

Just as in a mantra such as "devasya tvā savituḥ," because a certain word has a meaning connected with the actual performance [of the ritual], the remainder of the words serves as an auxiliary to that performance, so too the narratives found in the Vedāntas serve as auxiliaries to the performance.
Since all Vedāntas are thus subordinate to ritual action through their syntactical unity with those [narratives], there is no primacy of knowledge (*vidyā*). This is the sense.

However, considering that the narratives—by demonstrating the conduct between teacher and pupil—serve as auxiliaries to the proximate knowledge (*vidyā*) by way of facilitating the intellect, and that this is established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of their inherent capacity, the author concludes the final position (*siddhānta*) with the words "That is not so" (*tan na*), etc., maintaining that knowledge is indeed primary.

The meaning is that since the specific details of the stories have been stated in the supplements for each day— on the first day of the Aśvamedha sacrifice one should tell the story "Manu Vaivasvata," on the second day "Yama Vaivasvata," and on the third day "Varuṇa Āditya"— it is appropriate to restrict the initial general statement accordingly. //23//
And likewise, because of the connection as a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatā). (BBs 3.4.24)

Anticipating the objection, "In that case, where then is the application of these stories? he says, "And so," [indicating] that they apply to the *vidyās* (meditative knowledges) due to their proximity. [For example, the story] "That Prajāpati cut out his own omentum and offered it"—which serves as a supplement to the injunction, "One should sacrifice a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati"—is to be understood as such; likewise, the status of other stories as supplements to their respective injunctions should be seen in the same way. //24//
For this very reason, there is no dependence on the kindling of fire and so forth. (BBs 3.4.25)

Since there is a dispute among disputants as to whether the knowledge of Brahman (*brahma-vidyā*) requires ritual actions (*karman*) as auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) for the production of its own fruit, liberation (*mokṣa*), a doubt arises;
