"And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse.
(BBs 3.4.26) He states further: "dependence on all.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that just as there is no dependence on ritual action for the cessation of ignorance—since that is the fruit of valid knowledge (*pramā*)—so too, since knowledge (*vidyā*) is itself a form of valid knowledge (*pramā*) accomplished merely by its means, there is no dependence on ritual action even in that case.

In that regard, the difference is this: according to the ritualists (karmamīmāṃsakas), the performance of rituals does not achieve its purpose there [in knowledge]; whereas in the Siddhānta, its achievement of that [knowledge] is the result.

Here, in the case of the desire to know (vividiṣā) or in the knowledge being sought, the causality of rituals such as sacrifice is enjoined because it is something not previously established (apūrva).
For even valid knowledge (pramā) can be accomplished through ritual action by means of purification known as the destruction of the obstructions to its arising;
nor does this indirect sequence contradict the scriptural mention of the instrumental case (tṛtīyā-śruti),
since we observe the usage "he cooks with wood" even when the process is indirect, mediated by the flame.
Because the door [to liberation] is not something that can be obstructed; nor is there a lack of evidence for purity being the door [to knowledge], as it is said:
"Knowledge arises in men from the destruction of sinful karma."

He establishes his final position with the words "this" (*idam*), based on the Smṛti: "When the impurities have been cooked away by actions, then knowledge arises," and by Śrutis such as: "Having crossed over death through ignorance, one attains immortality through knowledge," which declare that liberation is attained through knowledge once evil has been removed by action. Now, an objection is raised: here, by the use of the fifth lakāra (the optative) in the word *vividiṣanti* ("they desire to know"), it appears that the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*) is the desire itself—the meaning of the desiderative suffix (*san*).

If it is argued that what is to be produced (*bhāvya*) by the rituals is the realization (*vedana*)—which transcends [the object] because it is obtainable through the beauty of its object—then why could liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the fruit of that realization, not likewise be produced by the rituals, since it too transcends [the object]?
To this he says: "And because of the connection with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

Since knowledge is explicitly presented as the fruit by the word [of the scripture] due to its being desired, liberation—which is not heard [in that context]—is not the fruit; otherwise, in the expression "he cooks with wood," it would follow that the wood is the cause of the satisfaction resulting from the cooking.
The state [of things].
Regarding the fact that ritual actions have knowledge as their purpose, he states the indicative marks and sentences beginning with "Now" (atha).
A certain portion of the Veda directly declares the state known as Brahman.
However, some, considering that [the Vedāntas] operate through the doors of knowledge, purpose, and action, have stated that "all the Vedāntas" [are concerned with Brahman].
The rest is clear. //26//

He should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and so forth; nevertheless, because those [qualities] are enjoined as being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of that [state], they too must necessarily be practiced. (BS 3.4.27)
Having thus described the external auxiliary rites for the arising of knowledge, he states the internal ones with the word "śama" (tranquility).

Since it is possible for these to form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) for the purpose of praising knowledge, it is improper to assume an injunction by breaking the use of the present tense, as that would result in the undesirable consequence of splitting the sentence from the passage concerning knowledge.

Therefore, having restated the opponent's intention—that knowledge is obtainable through the mere words [of the Upanishads] such as "That thou art"—he concedes this point with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi tu*).

The meaning is that since tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities are necessary, knowledge is not obtainable through words alone. Because one who knows thus is not tainted by evil action, it is understood as an injunction that one seeking knowledge should investigate while being endowed with tranquility and the rest; thus he says, "We say, 'No'.

Here, by the word *uparata* (restrained), renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is expressed; according to the view that renunciation is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to hearing (*śravaṇa*), what is enjoined here is hearing characterized by tranquility and the other qualities.

However, since renunciation— which arises as having its own fruit— is mentioned in such Śruti and Smṛti texts as "Those desiring the world go forth [as mendicants]" and "One should renounce, placing knowledge at the forefront," it cannot logically be a mere subsidiary (aṅga) to that [knowledge];

furthermore, if one were to enjoin multiple means of tranquility (śama) and so forth by way of restating the hearing (śravaṇa) already enjoined in the rule "It is to be heard," there would result the fault of sentence-splitting (vākyabheda).

Furthermore, because the word "should see" (*paśyet*) is used in its primary sense and because there is no defect in the characteristic of hearing (*śravaṇa*), renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to hearing;

rather, even though it is to be performed prior to that, the view is that like hearing, it is for the sake of knowledge (*jñāna*). In that case, the injunction for the combination of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth for the sake of knowledge—namely, "one should cultivate knowledge through the combination of tranquility and so forth"—is beyond reproach.

That which was previously accepted as the acceptance of the Vedic injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth for the sake of praise—done merely on the surface according to the maxim of the "sweetmeat on the tongue" (*guḍajihvikā-nyāya*) for the purpose of inducing the adoption of tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities—is now abandoned with the words "even sacrifices and so forth.

Since the connection of sacrifices and the like with the means of knowledge (*vidyā-sādhana*) is something not previously known (*apūrva*), an injunction is accepted through a syntactical split (*avāntara-vākya-bheda*);
the meaning is that there is a unity of purport (*ekavākyatā*) between the sentences concerning the knowledge of Brahman and the great sentence (*mahāvākya*).

Regarding the point that even in the context of the primary section (*prakaraṇa*) there is a subordinate injunction (*avāntaravidhi*), he cites the consensus of the *Pūrvatantṛ* (the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra): "Therefore, [it is said] *pūṣā*...
In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard: "Pūṣan has the ground portion as his share" (*pūṣā prapiṣṭabhāgaḥ*).
In that regard, neither Pūṣan as a deity nor a ground portion exists within the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

Therefore, since the relationship between the substance and the deity—understood through syntactic integration (*samāsa*) and untouched by the three times—necessarily implies the injunction of a sacrifice, one must supply a verbal injunctive word (*vidhipada*) for the sake of knowing the performance. By then elevating [the statement] from its context (*prakaraṇa*), the connection is established in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*) as follows: "A portion of flour is to be prepared for Pūṣan."

The meaning is that this has been deliberated upon in the Sūtra: "The grinding [of the grains] belongs to Pūṣan. There are also Smṛti texts such as: "By worshipping Him with one's own duty, a human being attains perfection.

If ritual actions were causes for knowledge in the same way as tranquility (śama) and other qualities, they would have to persist until the dawning of knowledge; in that case, there would be no possibility of renunciation (saṃnyāsa). To this, he says: "In that case also..."

The sense is that because tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities serve the purpose of knowledge by way of removing distractions of the mind, they persist; however, ritual actions do not persist because they serve the purpose of knowledge through an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*). //27//
In all cases, one may act with the permission [of the teacher], except in the event of a life-threatening emergency, because that is what is observed [in the scriptures]. (BBs 3.4.28)

And because there is no contradiction (abādhāt): "For one who knows thus, there is permission for all food" means that he possesses the meditation (dhyānavatī) that "everything is the food of the vital breath" (prāṇa). "Jagdham" means eaten (bhakṣita).
Because it is something not previously established and because no injunction is heard, there is doubt.
The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position argues that an injunction must be inferred—just as in the case of sacrifices and the like—on account of its being something new; thus he says, "an injunction.

Here, the result in the prima facie view is the establishment of the abandonment of rules regarding what is fit and unfit to be eaten as an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*), whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is the glorification of knowledge; this is the distinction.
The scriptural injunction "one should not eat *kalañja*" refers to those other than those who possess knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Just as the prohibition against another's wife refers to those other than the practitioner of the *vāmadevya-sāman* during sexual intercourse, so it was argued. To this, the author demonstrates the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) even outside the sutra itself: "This is not [an injunction]," because it is impossible for it to be an injunction due to its proximity to the injunction for the knowledge of the vital breath; rather, it is merely a praise, and an injunction cannot be assumed, as that would contradict the prohibitory scripture. For an already established injunction sublates a general scripture, but one that is merely assumed does not.

The meaning is as follows: stating the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that there is no permission for one who is healthy and knows the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to eat all kinds of food, he connects the Sūtra by saying, "He shows that.
When the crops in the land of the Kurus had been destroyed by *maṭaci*—small red birds—and a famine had arisen, [he lived] together with his young daughter.

While traveling to another country with his wife, the sage stayed in a village of merchants. There, he was given some half-eaten, contemptible beans by a merchant named Hastipālaka, whom he had requested for them; having been given them, he ate them.

When the merchant said, "Take water," he refused, saying, "I would indeed be drinking what is left over from another's meal. When the merchant asked, "Are these beans not also leftovers? the sage explained the reason for both eating the beans and refusing the water.
"I have a shortage of food, but water for drinking can be obtained at will from the pond and other sources," he said, and having eaten the beans, he gave the remainder to his wife.
She, though not herself in distress, learned of her husband's misfortune; she preserved the beans and gave them back to him in the morning.

The sense is that he, having eaten them, went to the king’s sacrifice, rebuked the *prastotṛ* and others, pointed out the deities of the *prastāva* and so forth as being the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so on, and remained there after obtaining wealth. Here, by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the conduct of the learned—consisting of eating leftovers and discarding water—it is indicated that even a wise person, when not in an emergency, must not eat what is forbidden by the Śruti; this is the intended meaning. // 28 // // 29 //
Moreover, it is also recorded in the Smṛti: BBs 3.4.30: "And it is also remembered."
Fearing that one might live even by drinking liquor, he says that it must never be done: "Likewise, [one should] always [abstain from] liquor, O Brahmin.
The word "avoid" (varjayed) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Anticipating the question "Why?", he says "of the drinker of liquor," because of the prescription of an expiation ending only in death.
"Hot" means excessively heated; the word "surā" (liquor) is understood from the context.
Furthermore, he states that she [the woman] should not be drunk from, saying: "those who drink liquor" (surāpaḥ). //30//
And from this [prohibition],
there is also the scriptural statement regarding the absence of acting according to one's own will. (BBs 3.4.31)

He states the source *śruti* for the aforementioned *smṛtis*: "And the word... [referring to the passage beginning] "kāmakāraḥ. Acting according to one's desire—that is, acting as one pleases—is also more appropriately negated, because the statement "na ha vā evaṃvidi" (*for indeed, not for one who knows thus*) is an *arthavāda*.

The intended meaning is this: if this were also a mandatory injunction (vidhi), then, because it would be both enjoined and prohibited, there would be an option (vikalpa) regarding the drinking of liquor—just as there is an option regarding the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup—and that would contradict all the Smṛtis as well as the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).
And because it has been enjoined, the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) must also be performed. (BS 3.4.32)
And because it is enjoined as an obligation of the stages of life (āśrama-karma),

since it is prescribed among the obligatory rites such as the Agnihotra, there arises a doubt due to the contradiction between its specific application and its general application; and just as the statement regarding "eating all food" is a mere praise because it contradicts other scriptures,
so too the scriptural injunction regarding its application toward the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) is a mere praise, because it contradicts the Vedic revelation of its obligatory application.
He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

If ritual actions are performed out of a desire for knowledge, they would be non-eternal and thus not mandatory; yet, because that [desire] is non-eternal, its eternity would have to be established by injunctions such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), which results in the occurrence of two contradictory attributes. Therefore, the conclusion of the prima facie view is that the scriptural passage concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā-śruti*) is merely a figurative praise (*stuti*).
In the established conclusion (siddhānta), however, the result is the performance in both ways. //32//
And by way of being a cooperative cause. (BBs 3.4.33)
"Cooperative actions" (sahakārīṇi karmāṇi) are those which, having come together, produce knowledge (*vidyā*) by way of purification.
The meaning is: "by that," namely, by their state of being such [cooperators].
He rejects the notion—derived from the word "cooperative"—that [knowledge] produces the fruit simultaneously with [the arising of] knowledge, by saying: "And this is not so."
Since knowledge (*vidyā*) is not enjoined [as a ritual act], it has no requirement for auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).

Therefore, enjoined rituals cannot be auxiliary factors for unenjoined knowledge; furthermore, because liberation is not something to be produced [by action], there is no possibility of actions serving as its auxiliaries—this is the meaning.
Because of two scriptural statements of equal force, there is a distinct application (*viniyoga-pṛthaktva*), which is a distinction of connection (*saṃyoga-bheda*); hence, there is no contradiction.
Even though desire is impermanent, ritual actions (*karman*) are not impermanent, because their performance is permanent due to the permanence of the injunction.
When desire exists, the permanence [of the rite] is established precisely through the performance of the optional rite; thus, there is no contradiction.
This point was deliberated upon in the sūtra: "But when one thing has both [purposes], there is the separateness of connection" (*ekasya tūbhayatve saṃyogapṛthaktvam*).

Just as the scriptural statement "the sacrificial post is made of khadira wood" establishes that the quality of being made of khadira serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*), while the scriptural statement "one desiring vigor [should use] khadira" establishes that it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatā*);
therefore, when there are two such statements, the application of what has already been applied is not contradictory—this is the meaning. //33//
In every way, those [same entities] are [the cause], because of the evidence for both characteristics. (3.4.34)

[Objection: But surely, let the Apūrva-yajñas and so forth, which are indeed distinct from the obligatory Agnihotra and other such rites, be enjoined toward the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*). In that case, how can there be an application of what has already been applied? To this he says: "In every way" (*sarvathāpi*).
This means whether they are obligatory (*nitya*) or optional (*kāmya*).

In the context of the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana* sacrifice, regarding the statement "They perform the Agnihotra for a month," because the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes a homa that is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the word "Agnihotra" which shares the same referent as that [suffix]— [...the word "Agnihotra" refers to the specific rite of that name, not the obligatory daily one.]

Since it is impossible for [the word "yajñena"] to refer back to an *agnihotra* sacrifice that is established as being separated [in context], it is logical that a different ritual action qualified by the attribute of "monthly" (*māsa*) is enjoined here.

However, in this case, because words ending in nominal suffixes such as "yajñena" lack unity of meaning with the verb, they cannot serve as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of an already established, though distant, ritual action; rather, the sense is that these very rituals are enjoined for the purpose of knowledge.

He states—“yasyaita” (for whom these)—that even the well-known status of perfected actions as *saṃskāra*s (purificatory rites) is a sign (*liṅga*) for the non-difference between knowledge and action whose purpose is [the attainment of] wisdom, by means of the purificatory rite called "purity" (*śuddhi*). //34//
And it demonstrates non-overpowering. (BBs 3.4.35)

He states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that practices such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) serve the purpose of knowledge (*vidyā*) by way of destroying obstacles: "And non-overpowering" (Sūtra 3.4.35).
But even in the interval, [the existence of the intermediate state is established] because that [state] is observed. (BBs 3.4.36)
Moreover, it is recorded in Smṛti:
"And even for those between [the stages], because that is seen.

Since there is doubt as to whether those who do not belong to a stage of life (āśrama) possess the qualification for knowledge—given that acts such as the recitation of prayers (*japa*) exist for them yet are also censured—the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they lack qualification, because scripture declares that the duties of the stages of life alone are the cause of knowledge and because those outside the stages are censured.

In that regard, the result is that the status of the duties of those not belonging to a specific stage of life (*anāśrama*) as causes for knowledge is not established [in the opponent's view], whereas it is established in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). // 36 // // 37 //
And there is a specific favor. (BsRp_3,4.9.38)
He raises an objection: "But [the text mentions] a mark (*liṅga*).

[The author] states the proof for the fact that duties pertaining solely to the caste (*varṇa*), which are not incompatible with being without an *āśrama*, serve the purpose of knowledge: "And so it is.
"Maitra" means compassionate.

[Objection: Granted that for those who do not belong to any stage of life (anāśramin), ritual action may be a cause for knowledge; nevertheless, they lack the qualification for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth because of the absence of renunciation (saṃnyāsa). To this, he says: "And it has a visible purpose. The qualification for hearing belongs to one who desires knowledge whose fruit is the destruction of the ignorance that binds.
Even renunciation, when performed at some time, assists in knowledge, since it is not a necessary constituent (aṅga) of hearing; such is the meaning. //38//
Therefore,
on the contrary, the other [state] is superior, both because of the scriptural indication and because of logical reasoning. (BS 3.4.39)
If it is asked, "In that case, the state of being an ascetic (āśramitva) is useless," he says: "But from this...
The meaning is that the one who performs meritorious deeds, who belongs to the Taijasa stage, and whose sattva is purified, proceeds by that path of knowledge and attains Brahman.

The sense here is that, because of the mark of being a performer of merit (*puṇyakṛttva*), the state of being a forest-dweller (*āśramitva*) is superior; for through the accumulation of merit, knowledge is swiftly attained, whereas one who does not belong to an āśrama is censured. //39//

But for one who has become that [the liberated soul], there is no non-becoming of that state, even according to Jaimini, because of the restrictive rule and because of the absence of the characteristics of that [prior state). (BS 3.4.40)

But for one who has fallen from the highest stage of life (uttamāśrama) and returned to a previous stage, even ritual action (karman) is a cause of knowledge, just like the actions of one who belongs to no stage of life (anāśramika); this is the logical connection,
and this is the result of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).
In the Siddhānta, however, the result is that for one who has fallen [from the state], action is not the cause.
Because of the intensity of passion and the like, and because of the prohibition against falling away, they express the doubt as to whether such falling away is authoritative or not.
He explains the restriction in the Siddhānta-sūtra with the words "tathā hi" (for it is thus).

"Exceedingly" (*atyantam*) refers to the rule of lifelong commitment (*naiṣṭhikatva*). "To the forest" (*araṇyam*) signifies the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) characterized by solitude. "He should go there" (*tadiyāt*) means he should depart; "from that [state] he should not return" (*na punareyāt*) means he should not fall away from that mendicancy—this is the secret of the *Upaniṣad*.

He explains the absence of proof regarding the loss of that nature with the words "And as... (yathā ca). He states the absence of the practice of the learned with the words "Nor is it thus" (na caivam).
The meaning is that, according to the Smṛti text, "Caṇḍālas are those who have fallen from their caste," the ritual action of those who have fallen is fruitless. //40//

Nor can it be argued that [the sin] pertains to one holding an office, because there is an inference of falling [from grace], and because such [office-holding] is incompatible with that state. (BBs 3.4.41)
Nor does it pertain to one who holds an office;
"would be defiled" (avakīryeta) means he would transgress.
One who has "defiled seed" (avakīrṇin) is so called because he possesses seed that has been spilled into a womb.

In this regard, there arises a doubt as to whether or not there should be an expiation for one who has fallen [from the status of a twice-born], because it is both a minor offense (*upapātaka*) and because there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) regarding his fall.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) argues that just as it was stated that sacrifices and other rites performed by one who has fallen are fruitless, so too an expiation would be fruitless; thus he says, "It is said: No.

In this context, the result is that for one who has performed the expiation, ritual action does not become a cause for knowledge according to the prima facie view, whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it does become so.
Just as at the time of initiation (*upanayana*), the fire-oblation (*homa*) must be performed in the common worldly fire (*laukikāgni*)—

because the formal establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), which is prescribed for the period after one has entered into marriage, has not yet reached its proper time and thus the *āhavanīya* fire does not exist— so too, in the sixth chapter concerning the characteristics of eligibility, it is stated that the donkey, the sacrificial animal for penance (*prāyaścitta-paśu*) for a student who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), is to be offered in the common worldly fire.

Having reached the conclusion that the prescribed expiation pertains only to the *upakurvāṇa* (the student who returns home) and not to the *naiṣṭhika* (the lifelong celibate), the author establishes the final position: //41//
However, some [teachers] hold that even when preceded by the prefix *upa*, it denotes a state (*bhāva*), just like the word *aśana*; this has already been stated. (BBs 3.4.42)
Regarding the term *upapūrva*:
it means that for which a minor offense (*upapātaka*) has a preceding word [denoting "minor"], it is an *upapātaka*.

Since the Smṛti statement "I see no expiation" (*prāyaścittaṃ na paśyāmi*)—which is a record of non-perception—is interpreted as intending the absence of expiation, the existence of an expiation is established by a previously established general Śruti even before one could postulate a specific Śruti as its source. Thus, the existence of the expiation is proven by that already established common Śruti.
The sense is that no such assumption arises because it would contradict established scriptural authority (*kḷpta-śruti*).

Although there is an equality between the establishment of the existence or non-existence of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the establishment of its existence must be accepted because it is rooted in scripture; regarding this, he states the consensus with the words "tad uktam" (so it has been said).

In the case of the injunction "a sacrificial pap made of barley" (*yavamayaś caruḥ*), some use the word "barley" (*yava*) for long-awned grain (*dīrghaśūka*), while others in certain regions use it for *priyaṅgu* beans.

Therefore, when a doubt arises as to for whom the *caru* (sacrificial porridge) should be prepared, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—based on the similarity of usage among the elders—is that the understanding [of who is meant] should be equal or identical through an option (*vikalpa*). However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: the understanding must be accepted as being rooted in scripture (*śāstra*), because knowledge of *dharma* and so forth has scripture as its cause. And thus it is said: "When other plants wither, then these barley grains remain rejoicing."

Thus, the meaning is that because it is rooted in the Śāstra, the practice involving long-awned barley (*dīrghaśūka*) alone is to be respected. He states the source for this Smṛti rule with the words "prāyaścitta" (expiation):
the meaning is that the venerable Atri said, "I do not see even a clear expiation," in order to make known that one must exert great effort for the sake of protecting celibacy (*brahmacarya*).

He states with the word "evam" (thus) that there is indeed an expiation for the violation of celibacy through negligence even for forest-dwellers and ascetics, just as for lifelong students (*naiṣṭhika*).
One should increase the *kṛcchra* penance known as *prājāpatya* by providing water and other necessities to a "great thicket"—a place abounding in grass and wood.
An ascetic (*yati*), however, should increase it except for the *soma* creeper.
"Even one who is addicted to every kind of sin, by meditating for even a moment on Acyuta,
becomes once more an ascetic and a purifier of the assembly;
so it is with regard to the multitudes of minor offenses and even the great sins."
Having entered the first watch of the night, one should practice meditation on Brahman.

The meaning is that a monk must also perform the refinements such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) prescribed in his own scriptures. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is implied: "The fire of yoga burns all defects born of mind, speech, and body—those arising from ignorance and those born of negligence—just as a flame consumes a heap of cotton."

"One should always perform sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas); performed daily, they purify even the killer of a fetus within a month"—such scriptural statements as these are to be accepted. //42//
But [the ritual] is outside [the village] in both cases, according to the Smṛti and because of established custom. (BBs 3.4.43)

But as for those outside [the fold], it is in both ways. There arises a doubt: whether the means of knowledge, such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth, performed together with those who have already performed penance (prāyaścitta), is effective or not; and since they have been purified, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that it is indeed a means. The author establishes the final conclusion (siddhānta)—that even if they are pure in the next world due to their penance, because they lack purity in this world, it is not a means—by saying: "If [they are pure] hereafter," and so on.
The commentary is easy to understand. //43//
"Because the scripture declares the fruit for the master [of the sacrifice], so says Ātreya. (BS 3.4.44)
Because the fruit is declared for the master [of the sacrifice],
there arises a doubt regarding the meditations based on the subordinate parts (aṅga), since it is possible for both [the master and the officiating priest] to be the performers.

Regarding the general rule that "one who has performed penance is fit for social intercourse," there is an exception in the case of perpetual students (naiṣṭhika) and others due to scriptural traditions of extreme censure.

He states the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position—that the general rule "he who is the performer of the subsidiary acts is the performer of that which depends upon them" is set aside by the scriptural declaration of the fruit for the agent—with the words "What [is the purpose]?

Here, the result [of the prima facie view] is the co-location of agency and enjoyership; whereas in the final conclusion (siddhānta), [the ritual acts] are performed by priests (ṛtvij) who are dependent on the subsidiary parts.

Even meditations (*upāstayaḥ*) have results that accrue to the sacrificer as independent fruits; how much more so, then, must the independence of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), which rests in itself, be stated?

Thus the result must be distinguished. Therefore, there is a connection with the chapter (*pāda*). The meaning of the scriptural passage is that for one who meditates on rain within the fivefold *sāman*—consisting of the *hiṅkāra*, *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratihāra*, and *nidhana*—the result is an abundance of rain.
To the question, "Why should the fruit of the *śruti* not belong to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)?", he says: "And that" (*tac ca*).

Just as the fruit of the *godohana* vessel belongs to the person authorized for the sacrifice because it is subordinate to the qualified performer of the sacrifice with its constituent parts (*sāṅga-kratu*), so too the fruit of the meditation on the auxiliary (*aṅga-upāsana*) belongs to that same person; this is the meaning.
To the objection, "Granted that its fruit belongs to him, why could the agent not be someone else?", he says: "And the fruit" (*phalaṃ ca*).
Regarding what was stated—that the fruit accrues to the sacrificer—he raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*).
The meaning is that [the fruit] is accomplished by means of the *udgāna*.
The purpose of the resolution is that the general rule (*utsarga*) that the fruit belongs to the sacrificer is established unless there is a statement that serves as an exception (*bādhaka*).
Therefore, the meaning is "because of being the enjoyer of the fruit. //44//
"It is the office of the officiating priest," says Auḍulomi, "for he is hired for that purpose. (BBs 3.4.45)
And because of the Vedic scripture (Śruti).
Since officiating at a sacrifice (*ārlijya*) as meditation (*upāsana*) is performed by a priest, [the author] states a scriptural indicative mark (*liṅga*), saying "and likewise" (*tathā ca*).

The meaning is that he meditated upon that *praṇava* called the *udgītha* through the vision of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and having so meditated, he became the *udgātṛ* priest for those performing a sacrificial session (*satrin*) at Naimiṣa.

Since the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) have been purchased by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) for the purpose of performing the complete ritual procedure (*sāṅgaprayoga`) which results in a fruit accruing to himself, it has been stated that even though they possess the status of agent (*kartṛtva*), they do not partake in that fruit because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) of the general rule (*utsarga*). Furthermore, the co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of agency and enjoyership through the medium of purchase is logically consistent; the sense is that it is like saying "the king fights and wins" in a battle whose actual agents are his servants. // 45 // // 46 //
There is an injunction for another auxiliary [to meditation] as a third [alternative], for one who possesses that [meditation], like the initial injunction; this is according to one view. (BS 3.4.47)
This is an injunction for another auxiliary means.

Since the ancient Brahmins, having known the Self and renounced, lived the life of mendicancy, therefore the present-day Brahmin as well—being a "paṇḍita" (wise one) by virtue of possessing the preliminary knowledge of the nature of the Self—must perform his duty of wisdom (*pāṇḍitya*), which is listening (*śravaṇa*); having become indifferent to that [preliminary knowledge], he should proceed.

Having attained certainty through the power of knowledge born of hearing (*śravaṇa*) by means of childhood (*bālya*), one should desire to abide in the state of a child—either by means of reflection (*manana*) which dispels doubt, or by means of a pure mind. Having thus performed both reflection and hearing, the sage (*muni*) should subsequently engage in meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). Thus, "non-silence" (*amauna*) refers to the pair of childhood and wisdom (*pāṇḍitya*), while "silence" (*mauna*) refers to meditative absorption.

The meaning is that, having obtained the fullness of the collection of means for knowledge (*jñānasāmagrī*), one subsequently becomes a *brāhmaṇa*—one who possesses the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) that "I am Brahman.
Because the word *mauna* is used both for the state of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*) in its perfected form and for the meditation (*dhyāna*) to be practiced, a doubt arises.

Just as in the supplementary passage beginning with "Baka [taught] him," the status of the *udgītha* meditation as a priestly function (*ārtvijya*) is determined, so too, from the supplementary passage "then he is a *brāhmaṇa*," which lacks an explicit injunction, it is certain that *mauna* is not something to be enjoined.
Thus he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "It is not enjoined.
Herein, the result is that meditation is not to be performed according to the prima facie view, whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is to be performed.

If "mauna" (the state of a sage) refers to the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*), then it is merely restated as being already established by another scriptural passage, for the purpose of praising the injunction regarding "childlike behavior" (*bālya*).
If it were knowledge, then it would have been obtained from the word *pāṇḍitya*; such is the meaning of the text of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
From the word *muni*, however, a preeminence of realized wisdom (*vijñāna*) is understood, and this is not obtained from the word *pāṇḍitya*, which denotes mere knowledge.
Nor does the word *muni* denote a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*), since it is used in reference to Vālmīki and others.

Therefore, he establishes the final position (siddhānta) with the words beginning "In this way" (*evam*), etc., that since silence (*mauna*) has not been previously established, it must be understood as an injunction (*vidhi*).
He explains the application of Āpastamba’s rule with the words "of the other stages of life" (*itarāśrama*).

Furthermore, he states that silence is to be enjoined because of the scriptural statement, "Having become indifferent to both non-silence and silence," which indicates that it is to be practiced just like hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*); thus he says, "because it is to be brought about through indifference" (*nirvedanīyatva*).

Nor is there the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the injunction of these three; the point is that such a syntactical split is accepted, as in the case of the *uparidhāraṇa* (holding [the fire] above).
To the question "For whom is this meditation enjoined?", he says: "for one who possesses that" (*tadvataḥ*).
The meaning is that the renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*) possessing indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) is the subject under discussion, as indicated by the phrase "having known the Self.

Anticipating the objection that meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth might be understood from common worldly practice as a means for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of subtle objects—such as the musical notes *ṣaḍja* and others—the author states a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) beginning with "Now then" (*nanu*).

If it is asked, "In a sentence devoted to the knowledge of Brahman, how can [meditation] be a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of knowledge?", he replies with the words "like the beginning of an injunction" (*vidhyādivat*), meaning: just like the injunction of subsidiaries within a sentence devoted to a sacrifice that yields its fruit.
The injunction (vidhi) extends from the primary rite down to its constituent parts (aṅga).
In this context, the meaning is that the primary sacrifice is the beginning of the injunction, and for that very reason, the subsidiary parts are called the "end of the injunction" (vidhyanta).
Those who are ignorant of the intent of this sūtra and its commentary claim that there is no injunction regarding such matters as hearing the duties of the renunciate (saṃnyāsa) stage of life.

For in this procedure, only the non-attainment [of the goal] is required, and that has been demonstrated due to the intensity of the perception of difference; so say those who know the tradition. //47//
But because [the knowledge] exists in its entirety, the conclusion is made with reference to the householder. (BS 3.4.48)

The meaning of the doubt is that since the conclusion states, "Having remained in the household after the *samāvartana* ceremony, one attains the world of Brahman and does not return again," there is no such thing as renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

The meaning of the resolution is that the conclusion was made with reference to the householder because of his abundance of duties involving great effort, and not because of the non-existence of renunciation. //48//
The same applies to the others as well, because of the instruction regarding silence. (BBs 3.4.49)

The author of the Sūtras has mentioned only two stages of life here: renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and the householder’s stage (gārhasthya). To dispel the misconception of someone who might think that there is no other stage of life besides these two, he says: "as in the case of silence" (maunavat). This means "like the two stages of life."

Although it should have been stated that this applies to the other two as well, the extensive explanation is given with regard to their internal subdivisions, which we have already demonstrated previously. //49//
One should follow [the path] without making it manifest. (BBs 3.4.50)
"Because it follows from the context, [the suffix] does not manifest [an action].

In this regard, concerning the subject of "childhood," since it is impossible for the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) to have the sense of a state (*bhāva*), one must accept that it has the sense of an action (*karman*). Then, because actions such as "urinating while standing" and the purity of state consisting in the non-development of the senses are equally "actions of a child," he states the doubt with the word "therein.

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the result is that even acts such as urinating while standing are to be performed as auxiliary parts of knowledge (*vidyā-aṅga*); whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), only the purity of state is to be practiced.
Since in the preceding case the word *mauna* (silence) is well-known to denote meditation (*dhyāna*) as a superior form of knowledge, it was stated that meditation is what is to be enjoined;

likewise, since the word *bālya* (childhood) is well-known to denote acting according to one's desire (*kāmacāra*) and so forth, he says "What then is that? to indicate that it is this [acting according to desire] which is to be enjoined. The meaning is: the state (*tattā*) of one who acts, speaks, and eats according to his own will (*kāmatas*).

The sense is that, according to what arises and what is possible, the state of one who possesses urine and so forth— that is, the reality of such a condition— is a matter for the scriptures on falling from grace (*pātitya-śāstra*) due to the force of the rules regarding childhood (*bālya-vidhi*);

thus, the scripture concerning the rules for purity, alms-seeking, and so forth— such as "But he who is without knowledge, who is mindless, and always impure, does not attain that state, but enters into *saṃsāra*"— is not a rule for acting as one pleases, because it is possible to follow the injunction of *bālya* known as "purity of intention" (*bhāva-śuddha*), which is not in contradiction with those rules.
He establishes the conclusion with the word "evam" (thus).

He states that there is no injunction for that [childhood] because it is contrary to the primary [purpose], using the words "pradhāna... (the primary...). The construction of the Sūtra is as follows: since the purity of being (*bhāva-śuddhi*) is connected as an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*), the meaning of the injunction regarding childhood (*bālya-vidhi*) is that one should remain without manifesting [one's spiritual status]. //50//
Even that which pertains to this life [occurs] when there is no obstruction of what is not yet begun, because that is observed. (BS 3.4.51)

Having explained the collection of means beginning with renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and ending with childhood (*bālya*), which pertain to this life, the author states the connection by saying that the arising of knowledge—which is to be accomplished by those means—is now being investigated. Then, stating the doubt because the fruit of a means can arise in two ways, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "all [means]" etc., namely, that hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth have a rule of having results in this life, like the *Kārīrī* sacrifice.

To the objection—"But how can there be a rule of results in this life for knowledge, which is accomplished by sacrifices and other means that have results in the next world?"—he replies: "Even sacrifices and so forth... and so on.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position holds that once purification through sacrifices and other means has been accomplished, and since hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth—the direct causes of knowledge—have been undertaken, a delay in the attainment of knowledge is not logical;

yet, such a delay is observed. Therefore, the result of this prima facie view is that the status of hearing and so forth as causes of knowledge is unestablished. The final conclusion (siddhānta), however, considers that even if there is a delay due to the influence of obstacles, their status as causes is still established. Thus, it concludes that hearing and so forth have an indefinite result, like the *Citrā* sacrifice, and establishes this with the word "evam" (thus).

Now, one might ask: why is the fruit of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth obstructed by a specific *prārabdha* karma? Why could the ripening of karma not be obstructed by hearing and the like themselves? To this he says: "And because its ripening is imminent. The meaning is that karmas ripen through the power of place and other such factors.
To the question of why hearing and so forth do not themselves ripen [into results], he says: "And those which...
Ripening-ness (vipācakatva) is the state of being a cause for the orientation toward the fruit (phalonmukhya).
If it is asked, "In that case, what is the nature of the place and other factors that ripen hearing and so forth?", he says: "The scripture also...
The intention is that the knowledge of the place and so forth arises through the power of the result (*phala*).
Nevertheless, regarding the reason why the very *karma* constitutes an obstacle to hearing and so forth—and not the reverse—he states: "By the means... (*sādhanena*).
The sense is that the power of being an obstacle must also be understood from the force of the result.
He states the scriptural and traditional indicators (*liṅga*) for the existence of such an obstacle with the words "And thus," and so forth.
The establishment of the obstacle follows from the statement: "Even though they hear, they do not know."
Even one who speaks of the self as it truly is is a marvel, being like something extraordinary;
let alone one who has attained direct realization,
even one who knows it through indirect means is a marvel.
The meaning is: even though instructed by a virtuous teacher. //51//
Thus,
there is no restriction regarding the fruit of liberation, because that state has been definitively ascertained; because that state has been definitively ascertained.

When there is no obstruction by *prārabdha-karma*, the dawn of knowledge (*vidyā*) occurs right here in this life, because obstructions consisting of accumulated sins have been removed by sacrifices and other such acts. But when there is an obstruction, it is removed through experience (*bhoga*), and thus [knowledge] arises in the next world. Just as this specific rule regarding whether knowledge is attained in this life or the next has been stated, one might think that there could likewise be some distinction such as excellence (*utkarṣa*) in the fruit, which is liberation (*mokṣa*). To this he says: "Thus, there is no such restriction regarding the fruit of liberation, because that state is definitively determined; because that state is definitively determined."

Liberation (*mukti*) is the subject here. Since liberation can occur in both ways—whether there is a restriction of specific qualities (*viśeṣa-niyama*) in it as there is in knowledge (*vidyā*), or not—a doubt arises. To state the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he says "as" (*yathā*).
Liberation possesses specific qualities.
Therefore, because it is a fruit [of knowledge], liberation is something to be accomplished by action; this is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

However, in the final conclusion (siddhānta), since inference is sublated by the scriptural texts that determine the absence of distinctions [in Brahman], liberation is manifested solely by knowledge; this is the result.

Furthermore, having admitted some degree of excellence in knowledge due to the varying degrees of hearing and other means, he states—beginning with "Moreover, the means to knowledge"—that there is no excellence in the liberation obtained through that knowledge.

Now, one might object: since Brahman is eternally established, if the cessation of ignorance were different from it, duality would result; yet if it were non-different, it could not be something to be accomplished, and thus it could not be the fruit of knowledge. To this, he says: "For that... Because it is manifested by knowledge, the bliss of Brahman itself is the primary fruit. This manifestation—the cessation of ignorance—is accomplished by knowledge as the absence of the obstacle to the dawning of the nature of bliss; and that [cessation] is indeterminable (anirvācya).
There is no consequence of falling into dualism;
others, however, say that she (Māyā) is non-different from Brahman.
Nor should it be argued that knowledge is useless in that regard because of the impossibility of its being something to be accomplished.

The entire world proceeds from the knowledge that "in the absence of X, Y is absent," whereby X is established as the means to achieve Y. Just so, in the absence of *vidyā* (knowledge), there is the absence of liberation, which is the true nature of Brahman; for it is precisely this *avidyā* (ignorance) that exists in the form of misfortune, since it is the object of the conventional expression "there is no liberation" due to its being the non-existence of liberation.

And thus, because of the certainty that there is no liberation without knowledge (*vidyā*), one acquires knowledge; and upon the arising of knowledge, one abides as the Self which is the bliss of Brahman—self-luminous and eternally free from all evils that are established by their own nature. This is irreproachable.
Now, he abandons the acceptance of any excellence (*atiśaya*) in knowledge, saying "nor... [i.e., *na ca*].
The meaning is that in the case of a single form as an object, a gradation (tāratamya) in the resulting valid cognition is untenable.
[Objection: How then was a distinction among forms of knowledge stated in the previous section?
To this he says: "Therefore," etc.
The meaning is that even when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present, a delay in knowledge has been mentioned, but not a gradation [of intensity].
To the question, "In that case, why might there not be a delay in liberation even when knowledge exists?", he says: "But not...

The point is that although there may be a delay in the production of a lamp due to obstructions such as wind, once it has been produced, no delay is observed in the cessation of darkness; likewise, when knowledge exists, there is no delay in the cessation of ignorance.
Furthermore, it is logical that there is a gradation of fruits corresponding to the gradation of qualities in ritual actions and meditations;

however, since the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa-vidyā) is of a single uniform nature, its fruit is likewise of a single uniform nature—this he states with the words beginning "vidyābheda" etc.
In the Smṛti, the meaning is "of a certain knower of the attributeless."
Therefore, it is established that liberation occurs at the very same time as knowledge. //52//
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavat.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter, titled "An Investigation into the Internal and External Means for Knowledge Devoid of Attributes (*Nirguṇavidyā*)."
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Means of Attainment" (*Sādhana*), in the venerable *Śaṅkara-bhāṣya* on the *Brahma-sūtras*.
